title_r: Exploring multi-agent contexts: a replication study
abstract_r: This study will replicate and extent Capozzi et al. (2018). Humans tend to follow where others are looking to orient their attention spontaneously. However, researchers have recently begun investigating how this behaviour may change when we are presented with multiple faces that could be looking in different directions. Capozzi et al. (2018) found that when participants saw small groups of three human faces, it took only one face (33%) to look toward a target location to facilitate response times in a cueing task. However, three faces (66%) were needed to create the same results when the group size increased to five human faces. These results suggest that the way in which humans perceive multiple consistent or inconsistent cues may follow a quorum-like evaluation. Thus, the percentage of gaze cues needed to orient our attention changes as a function of group size rather than just following a majority rule. The present study seeks to replicate this finding with faces. In addition, we will include a control condition where non-social directional arrows are used as stimuli in the same manner as faces.

title_r: Speaker Knowledge Influences the Comprehension of Pragmatic Inferences - A Replication Study
abstract_r: This study tests the extent to which perceived speaker knowledge affects the generation of scalar implicatures (either strong or weak). It is a replication of Bergen & Grodner 2012 with the same title. In the original study, the researchers determined that speaker knowledge does affect the likelihood of generating a strong or weak implicature from the following findings: 1) Full speaker knowledge causes greater processing difficulty in the following trigger sentence because of the integration of extra information associated with a strong implicature and 2) When referring back to a complement set evoked by a strong scalar implicature, the full speaker knowledge context facilitated processing. These are the results I hope to replicate in order to reach the same conclusion.

abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Replication Recipe (Brandt et al., 2013): Post-Completion

item30: The effect size of the replication is the effect size of job search purpose, F(1, 121) = 5.37, p = .022, η2p = .042, d = 0.429 which is the largest effect size found. The main effect of goal framing, F(2, 121) = 1.02, p = .364, η2p = .017, was not significant at α = .05. It was found that there is also no significant interaction between framing and job search purpose, F(2, 121) = .262, p = .770, η2p = .004, as opposed to the results found in the original study at α = .05.

item31: The confidence interval of the replication effect size is 95CI [0.21, 0.79] around the standardized mean difference between the two groups of job search purpose.

item32: significantly different from the original effect size

item33: practical failure to replicate

item34: Practical failure to replicate defines the replication effect size to be both signiﬁcantly different from the null and from the original effect size (Brandt et al., 2014). For our replication study, the effect size of job search purpose was significantly different from null, but also significantly different from the original effect size based on comparison of the two 95CIs. 
The effect size of goal framing was however, not significantly different from null, suggesting that it is an informative failure to replicate, which is defined as the replication effect size being either not different from null, or significantly different from original effect size and in the opposite direction (Brandt et al., 2014). However, since the effect size of job search purpose is the main finding to be replicated, the replication study is deemed to be a practical failure to replicate.

item37: a.	Survey format - we had no access to the format of the original survey administered by Foster and Diab (2017).  During the process of replicating this study, we encountered difficulties when designing the online survey.  We had to make assumptions about the format of the survey with regards to the arrangement of the survey questions and the participants’ access to the job vignettes after reading them.  Hence, we were unable to replicate the study to the standards we had hoped. 
b.	Ensuring participant engagement - another limitation and challenge faced by the research team was ensuring that participants paid attention not just to the manipulation and quality checks, but to the hypothetical scenario and the study itself as well. As per the design of the original study, an online survey was used for data collection. Participants were free to complete the study at any time and location, without any time limits or restrictions on concurrent tasks (e.g. attending classes, listening to music, or talking to others). As such, there was no way to control the conditions in which participants did the survey or ensure that they were paying sufficient attention. This may result in participants not engaging fully with the information in the hypothetical scenarios, which would ultimately have the potential to decrease the quality or accuracy of the findings. It is likely that this may have also been a limitation of the original study. However, unlike this study, the original study had rather stringent requirements when recruiting participants, which adequately addressed this problem.


c.	Sample size - a major limitation of this study is its small sample size. Due to the limitations on time and resources, only 182 out of the target of 450 responses were obtained, of which 127 were valid and used for analysis. Although the main effect of job search purpose was still found to be significant, our small sample size may have played a role in leading us conclude that the other effects were not significant, since a small sample size would decrease the overall statistical power of this study. This is especially relevant since smaller effects are harder to detect and typically require a larger sample size, and this limitation may have prevented us from detecting the main effect of framing and the interaction effect between job search purpose and framing at a significant level, as both have effect sizes (in the original study) that are smaller than that of the main effect of job search purpose.
d.	Use of college sample – since a small effect size was found in our replication study, the use of a college sample could have been a bigger limitation than we have expected. The college sample, with mostly little or no work experience, may not be a fit for the vignettes approach of the study. Even though the status of unemployment could facilitate the students’ ability to imagine they are looking for a job, the imagined cost of being laid off verses switching careers could be skewed due to their lack of prior job experience. Losing a job may not be as painful for students that have never had a job, especially for those who were under the financial support from their families. It is important that future research utilize a sample that is more representative of the real-world job market or examine inaction inertia in a real job search context.
e.	Differences in job offer vignettes - a limitation raised by the authors of the original study was the differences between the vignettes read by those in the laid off condition versus the switching careers condition. Participants in the laid off condition were told that they had foregone the offer due to personal family matters, as opposed to those in the switching careers condition who were told that they had foregone the offer due to obligations to their current company. The difference in reasons for turning down the job offer may therefore have affected the findings, and future research should make this a constant as part of the experimental design to verify the findings.

title_r: How does a target's level of caring about a social issue influence perceived trustworthiness? A direct replication.
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

This study aims at investigating if the effect of study 2 of Zlatev (2019) that perceived trustworthiness increases with a target’s level of caring about a social issue can be replicated.

summary: As our study will be a direct replication, our materials, design plan and analyses will be vastly the same as Zlatev’s. The social issue that Zlatev considered in study 2 was capital punishment. Given that the study will be replicated in Germany where capital punishment has been abolished, we decided to substitute it with another social issue of higher national relevance which has been used in study 1 and has produced the same effect: abortion.

The main dependent measure is participants' ratings of the integrity of a fictitious character named “Person A” after being told about their opinion (legality/illegality of the social issue) and their related level of caring (between 1 “not at all important” and 100 “extremely important”). These ratings will be both generated randomly. 
The items designed to measure integrity-based trust will be: “Person A has a great deal of integrity”, “I can trust Person A´s word” and “Person A cares about honesty and truth”. We will also include a measure of how benevolent the character is (measured using three items: “Person A is kind”, “Person A is nice” and “Person A is selfish”). 
This replication is part of the project “Expra 2020” of the Psychology Department of the University of Cologne and will be based on data obtained in an online survey via Qualtrics. There will be two other conceptual replications of Zlatev’ study. The time frame will be June-July 2020.

title_r: Can Research Participants Comment Authoritatively on the Validity of Their Self-Reports of Mind Wandering and Task Engagement? A Replication and Extension of Seli, Jonker, Cheyne, Cortes, and Smilek
abstract_r: Seli, Jonker, Cheyne, Cortes, and Smilek (2015) found that, through retrospective confidence reports, subjects can distinguish the validity of their mind wandering reports during a sustained attention (“metronome response”) task. In addition, some subjects were better able to make this distinction than others. Here, I sought to replicate both the within and between-subjects’ effects of confidence judgments on thought probe validity. To this end, I executed a preregistered close replication of Seli et al. (2015) and extended this work by administering the metronome response task twice and by measuring potential individual difference markers for which subjects may be better than others at monitoring their thoughts: working memory capacity, conscientiousness, neuroticism, and dispositional mindfulness. With data from 291 subjects, I found only weak evidence for a within-subjects effect of confidence on thought-report validity in the first administration of the metronome response task and weak to non-existent evidence for individual differences in thought monitoring. No evidence was found for individual differences in the ability to provide valid thought reports.

title_r: The Artificial Harm-Made Mind: A Replication Study On The Relationship Between Intentional Harm and Mind Perception In Robots.
abstract_r: Ward, Olsen and Wegner (2013) found that witnessing intentional harm towards a robot increases the perception that the robot is capable of experiencing pain. This served as a catalyst for mind perception more broadly. The discovery of the “harm-made mind” carries crucial consequences for the ethics surrounding artificial agents. However, the advanced emotional capabilities of the robot described in the vignette used by Ward et al. (2013) may have amplified the reported effects. This paper therefore aims to replicate the original study (Ward et al., 2013) and expand it in two ways. First, we will add a separate condition in which the robot is described as lacking emotional capabilities. Second, we test whether perceiving intentional harm towards a robot influences the perception of the “perpetrator”, i.e., the person who inflicts harm to the robot. The findings of this study have implications for policies concerning artificial social agents.

title_r: Conceptual Replication of Ferguson and Sheldon (2013)
abstract_r:

summary: Study Information
Trying to be happier really can work: Happiness and paintings
Conceptual Replication of Ferguson, Yuna & Sheldon, Kennon. (2013). Trying to be happier really can work: Two experimental studies. The Journal of Positive Psychology. 8. 23-33. 10.1080/17439760.2012.747000. 

Authorship
Brianna Chmielewski, Kamila Plaza, Meagan Rosario, Tyra Watkins
Research Questions

1.	Does the manipulation of mood encouragement have an impact on how individuals feel about an image? 
2.	Does the manipulation of the type of image have an impact on how individuals feel about an image?
3.	Is there an interaction between mood encouragement and type of image on mood? 

Hypotheses
•	Does the manipulation of mood encouragement have an impact on how individuals feel about an image? 
More specifically, do emotionally encouraged versus not encouraged groups feel more or less happy when analyzing an “ambiguous” and “happy” painting?
Our hypothesis is that the manipulation will be very effective. In the original study by Ferguson and Sheldon (2013), those who were part of the encouraged-to-improve-mood group felt a greater boost in mood when they listened to the positive classical song (p= 0.001, d= 0.76) and felt less of a positive mood when they listened to the ambiguous classical song (p= 0.72, d= 0.08). There was no difference in reported mood for the ambiguous song based on the group they were in (p= 0.82, d= 0.05).
•	Does the manipulation of the type of image have an impact on how individuals feel about an image?
	
Our hypothesis is that those viewing the positive image will report higher levels of mood compared to those viewing the ambiguous image. In the original study, Ferguson and Sheldon (2013) found that there was a significant effect of type of music on positive mood (p = .002). Since this is a conceptual replication, we expect to see similar results as this study. 

•	Is there an interaction between mood encouragement and type of image on mood? 

We expect to see those in the encouraged condition will be more impacted if in the positive condition rather than the ambiguous condition. We expect to see this because similar results were found in Ferguson and Sheldon’s study (2013). 

Sampling Plan
Data collection procedures

We plan to collect our data by using convenience sampling on students at Dominican University. Participants will be recruited by letting friends know about the study and asking our professors to send information to other classes to maximize our recruitment. There will be no compensation for this study other than credit that will be awarded to those currently enrolled in PSYC 101 and/or NEUR 105. Participants will be excluded from the initial pool if they fail the manipulation check or if they do not complete a substantial portion of the survey.
Sample size
Sample goal is at least 100 participants.
Sample size rationale
Based on the Dominican University population, we predicted that a sample size of at least 100 participants will satisfy our study to get an acceptable amount of results. 
Stopping rule
Sample size will not be limited to a certain amount; the more participants, the better. 

Variables
Manipulated variables
•	Type of images (ambiguous or happy) 
•	Encouraged to boost mood vs not encouraged to boost mood
Measured variables
•	How participants felt after viewing their assigned image. 
 2 measures:  
→ Rate their agreement (1= not at all, 15= extremely) on six different mood descriptors: happy, joyful, enjoyment/fun, pleased, content, and satisfied. Ratings were averaged.
→  Continuous line asked participants to indicate how positive they felt (line extended from “very negative” to “very positive”) relative to their negative feelings. Distance between positive and negative marks was measured using a ruler and converted into a proportion of entire line. 
 
Design Plan
Blind
Both the researchers and the participants are blind to the image manipulation. Computers will not be assigned to specific images, therefore we will not know who is in what group, and the participants will not be aware of the ambiguous and happy images until debriefing. 
Study design
2 x 2 factorial between-subject design .
Participants are randomly assigned within the online survey. 
Analysis Plan
Statistical models
TWO-WAY ANOVA

•	2x2 factorial ANOVA 
•	Analyze main effects and interactions between the two groups

Data exclusion

•	Participants who do not finish the survey.
•	Participants under the age of 18
•	Participants who do not pass the manipulation check.
•	Any participant who voices suspicion about the nature of the study
Missing data
Excluding participants entirely (except if missed demographic questions).

title_r: Characteristics of popular climate policies. A replication study.
abstract_r: This study attempts to replicate the findings from de Groot & Schuitema’s (2012) paper “How to make the unpopular popular? Policy characteristics, social norms and the acceptability of environmental policies” in a German sample. It aims to broaden the understanding on what contributes to the acceptability of climate policies. To that end, we focus on three influencing factors: level of coerciveness, behavioral targets and social norm . Those factors are implemented through texts describing the policy (scenarios) that subjects read and then rate the policy’s acceptability. Policy coerciveness represents how much a policy enforces exhibiting a certain behavior (De Groot & Schuitema, 2012). As in the original study, this distinguishes push and pull measures. While pull measures reward the desired behavior, push measures punish an undesired behavior (Loukopoulos et al., 2005, Eriksson et al., 2006, Hrelja & Rye, 2023). In this study, push measures are in all scenarios implemented as monetary punishments (through taxes or fines), pull measures are monetary incentives (vouchers) and measures to ease. The behavioral target variable is referring to the cost of behaviors targeted by a policy. This includes not only the monetary cost to implement a behavior, but also non-monetary costs, such as cognitive and organisational effort (Diekmann & Preisendörfer, 2003, Farjam et al., 2019). The behavioral target variable distinguishes high-cost and low-cost behaviors, in this case mobility choices and (not) littering , respectively. The variable social norm represents a behavioral default that is given by others for a specific situation, or as Chung & Rimal (2016) put it “perceptions about the prevalence of behavior and pressures to conform”. In this case it is operationalised through an information about how much others approve of a climate policy giving a direction for the individual on how to behave. Generally, it is hypothesized that policies that are push measures, require a high behavioral cost and are less approved of by others will be rated as less acceptable. We will test main and interaction effects of those three predictors in an analysis of variance, the specific hypotheses are presented in the following.

title_r: The Artificial Harm-Made Mind: A Replication Study On The Relationship Between Intentional Harm and Mind Perception In Robots. 2 (Anonymised Version)
abstract_r: ! THIS PREREGISTRATION IS AN ANONYMISED COPY OF THE ORIGINAL PREREGISTRATION FOR REVIEWING PURPOSES. THE ORIGINAL PREREGISTRATION WAS PUBLISHED OCTOBER 13, 2020 ! Ward, Olsen and Wegner (2013) found that witnessing intentional harm towards a robot increases the perception that the robot is capable of experiencing pain. This served as a catalyst for mind perception more broadly. In a previous registered study, we replicated the original study (Ward et al., 2013) and expanded it in two ways. First, we added a separate condition in which the robot is described as lacking emotional capabilities. Second, we tested whether perceiving intentional harm towards a robot influences the perception of the “perpetrator”, i.e., the person who inflicts harm to the robot. In this follow-up study, we made changes to the original stimulus material. Specifically, we changed the motivation for harming the robot, so that the actions of the “perpetrator” are targeted directly against the robot, rather than indirectly targeted at another human being.

title_r: A replication study investigating individual differences in online communication and jealousy.
abstract_r: The aim of this study is to investigate the effects of attachment style and attitudes surrounding online communication while dating on jealousy in romantic relationships. As it is a replication study, the secondary aim is to replicate the findings of the original publication (Sullivan, 2021). Participants will be asked to complete a survey measuring attachment anxiety, attitudes to online communication and jealousy in relationships caused by social media. A total of three questionnaires that were used in the original publication (Sullivan, 2021) will be used in this study. The first that the participants would complete is the anxiety subscale of the Revised Adult Attachment Scale (Collins & Read, 1990) which measures attachment anxiety. The second questionnaire participants will be presented with includes adapted questions from the Facebook Jealousy Scale (Muise et al, 2009) that assesses online jealousy, and the third questionnaire will be questions from the misunderstanding and apprehension subscales of the Online Attitudes Questionnaire (Ledbetter, 2009), which assesses attitudes about communicating online. Previous research has found that those with insecure attachment styles can experience more negative emotions in relationships (Simpson, 1990) and behavioural jealousy was significantly affected by attachment style as those with insecure attachments were reported to be more fearful of rejection and abandonment (Karakurt, 2001). This topic is therefore a vital area to research as those with insecure attachments often struggle to develop healthy and fulfilling relationships, which can result in poor mental wellbeing and low self-esteem (Stackert & Bursik, 2003). Although there is some previous research exploring the impact of attachment styles on romantic relationships and how this also impacts social media stalking and surveillance of a partner’s phone, it is crucial to investigate this topic further in order to further our understanding of how these factors influence each other.

title_r: Novel Approaches to Online Hypnosis: Norming and Replication Studies
abstract_r: Although Palfi et al. (2019) demonstrated the practicality of online hypnosis, standard procedures for interpreting the results of online hypnotizability scales still require experimenters to manually score several items. Our first study is designed to provide norms for online hypnosis (with a text introduction in an Australian student undergraduate population), while also testing a modified scoring system that might allow for more automatization of the online hypnosis procedure. This is achieved by measuring the accuracy of participants’ self-scoring for several items of the Sussex Waterloo Scale of Hypnotizability (SWASH; Lush et al., 2018) that would otherwise need to be coded by an experimenter. Our second study expands on the work of Palfi et al. to explore the limits of online hypnosis by testing a series of experimentally relevant suggestions. Specifically, we aim to conceptually replicate a series of results from Polito et al.’s (2018) hypnotic Clever Hands (CH) task and Schmidt et al.’s (2017) hypnotic visual oddball (VO) paradigm. In the original CH task, Wegner et al. (2003) observed that participants responded more accurately on easy questions than hard questions despite explicit instructions to answer all questions randomly. In Polito et al.’s hypnotic CH version, Polito et al. found that a hypnotic suggestion for alien control inhibited this effect as participants responded close to chance (56%) on easy items following the suggestion. However, this result was merely nonsignificant. Accordingly, in our current paradigm, we apply a Bayesian approach to determine whether we find evidence in favor of the null hypothesis (i.e., no difference from chance). In a VO paradigm, participants must count the number of target shapes presented on screen while ignoring distractor shapes. Schmidt et al. (2017) reported that a hypnotic suggestion to visualize a block of wood in front of the screen inhibited participant performance, specifically in relation to hypnotic highs. Replicating Shmidt et al.’s finding would provide additional support for the efficacy of online hypnotic by demonstrating that suggestion effects extend beyond the domain of standard scale suggestions.

title_r: Social Comparision and Self-Construal: A replication study
abstract_r: Research question: Does self-construal have an influence on the consequences of social comparison (as in Gardner et al., 2002)? Gardner et al. (2002, study 1) found that interdependent self-construal is a factor that influences the consequences of social comparison on self-evaluation. Participants were primed with interdependent or independent self-construal and then asked to compare themselves to a friend and a stranger, in a self-relevant and a self-irrelevant task. As a measurement for the influence of social-comparison participants guessed if the stranger and the friend got the answers in a knowledge task correct. In the self-relevant task men projected a better performance for strangers than their friends, when primed with the independent self-construal. When primed with the interdependent self-construal men projected in both tasks a better performance for the friend compared to the stranger. For women there was no significant three-way interaction (prime, self-relevance, relationship). We will conceptually replicate this finding with a few adaptations. In the present study there will only be a self-relevant task, because social-comparison has no consequences in the self-irrelevant task ("Self-Evaluation Maintenance Model—IResearchNet", 2016). Furthermore, Gardner et al. (2002) explained the gender differences, with men and women having a different chronic self-construal. We will not merely assume these gender differences in chronic self-construal but measure it directly and look at its influences. The present research question is if self-construal (primed and chronic) influences the consequences of social comparison on self-evaluation (as in Gardner et al. 2002).

title_r: Selecting the special or choosing the common? A high-powered conceptual replication of Kim and Markus’ (1999) pen study
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

Kim and Markus (1999; Study 3) found that 74% of European Americans selected a pen with an uncommon (vs. common) color, whereas only 24% of East Asians made such a choice, highlighting a pronounced cross-cultural difference in the extent to which people opt for originality or make majority-based choices.   The present high-powered study   (N  =   729) conceptually replicates the results from Kim and Markus (1999; Study 3), although our effect size (r = .12) is significantly weaker than that of the original study (r = .52). Interestingly, a larger proportion of Chinese, but not the US, participants selected a pen with an uncommon color now than during the original study. Thus, our findings indicate a potential transmission of certain western values to cultures traditionally characterized by collectivism and conformity, likely exacerbated by the globalization of mass media and the rapid economic growth in many East Asian countries.

item30: For H1, the effect size refers to the mean differences in scores between the honest and faking conditions (Cohen’s d). For H2, the effect size refers to the change in the percentage of variance in the ability to fake that is explained by trait EI only, as indicated by the change in coefficient of determination (ΔR2). For the file clerk position, there is a significant increase in explained variance by trait EI (ΔR2 file clerk =.17, p =.02) whereas for the lawyer position, there is no significant increase in explained variance by trait EI (ΔR2 lawyer =.01, p =.55).

item31: For the effect of trait EI on overall ability to fake towards the file clerk profile, the 95% confidence interval was -0.142 ≤ ρ ≤ 0.560. For the effect of trait EI on overall ability to fake towards the lawyer profile, the 95% confidence interval was - 0.485 ≤ ρ ≤ 0.242.

item32: not significantly different from the original effect size

item33: inconclusive

item34: The replication effect size is not significantly different from the original effect size. Comparing confidence intervals, for the original study’s effect of trait EI on overall ability to fake towards the file clerk profile, the 95% confidence interval was 0.215 ≤ ρ ≤ 0.472, whereas for the replicated study’s effect of trait EI on overall ability to fake towards the file clerk profile, the 95% confidence interval was -0.142 ≤ ρ ≤ 0.560. The two confidence intervals do overlap and as such we can conclude that there is no statistically significant difference in the two population values at the given level of confidence. Similarly, for the original study’s effect of trait EI on overall ability to fake towards the lawyer profile, the 95% confidence interval was - 0.327 ≤ ρ ≤ - 0.045, whereas for the replicated study’s effect of trait EI on overall ability to fake towards the lawyer profile, the 95% confidence interval was - 0.485 ≤ ρ ≤ 0.242. The two confidence intervals do overlap and as such we can conclude that there is no statistically significant difference in the two population values at the given level of confidence.

Hence, we judge the replication to be inconclusive given that the replication was neither significantly different from the null nor the original.

The replication for our study is inconclusive because comparing the original study and replicated study’s Cohen’s d for H1, there seems to be consistency in which Cohen’s d value is greatest for the positive facets (original study: 1.89; replicated study: 2.15), followed by negative facets (original study: 1.08; replicated study: 1.03) and smallest for neutral facets (original study: 1.06; replicated study: 0.70). However, the values should be examined with discretion due to the limitations of our team’s replication study. Along the same vein, due caution should be paid in interpreting the statistical significance and non-significance for the file clerk and lawyer condition for H2 (original study: ΔR2 file clerk  = .03, p = .02, ΔR2 lawyer = .04, p = .00; replicated study: ΔR2 file clerk =.17, p =.02, ΔR2 lawyer =.01, p =.55).

item37: There are mainly 3 limitations for our team’s replication study:
(a) The small sample size of our study undermines the results obtained as it reduces the chance of detecting a true effect. 
(b) Overly lengthy questionnaire consisting of 458 questions that requires at least 40 minutes or more to complete the questionnaire. This could incur respondent fatigue and as a result undermine participants’ true ability to fake. 
(c) Absence of incentives provided to participants - Participants were not motivated to complete the questionnaire as incentives were not made available to them. This could have led them to not answer the questions with much effort, thus resulting in inconclusive results.

title_r: How can clinicians choose between conflicting and discordant systematic reviews? A replication study of the Jadad algorithm
abstract_r: Abstract Introduction The exponential growth of published systematic reviews (SRs) presents challenges for decision makers seeking to answer clinical, public health or policy questions. In 1997, an algorithm was created by Jadad et al. to choose the best SR across multiple. Our study aims to replicate author assessments using the Jadad algorithm to determine: (i) if we chose the same SR as the authors; and (ii) if we reach the same results. Methods We searched MEDLINE, Epistemonikos, and Cochrane Database of SRs. We included any study using the Jadad algorithm. We used consensus building strategies to operationalise the algorithm and to ensure a consistent approach to interpretation. Results We identified 21 studies that used the Jadad algorithm to choose one or more SRs. In 62% (13/21) of cases, we were unable to replicate the Jadad assessment and ultimately chose a different SR than the authors. Overall, 18 out of the 21 (86%) independent Jadad assessments agreed in direction of the findings despite 13 having chosen a different SR. Conclusions Our results suggest that the Jadad algorithm is not reproducible between users as there are no prescriptive instructions about how to operationalise the algorithm. In the absence of a validated algorithm, we recommend that healthcare providers, policy makers, patients and researchers address conflicts between review findings by choosing the SR(s) with meta-analysis of RCTs that most closely resemble their clinical, public health, or policy question, are the most recent, comprehensive (i.e. number of included RCTs), and at the lowest risk of bias.

title_r: Do environmental messages emphasising binding morals promote conservatives’ pro-environmentalism? A pre-registered replication
abstract_r: Past studies indicated that environmental messages incorporating binding morals (i.e., loyalty/betrayal, authority/subversion, purity/degradation morals) were effective in reducing the negative association between political conservatism and pro-environmentalism. We conceptually replicated and extended this finding through open science practices. In a pilot study, we constructed three environmental messages incorporating each binding moral based on previous relevant studies, and confirmed their validity (96 U.S. adults, 50% woman). We then investigated the independent effects of these binding moral messages on pro-environmentalism across the political spectrum (705 U.S. adults, 56.6% woman). Contrasting with our expectations and previous findings, we found no evidence that these environmental messages emphasising distinct binding morals were more effective than a control environmental message in attenuating the political polarisations on conservation intentions and willingness to receive more information about environmental protection. Simply adding binding morals content in environmental messaging may not be useful in promoting conservatives’ pro-environmental engagement. We further discussed future research as well as limitations of this research.

title_r: Evidence That Tetris Reduces Immediate but Not Subsequent Daily Intrusions of a Trauma Film: A Multilab Replication Study
abstract_r: Reactivating a target memory and subsequently playing the computer game Tetris is thought to reduce intrusive memories and is being explored clinically. However, the current literature on the effect of Tetris on intrusions has limitations. To examine whether the previous finding from experimental research that Tetris reduces trauma film related intrusions is replicable in a large sample, we conducted a preregistered, multi-site study in healthy participants. Experiment 1 (N = 141) showed similar intrusion rates of an updated trauma film that was then used in Experiment 2. In line with previous findings, Experiment 2 (N = 433) showed that compared to a perceptual vigilance control task, Tetris reduced retrospective ratings of trauma film related intrusions during the task. In contrast to such an immediate effect, the hypothesis that Tetris reduces intrusions over the course of one week was not corroborated. Future research may examine the role of the format of delivering the experiment (i.e., in-person versus online sessions) and type of control condition (i.e., no-task versus active control). This may inform studies on whether, and in what settings, Tetris is a suitable intervention for clinical use.

title_r: Do environmental messages emphasising binding morals promote conservatives’ pro-environmentalism? A pre-registered replication
abstract_r: Past studies indicated that environmental messages incorporating binding morals (i.e., loyalty/betrayal, authority/subversion, purity/degradation) were effective in reducing the negative association between political conservatism and pro-environmentalism. We conceptually replicated and extended this finding through open science practices. In a pilot study, we constructed three environmental messages incorporating each binding moral based on previous relevant studies, and confirmed their validity (96 U.S. adults, 50% women). We then investigated the independent effects of these binding moral messages on pro-environmentalism across the political spectrum (705 U.S. adults, 56.6% women). Contrasting with our expectations and previous findings, we found no evidence that these environmental messages emphasising distinct binding morals were more effective than a control environmental message in attenuating the political polarisation on conservation intentions and willingness to receive more information about environmental protection. Simply adding binding morals content in environmental messaging may not be useful in promoting conservatives’ pro-environmental engagement. We further discuss future research as well as the limitations of this research.

title_r: Calibration information reduces bias during estimation of factorials: A (partial) replication and extension of Tversky and Kahneman (1973)
abstract_r: Tversky and Kahneman (1973) found that, under time pressure, people massively underestimated the expansion of 8! (correct value 40,320), and this bias was mitigated for participants presented the descending (8x7x6x5x4x3x2x1; Median=2,250) vs. ascending order (1x2x3x4x5x6x7x8; Median=512). In a first-ever replication (N=140), we also found predominant underestimation, but no significant between-subjects descending vs. ascending order effect. However, when participants then estimated the opposite order, we reproduced this order effect within-subjects. Finally, participants received calibration information (the correct value of 6! or 10!) and again estimated both orders of 8!. Participants who received 10! made more accurate estimates for 8! (Median=38,000), which did not differ statistically from the correct value. Participants who received 6! still grossly underestimated (Median=2,678.5), despite 8! being closer to 6! than 10! in linear and log units. Thus, we surprisingly found the classic factorial estimation bias only within-subjects, and provide evidence for how calibration can reduce it.

title_r: Assessment of Off-the-Shelf SE-specific Sentiment Analysis Tools: An Extended Replication Study
abstract_r: Sentiment analysis methods have become popular for investigating human communication, including discussions related to software projects. Since general-purpose sentiment analysis tools do not fit well with the information exchanged by software developers, new tools, specific for software engineering (SE), have been developed. We investigate to what extent SE-specific tools for sentiment analysis mitigate the threats to conclusion validity of empirical studies in software engineering, highlighted by previous research. First, we replicate two studies addressing the role of sentiment in security discussions on GitHub and in question-writing on Stack Overflow. Then, we extend the previous studies by assessing to what extent the tools agree with each other and with the manual annotation on a gold standard of 600 documents. We find that different SE-specific sentiment analysis tools might lead to contradictory results at a fine-grain level, when used 'off-the-shelf'. Conversely, platform-specific tuning or retraining might be needed to take into account differences in platform conventions, jargon, or document lengths.

title_r: Automatic Classification of User Requirements from Online Feedback -- A Replication Study
abstract_r: Natural language processing (NLP) techniques have been widely applied in the requirements engineering (RE) field to support tasks such as classification and ambiguity detection. Although RE research is rooted in empirical investigation, it has paid limited attention to replicating NLP for RE (NLP4RE) studies. The rapidly advancing realm of NLP is creating new opportunities for efficient, machine-assisted workflows, which can bring new perspectives and results to the forefront. Thus, we replicate and extend a previous NLP4RE study (baseline), "Classifying User Requirements from Online Feedback in Small Dataset Environments using Deep Learning", which evaluated different deep learning models for requirement classification from user reviews. We reproduced the original results using publicly released source code, thereby helping to strengthen the external validity of the baseline study. We then extended the setup by evaluating model performance on an external dataset and comparing results to a GPT-4o zero-shot classifier. Furthermore, we prepared the replication study ID-card for the baseline study, important for evaluating replication readiness. Results showed diverse reproducibility levels across different models, with Naive Bayes demonstrating perfect reproducibility. In contrast, BERT and other models showed mixed results. Our findings revealed that baseline deep learning models, BERT and ELMo, exhibited good generalization capabilities on an external dataset, and GPT-4o showed performance comparable to traditional baseline machine learning models. Additionally, our assessment confirmed the baseline study's replication readiness; however missing environment setup files would have further enhanced readiness. We include this missing information in our replication package and provide the replication study ID-card for our study to further encourage and support the replication of our study.

title_r: Searching for the Synchrotron Cosmic Web Again: A replication attempt
abstract_r: We follow up on the surprising recent announcement by Vernstrom et al. (2021) of the detection of the synchrotron cosmic web. We attempt to reproduce their detection with new observations with the Phase II, extended configuration of the Murchison Widefield Array at \SI{118.5}{\mega \hertz}. We reproduce their detection methodology by stacking pairs of nearby luminous red galaxies (LRGs) -- used as tracers for clusters and galaxy groups -- contained in our low frequency radio observations. We show that our observations are significantly more sensitive than those used in Vernstrom et al., and that our angular sensitivity is sufficient. And yet, we make no statistically significant detection of excess radio emission along the bridge spanning the LRG pairs. This non-detection is true both for the original LRG pair catalogue as used in Vernstrom et al., as well as for other larger catalogues with modified selection criteria. Finally, we return to the original data sets used in Vernstrom et al., and find that whilst we clearly reproduce the excess X-ray emission from ROSAT, we are not able to reproduce any kind of broad and extended excess intercluster filamentary emission using the original 118.5 MHz MWA survey data. In the interests of understanding this result, as part of this paper we release images of the 14 fields used in this study, the final stacked images, as well as key components of our stacking and modelling code.

title_r: Modeling Help Seeking Intentions In Victims Of Intimate Partner Violence: A Conceptual Replication Of Fleming And Resick (2017)
abstract_r: Victims of intimate partner violence come forward and seek services and help for the crimes committed upon them at much lower rates than victims of other interpersonal crimes. In this study, the Theory of Planned Behavior was used to assess individual behavioral predictors of formal help-seeking in victims of intimate partner violence in order to better understand factors that promote or inhibit help-seeking in this vulnerable population, including victims’ attitudes about help seeking, the subjective norms they feel about help seeking, their perceived ability to get help, and the relationship these factors have with prior experiences. Partial support was found for the full Theory of Planned Behavior model predicting intentions for all resource types, with attitudes and perceived behavioral control predicting intentions for most resources, while norms rarely contributed to the variance. Prior experience was related to attitudes about several of the resources.

title_r: Multiple Aspects and Correlates of Body Figure Ratings: A Replication and Extension of Fallon and Rozin (1985)
abstract_r: College females, using a set of nine figure drawings reflecting very thin to very heavy figures, rated their current figure (based on how they thought they looked versus how they felt), ideal figure, how they appeared to others, and the figure they deemed most attractive to men. A subsample of the 123 subjects also completed measures of body satisfaction, depression, eating disturbance, teasing, and noted the age of menarche. The results replicated and extended the findings of Fallon and Rozin (1985), who found that ideal figures were smaller than ratings of current size. Additionally, there was a significant difference between the two protocols for current size, indicating that subjects rated their size as larger when asked to rate based on affective instructions. Figure ratings based on cognitive/rational instructions did not differ from those based on how they conceptualized others' views of their bodies. Significant correlations were observed among figure ratings, body satisfaction, eating disturbance, depression, and teasing. The need to focus on etiological mechanisms of disturbed body image and eating behavior is addressed, and the role of teasing as a possible precipitant is examined.

title_r: College students’ beliefs about domestic violence: A replication and extension.
abstract_r: In recent decades, significant effort and money have been spent to change social and legal responses to domestic violence and affect public perceptions. A small body of research has examined individuals’ opinions about what behaviors are considered domestic violence. Using a sample of college students, the present study examined a modified version of a somewhat popular instrument used to measure beliefs about domestic violence, extending previous work done by Carlson and Worden. Results indicated beliefs about domestic violence are multidimensional, depending on the nature of the behavior and, in part, the gender of the perpetrator. Opinions about the lawfulness of these behaviors fit the same factor structure as beliefs about domestic violence. Demographic characteristics, current relationship status, secondhand experiences with domestic violence, and perceived prevalence of domestic violence in the community are generally not related to beliefs about domestic violence or the lawfulness of these behaviors. However, attributions of blame on the victim are negatively related to domestic violence beliefs and lawfulness. Moreover, lawfulness is a key covariate for domestic violence beliefs. In addition, results also indicate that the gender of the perpetrator is an important variable affecting student’s beliefs about sexual assault behaviors. Results from this study support the prevailing ideas behind the Battered Women’s Movement that enacting policies and educational programs deeming domestic violence socially, morally, and legally wrong could shift long-standing sociocultural beliefs about men’s use of violence against women. Implications of this study for research and policy specific to college students are discussed.

title_r: The near-miss effect in online slot-machine gambling : a series of conceptual replications
abstract_r: The field of gambling studies is beginning to recognize the need to conduct targeted replications of influential effects throughout the field. Given the limited resources afforded to researchers, we must be systematic in our approach to selecting which effects are most in need of replication. Following a systematic approach to replication selection, a series of conceptual replications of the ‘near-miss effect’ in slot machine gambling was conducted, on online community samples. Near-miss outcomes on a slot machine are those that appear proximal to a win, though they are functionally identical to other losing outcomes (herein termed ‘full misses’). Near-misses have been shown to elicit a range of differential psychological effects compared to full-misses. Experiment 1a and 1b attempted to replicate a previous study by Clark et al. 2009 that 1) near-misses are experienced as more negative, 2) near-misses are rated as more motivating to continue playing a slot machine. Experiment 2 tested the effects on speed of gambling (a replication of Dixon et al. 2013) that near-miss outcomes speed up participant speed of play compared to full miss outcomes. Experiment 3 tested whether near-miss outcomes influence subsequent bet size. I replicated the motivation hypothesis of Clark et el., (2009), but found a significant effect in the opposite direction for the valence hypothesis. Across both study 1a and 1b, near-miss outcomes were more positive relative to full-misses. Experiment 2 replicated the hypothesis that near-miss outcomes increase speed of play (Dixon et al., 2013). Experiment 3 observed near-miss outcomes led to a significant increase in bet size on the subsequent spin relative to full-miss outcomes. I consider how this pattern of results across 3 different dependent variables speak to the different theoretical accounts of how near-misses operate.

title_r: Intertemporal consumption and debt aversion: a replication and extension
abstract_r: We replicate Meissner (Exp Econ 19:281–298, 2016), where debt aversion was reported for the first time in an intertemporal consumption and saving problem. While Meissner (2016) uses a German sample, our participants are US undergraduate students. All of the original study’s main findings replicate with similar effect sizes. Additionally, we extend the original analysis by introducing a new individual index of debt aversion, which we use to compare debt aversion across countries. Interestingly, we find no significant differences in debt aversion between the original German and the new US sample. We then test whether debt aversion correlates with individual characteristics such as gender, cognitive reflection ability, and risk aversion. Overall, this paper confirms the importance of debt aversion in intertemporal consumption and saving problems and validates the approach of Meissner (2016).

title_r: The Possible Unemployment Cost of Average Inflation Below a Credible Target. A Replication Study of Svensson (American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics, 2015). Data.
abstract_r: These are the replication files for Oraby (JCRE, 2022). The paper aims to replicate Svensson (American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics, 2015). Abstract: This paper replicates the main analysis of Svensson (2015) with some expansion to the original analysis, mainly for the United States. Overall, the replication exercise successfully confirms the conclusions of Svensson (2015). In both Sweden and the United States, empirical evidence supports the existence of a non-vertical long run Phillips curve. The slope of the long run Phillips curve recorded -0.75 in Sweden and -0.23 in the United States. While the average inflation rate in the United States was very close to its targeted level, the average inflation rate in Sweden was 0.6 percentage points below its targeted level over the sample period. The deviation of inflation rate from its targeted level in Sweden resulted in an unemployment cost equivalent to 0.8 percentage points over the sample period where the average unemployment rate recorded 7.4 percent compared with an estimated 6.6 percent had the average inflation rate been at its targeted level.

title_r: Productivity premia for many modes of internationalization. A replication study of Békés and Muraközy (Economics Letters, 2016) (replication study)
abstract_r: This study attempts to replicate estimation results from Gábor Békés and Balázs Muraközy, Measuring productivity premia with many modes of internationalization, published in Economics Letters (2016). In this paper the authors use comparable firm-level data for seven European countries based on the EFIGE dataset to estimate the productivity premia of firms with various modes of internationalization by several empirical methods to demonstrate how results differ due to the method applied. While the EFIGE data are available free of charge from the web one core variable used by Békés and Muraközy is not, because total factor productivity (tfp) as computed by the authors is based on data from a commercial data base and, therefore, is available for users with a license to this database only. The freely available EFIGE data, however, come with another tfp-variable that can be used instead. In this replication study I use the EFIGE data with this publicly available tfp-variable to replicate (parts of) the estimations of Békés and Muraközy (2016) to see whether their results hold with the widely used public use version of the EFIGE data, too. It turns out that the big picture that emerges from using both productivity measures tends to be very similar. The use of the public use version of the EFIGE data for empirical investigations that deal with productivity, therefore, seems to be feasible.

abstract_r: Summary: These codes replicate Autor et al. (2008) and extend their analysis through 2022. Findings: The extension to an additional 17 years of analysis underscores the original finding that rising wage inequality was not an episodic event of the 1980s. That being said, overall 90/10 inequality and the college wage premium have plateaued since 2005. Despite overall inequality plateauing, upper-tail 90/50 inequality has continued to increase since 1980 for both men and women. I also find that the composition-adjusted real wages of high school dropouts has caught up with high school graduates in the last decade. The combination of these findings is consistent with rising polarization in which employment and wages expand for high-wage and low-wage work.

title_r: The Long-Term Effects of Measles Vaccination on Earnings and Employment. A Replication Study of Atwood (American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 2022)
abstract_r: The replication package reproduces the results presented in the paper "The Long-Term Effects of Measles Vaccination on Earnings and Employment. A Replication Study of Atwood (American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 2022)" by Mara Barschkett, Mathias Huebener, Andreas Leibing, Jan Marcus and Shushanik Margaryan, published in: Journal of Comments and Replications in Economics, Volume 2, 2023-4. Data are available at http://doi.org/10.3886/E138401V1. Abstract: Atwood analyzes the effects of the 1963 U.S. measles vaccination on long-run labor market outcomes, using a generalized difference-in-differences approach. We reproduce the results of this paper and perform a battery of robustness checks. Overall, we confirm that the measles vaccination had positive labor market effects. While the negative effect on the likelihood of living in poverty and the positive effect on the probability of being employed are very robust across the different specifications, the headline estimate—the effect on earnings—is more sensitive to the exclusion of certain regions and survey years.

title_r: Does generation benefit learning for narrative and expository texts? A direct replication attempt
abstract_r: Generated information is better recognized and recalled than information that is read. This generation effect has been replicated several times for different types of material, including texts. Perhaps the most influential demonstration is by McDaniel, Einstein, Dunay, and Cobb (Journal of Memory and Language, 1986, 25(6), 645–656; henceforth MEDC). This group tested whether the generation effect occurs only if the generation task stimulates cognitive processes not already stimulated by the text. Numerous studies, however, report difficulties replicating this text by generation-task interaction, which suggests that the effect might only be found under conditions closer to the original method of MEDC. To test this assumption, the present study closely replicated MEDC's Experiment 2 in two separate German and English-speaking samples. The present study provided partial evidence in favor of the expected interaction, which ultimately depended on successful completion of the generation task (with near-to-perfect accuracy). Moreover, it indicates that sentence unscrambling might enhance learning across genres.

summary: Implicit Candidate Traits in the 2016 Presidential Election: Evidence From a Nationally Representative Sample

Joseph A. Vitriol
Aleks Ksiazkiewicz
Christina E. Farhart 

Abstract
A major challenge to understanding how citizens assess political candidates, and how these assessments translate into political judgment and behavior, is the extent to which socially and politically relevant psychological processes and attitudinal evaluations are accessible at the conscious versus unconscious level. The current research seeks additional evidence for our dual-process model of candidate trait perceptions (Ksiazkiewicz, Vitriol, & Farhart R&R) using a nationally representative sample in the context of the 2016 U.S. Presidential elections. We expect that implicit evaluations of the warmth and competence of major party candidates, Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton, would predict candidate evaluations, economic attitudes, vote intentions, and actual vote behaviors in the 2016 election. Consistent with prior research, we expect these implicit constructs (measured in September 2016) to demonstrate predictive validity for vote choice in the 2016 Presidential Election, above and beyond explicit analogs, demographics variables, partisan identification and ideological self-placement. We also expect these effects to be moderated by strength of partisan identification and strength of candidate preferences, which was measured in July of 2016.  Further, we explore additional potential moderators (e.g., gender bias; attitude certainty; cognitive style) and mediators for the correspondence between implicit-explicit attitudes (e.g., information search/exposure) to better understand the condition under which implicit constructs show incremental effects above and beyond explicit judgments. 

Keywords:  IAT, gender, vote choice, implicit warmth and competence, election
 

Implicit Candidate Traits in the 2016 Presidential Election: Evidence From a Nationally Representative Sample
	Research in political science investigating voter decision-making has traditionally assumed that voters have introspective access to their attitudes, preferences, and beliefs when making an electoral decision. However, much research in social psychology indicates that many types of cognitive processes, associations, and structures that give rise to attitudinal preferences are inaccessible to conscious awareness, either because such mental content is operating at the unconscious level or because it cannot be retrieved through deliberate introspection (Nisbett & Wilson, 1977; Winkielman & Schooler, 2011). A major challenge to understanding how citizens assess political candidates, and how these assessments translate into political judgment and behavior, is the extent to which socially and politically relevant psychological processes and attitudinal evaluations are accessible at the conscious versus unconscious level. 
	Political psychologists have begun to supplement theories of conscious, explicit processes with theories regarding unconscious, implicit processes in voter decision-making (e.g., Lodge & Taber, 2013; for a review of implicit research as it applies to political topics, see Ksiazkiewicz & Hedrick 2013). For example, in the 2012 Presidential Election, we examined the unique effects of implicit and explicit trait (i.e., Warmth and Competence) judgments on vote choice and evaluations of the presidential candidates, Barack Obama and Mitt Romney, in the 2012 US election. This line of inquiry suggests that 1) implicit candidate trait associations demonstrate predictive validity above and beyond its explicit counterpart, and 2) implicit trait associations are more consequential for undecided voters. This work is currently under review (Ksiazkiewicz, Vitriol, & Farhart, revise and resubmit). However, this previous study relied upon a convenience sample, so its generalizability to representative samples is untested. 
	The current study seeks to extend and replicate our dual-process model of trait perceptions to a large sample weighted to be nationally representative and recruited in the context of the 2016 U.S. Presidential Election. First, we examine the incremental effect of implicit evaluations of the warmth and competence of major party candidates, Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton, expecting these constructs to predict candidate evaluations, economic attitudes, vote intentions, and actual vote behaviors in the 2016 election above and beyond each other, explicit analogs, demographics variables, partisan identification and ideological self-placement. Second, consistent with previous research, we also expect these effects to be moderated by strength of partisan identification and strength of candidate preferences, which was measured in July of 2016.  Third, we explore potential moderators (e.g., gender bias; attitude certainty; cognitive style) and mediators for the correspondence between implicit-explicit attitudes (e.g., information search/exposure) to better understand the condition under which these implicit constructs show incremental effects above and beyond explicit judgments. 
	To our knowledge, few panel studies that include implicit measures has been undertaken to examine the effects of these constructs on changes in political judgment and behavior over the course of a political campaign (e.g., Ksiazkiewicz, Vitriol, & Farhart, revise and resubmit), and even fewer studies have included implicit measures in nationally representative samples. The broad aim of the current proposal is to advance the burgeoning literature on implicit processes in political contexts by investigating the consequences of implicit candidate-trait associations (i.e., using 2 versions of the Brief-IAT) on change in political attitudes and actual vote behavior in the 2016 U.S. Presidential Election using a large, national representative sample. 

Implicit Processes in Political Contexts
The study of implicit political attitudes and its electoral consequence can contribute to our understanding of the psychological processes that underlie voter decision-making in a number of ways. First, implicit associations are likely to account for unexplained variance in traditional models of voter decision-making. Implicit processes have incremental predictive validity across a wide range of domains traditionally examined exclusively at the explicit level (e.g., Greenwald Poehlman, Uhlmann, and Banaji 2009). In political contexts, implicit processes may be particularly useful for explaining the behavior of individuals whose behaviors are not well described by traditional political science theory (e.g., independents and undecided voters; Arcuri et al. 2008; Galdi, Arcuri, and Gawronski 2008; Galdi, Gawronski, Arcuri, and Friese 2012; Hawkins and Nosek 2012; but see Friese et al. 2012). 
Second, it is unlikely that this unexplained variance could be accounted for by traditional measurement techniques that focus exclusively on explicit attitudes. Implicit associations cannot be captured by traditional survey techniques because individuals are usually unaware of the impact of their implicit associations on their judgments and behaviors (Gawronski, Hofmann, and Wilbur 2006). Across a variety of domains, implicit processes have been shown to be related, but not reducible, to explicit processes (Hofmann et al., 2005; Nosek and Smyth 2007). Indeed, as demonstrated by meta-analysis (Greenwald et al. 2009), implicit and explicit measures of attitudes both show incremental predictive validity across behavioral domains, suggesting that each measure distinct psychological processes or cognitive structures that account for distinct portions of the variance in attitudinal and behavioral outcomes. 
Third, and most importantly for the current work, because implicit measures are largely unaffected by social desirability bias, they can be particularly useful in situations and on topics where traditional survey techniques may not capture participants’ “true” beliefs (Banse, Seise, & Zerbes, 2001; Boysen, Vogel, & Madon, 2006). For example, in the context of an election where at least one of the major party candidates is a woman, like the 2016 US presidential election, some voters may conceal their true assessments of candidates in order to appear unprejudiced (Redlawsk, Tolbert, and Franko 2010).  Similarly, some respondents may feel that it is socially undesirable to express support for Trump. 
Thus, implicit and explicit attitudes are not interchangeable, redundant constructs, but instead represent psychologically independent, and at times divergent (see Nosek 2005), attitudinal orientations that may have different evaluative and behavioral implications (e.g., Fazio 1990), even when no clear motivation for impression-management is present (e.g., Teubel, Asendorpf, Banse, and Schnabel 2011). Instead, automatic, unconscious associations may be incongruent with explicit attitudes and judgments. Accordingly, the correspondence between implicit and explicit attitudes may have important electoral consequences.

On the Correspondence Between Implicit and Explicit Attitudes
	Of central importance to the current investigation is the relation between implicit and explicit attitudes, as it speaks directly to the conditions under which and the individuals for whom unconscious associations matter. Meta-analytic investigations of implicit-explicit correspondence across a broad range of attitudinal domains generally indicate an average correlation that is positive and moderate (e.g., Nosek, 2005), but varies across content areas and individuals (Blair, 2001). Psychological factors that could potentially mediate the correspondence between implicit and explicit political attitudes remain largely unexamined.
	Implicit measures can be understood as capturing attitudinal preferences prior to the initiation of conscious, deliberative thought that could potentially change or “edit” individuals’ evaluation or response (Nosek, 2005). This suggests that attitudinally relevant cognitions and elaborations should increase the correspondence between implicit and explicit attitudes by increasing the likelihood that individuals obtain a more accurate conscious representation of their underlying implicit preferences, which should reduce its incremental predictive validity. Voters less interested in politics or who have weaker partisan identifications and candidate preferences are generally less likely to engage in the kind of cognitive elaboration that renders implicit and explicit attitudes highly congruent. For these individuals, we expect implicit candidate trait associations to demonstrate incremental predictive validity.
	Cognitive elaboration is expected to increase the correspondence between implicit and explicit attitudes because it increases the accessibility of underlying, unconscious preferences. Cognitive accessibility is indeed a critical psychological mechanism through which implicit associations may be incorporated into explicit judgments. Accordingly, we examine the possibility that individual differences associated with cognitive elaboration, including need to evaluate, need for cognition, need for closure, defensive confidence, political knowledge and interest, and strength of partisan identification moderate the relationship between implicit and explicit trait associations for each candidate. Similarly, consistent with prior research on gender bias in warmth assessments (Winter, 2010), we expect that ambivalent sexism, separate spheres ideology, or negative explicit attitudes towards women (i.e., feeling thermometers) will moderate the relationship between implicit trait associations and actual vote behavior, such that implicit warmth assessments will matter more and implicit competence assessments will matter less for individuals characterized by gender bias.
	Finally, we also explore several behaviors that may reinforce implicit trait associations and therefore potentially mediate the relationship between these constructs and explicit attitudes and behavior. Specifically, we expect that implicit constructs will direct political engagement and participation, confirmatory information-search, biased consumption of attitudinally-congruent media, and selection into politically homogenous (vs. heterogeneous) social networks. These behaviors will, in turn, increase the likelihood that individuals’ explicit attitudes, behavioral intentions, and actual behaviors will be more consistent with the evaluative implications of the implicit constructs.
The Present Study
The major questions we address in this project is 1) if implicit trait associations shape explicit political judgment, preferences, and behavior (i.e., incremental predictive validity) for a nationally representative sample, 2) for whom (i.e., less politically knowledgeable, engaged, and interested members of the electorate; individuals engaged in low levels of cognitive elaboration; voters characterized by gender bias or not), and 3) what behaviors may mediate implicit-explicit congruence. We advance the following confirmatory hypotheses, based on the findings reported in Ksiazkiewicz, Vitriol, and Farhart (R&R). Below, we also advance several exploratory hypotheses, which are an extrapolation of prior research in psychology on implicit processes to the political domain:
1.	Confirmatory Hypothesis 1: Implicit trait associations about candidate’s warmth and competence will independently predict explicit candidate evaluations and preferences, economic evaluations, behavioral intentions, and actual voting at the time of the election.
a.	Confirmatory Hypothesis 1a: These effects of implicit constructs will emerge above/beyond demographics, explicit trait associations, partisan identification, and ideological self-placement.
b.	Confirmatory Hypothesis 1b: In addition to demographics, explicit candidate traits, partisan identification, and ideology, each implicit construct will demonstrate incremental validity independent of each other.
2.	Confirmatory Hypothesis 2: Implicit trait associations about candidate’s warmth and competence will more strongly predict explicit candidate evaluations and preferences, economic evaluations, behavioral intentions, and actual voting at the time of the election among individuals with weak partisan identifications or candidate preferences.	
a.	Confirmatory Hypothesis 2a: This interaction between implicit constructs and strength of attitudes and identification will emerge above/beyond demographics, explicit trait associations, and ideological self-placement.
b.	Confirmatory Hypothesis 2b: In addition to demographics, explicit candidate traits, partisan identification, and ideology, this interaction between each implicit constructs and strength of attitudes and identification will obtain significance when both implicit constructs are included in the model.
3.	Exploratory Hypothesis 1: Individual differences associated with cognitive elaboration, including need to evaluate, need for cognition, need for closure, defensive confidence, political knowledge and interest, and strength of partisan identification, will moderate the relationship between implicit and explicit trait associations for each candidate, such that at high levels of cognitive elaboration implicit and explicit constructs will be more strongly related.
4.	Exploratory Hypothesis 2: Political engagement and participation, confirmatory information-search, biased consumption of attitudinally-congruent media, and selection into politically homogenous (vs. heterogeneous) social networks will mediate the relationship between implicit constructs and the likelihood that individuals’ explicit attitudes, behavioral intentions, and actual behaviors are more consistent with the evaluative implications of the implicit constructs.


Method
Data were collected as part of a large, multi-investigator panel study of the 2016 U.S. presidential election, utilizing a 4-wave panel design. At Wave 2, participants completed a warmth and competence IAT, in random order. The other measures used in this analysis were also administered to the same participants. Participants were recruited using Survey Sampling International.

Measures
All participants will complete a competence-IAT and warmth IAT, explicit measures of candidate trait evaluations, partisan identification and strength of partisan identification, need to evaluate, need for cognition, need for closure, defensive confidence, political knowledge and interest, economic evaluations, candidate evaluations, vote preferences and choice,
political engagement and participation, media consumption and exposure, social network, ideological self-placement, and demographics. Below, we describe the implicit and explicit measures of candidate trait judgments and any additional transformations we intend to conduct on the variables. The appendix includes the language used to measure these other variables.

Measures
Implicit trait associations. The most commonly used method to measure implicit attitudes is a computer-administered categorization task, called the implicit association test (IAT, Greenwald, McGhee, and Schwartz 1998). Individuals are repeatedly presented with pairs of concepts and faster response latencies indicate stronger implicit associations between the concepts. Participants completed separate IATs at each wave for judgments of competence and warmth with a word-completion distractor task between the IATs. The order of the IATs was randomized for each respondent at the first wave and kept constant at subsequent waves. Each IAT paired adjectives categorized as warm or cold or as competent or incompetent with pictures of Obama and Romney.  These category labels were selected to reflect the underlying constructs of interest, as the choice of category labels on IATs has been found to affect measurement of implicit associations (Mitchell et al. 2003). Higher scores on each of these indicators represent stronger associations of the positive trait with Obama, relative to Romney. IAT scores were computed using the most recent algorithm from Greenwald, Nosek, and Banaji (2003).

Explicit trait judgments.
Explicit candidate-trait of warmth/competence were measuring using a single item. In some analyses, explicit candidate traits will be combined into a single variable if they are highly correlated, but not otherwise.

Data Analysis Plan
Survey weights 
We will follow the instructions provided by the survey research firm SSI to appropriately weight the data in all analyses.

Data Transformation 
IAT response times will be recoded into D-scores using the standard techniques (i.e., Greenwald, Nosek, & Banaji, 2003). D-scores will be recoded to run from -1 to 1, where 0 indicates no association, -1 indicates the theoretically maximal Hillary association (i.e., a D-score of -2) and 1 indicates the theoretically maximal Trump association (i.e., a D-score of 2). Vote choice will be analyzed in a number of ways. First, it will be dichotomized between Trump and Clinton (excluding others). Second, it will be treated as a multinomial logistic regression with categories including Trump, Clinton, third party, and not voting. Scale variables will be calculated as additive indexes. Candidate evaluations (e.g., feeling thermometers) will be differenced to provide a single scale (degree of preference for Trump/Hillary). All continuous and ordinal variables besides the IAT will be coded 0 to 1. Higher values will either indicate greater presence of the trait or greater Trump support/conservatism/Republicanism, as appropriate.


Hypothesis Testing
All models will include age, gender, race, and ideological self-placement as covariates. For analyses not utilizing partisan strength as a mediator/moderator, party ID will also be included as a covariate. For each set of analyses, we present four models, all of which include the aforementioned covariates. First, we regress dependent variables on implicit competence. Second, we regress dependent variables on implicit warmth. Third, we include both implicit warmth and competence in the model. Finally, we regress the dependent variables on the average of implicit warmth and competence (pooled implicit trait association). We present each of these models with and without covariates included. Below, we describe in greater detail how we intend to test each hypothesis.

Confirmatory hypothesis 1, 1a, 1b: Weighted OLS regression will be used for differenced candidate evaluations, economic evaluations, and behavioral intentions. Voting will be analyzed using a probit model or multinomial probit model, depending on whether there are two categories or more than two categories. For dependent variables that are measured repeatedly across waves, we will also explore the extent to which implicit constructs predict change by including lagged indicators of these dependent variables.

Confirmatory Hypothesis 2, 2a, 2b: Weighted OLS regression will be used for differenced candidate evaluations, economic evaluations, and behavioral intentions. Voting will be analyzed using a probit model or multinomial probit model, depending on whether there are two categories or more than two categories. In separate models, each implicit construct will be interacted with strength of partisanship or candidate preference. Simple slope analyses will be conducted at 1 SD Above/Below the mean of the moderator.

Exploratory Hypothesis 1: Weighted OLS regression will be used for differenced candidate evaluations, economic evaluations, and behavioral intentions. Voting will be analyzed using a probit model or multinomial probit model, depending on whether there are two categories or more than two categories.  In separate models, each implicit regressors will be interacted with need to evaluate, need for cognition, need for closure, defensive confidence, political knowledge, and political interest. Simple slope analyses will be conducted at 1 SD Above/Below the mean of the moderator.

Exploratory Hypothesis 2: Weighted OLS regression will be used for differenced candidate evaluations, economic evaluations, and behavioral intentions. Voting will be analyzed using a probit model or multinomial probit model, depending on whether there are two categories or more than two categories. In separate models, the mediating role of 1) political engagement and participation, 2) confirmatory information-search, 3) biased consumption of attitudinally-congruent media, and 4) selection into politically homogenous (vs. heterogeneous) social networks will be tested separately for each implicit construct. Finally, mediation analyses were conducted by following the steps for bootstrapping recommended by Preacher & Hayes (2004; also see Zhao, Lynch, & Chen, 2010).
