title_r: Pre-peer review: Investigating information and skill transfer in neurodiverse groups using diffusion chain methodology: a replication study V2
abstract_r: Background: There have been many anecdotal reports that autistic people feel more comfortable and relaxed in autistic company. Our recent Diversity in Social Intelligence study examined this empirically, and found that an autism-specific environment facilitates learning and interaction for autistic people (Crompton et al., 2020). Our key findings indicate that (1) Autistic people transfer information with other autistic people as effectively as non-autistic people share information with one another; (2) information sharing breaks down when pairs are mis-matched: when one person is autistic and the other non-autistic, (3) feelings of rapport between people of the same neurotype accompany these info-sharing benefits; and (4) external observers can detect the lack of rapport apparent in mixed autistic / non-autistic interactions. These findings, for the first time, demonstrate that autistic people’s social behaviour includes effective communication (information, and skill sharing) and effective social interaction (positive rapport), which is in direct violation of the diagnostic criteria for autism. This represents the first empirical evidence that autistic people have their own repertoire social norms and cues, amounting to a uniquely autistic form of 'social intelligence'" This ground-breaking finding has profound implications for the characterisation of autism as a disorder, and practical implications for policy makers, practitioners, educators, clinicians and psychologists. However, pushing for dramatic changes in policy and practice would be premature without replication. This pre-registration is for a direct replication of the Diversity in Social Intelligence study in two parallel sites, from two continents, with both labs independent of the initial study. It will allow us to investigate whether these findings are replicated in independent samples. This rapid replication will allow us to explore this in a timely way and, if analogous results are found, make evidence-based recommendations to practitioners and policymakers. Replication Methodology: This replication study uses a diffusion chain methodology - a controlled, experimental form of the game "Telephone" - which has been effective in probing cultural learning between individuals in a social group (e.g. Flynn & Whiten, 2008; McGuigan & Graham, 2010). In this method, an experimenter models a complex behaviour to the first person in the chain. The person then has a chance to replicate the behaviour alone, before being paired with the next person in the chain and instructed to demonstrate the behaviour to them. Once more the second participant can practice the behaviour and then must pass it on to the next individual, and so on (see Figure 1 for an illustration of the diffusion chain technique). The diffusion chain methodology involves sequential pairs of participants completing the task, with two people in the lab at any one time, rather than a group task with all participants in the room. Tasks: We will replicate two of the diffusion chain tasks used in the original study: a storytelling task and a Rubik’s twist task. These tasks will provide raw data allowing us to operationalise the effectiveness of information transfer, and skill learning, between people. Measures: In addition, self-rated rapport will be measured after each diffusion chain interaction. We expect to find higher interactive rapport between two people of the same neurotype. Our hypothesis is that single neurotype chains (i.e. chains of all autistic people or chains of all non-autistic people) will result in more accurate and efficient transmission of information between people, and higher interactive rapport than mixed neurotype (i.e. mixed autistic-non-autistic) chains. Participants: Conditions: 216 participants (108 autistic and 108 non-autistic), matched for age and gender will be recruited and remunerated for their time. Participants will be allocated into one of three conditions: (1) Autistic: all participants are autistic (n = 72) (2) Non-autistic: all participants are non-autistic (n = 72) (3) Mixed: where half the participants are autistic, and half the participants are non-autistic (n = 72) For each of the three conditions, we will run twelve diffusion chains, each with six participants (n = 6 participants * n = 12 chains * n = 3 conditions = 216 participants). In the Mixed condition, participants will be arranged in an alternating order (autistic, non-autistic, autistic, etc.) so that each pair of people in the chain is “mis-matched” with a participant from the other diagnostic group. In the original study diffusion chains were eight participants long. Here we plan for chains of six people in length. The reason for this amendment is to maximise the value of the data collected, as explained below. Variations on the original study: In the original study we observed clear floor effects for participants in positions 7 and 8 in the chain (see Crompton, Ropar, Evans-Williams, Flynn & Fletcher-Watson, 2020). This occurred across all conditions and individual chains. In effect, by the time the information had been passed along six times, it was so degraded that participants had a minimal amount of information available to transfer. The mean difference in number of details recalled from the 1st to the 6th person in the chain was 21.56 (4.312 details per step) while the mean difference in number of details recalled from the 6th to the 8th person was 2.94 (1.47 details per step). On average the 6th person in the chain recalled 7.56 details while the 8th person in the chain recalled 4.61 details. Thus, we can clearly see how little information is available in the last part of a chain of 8 people. By reducing the number of participants in each diffusion chain to six, and increasing the number of diffusion chains, every participant will have a chance to provide meaningful data for analysis without floor effects. Having shorter chains will yield more powerful data (more chains, with the same number of participants), be more logistically achievable and cost-effective. The chains remain a direct replication of the data collected from the first six placed participants per chain, from the original study. Our research questions are: (1) Does performance on transmission tasks differ between autistic, non-autistic, and mixed conditions? (2) Does self-rated interactional rapport differ between autistic, non-autistic, and mixed conditions?

Escalation of commitment refers to the decision error in which people stick to their original decision despite negative feedback (Sleesman, Conlon, McNamara & Miles, 2012; Staw, 1976; Staw & Fox, 1977). In 1976, Staw initiated experimental research on escalating commitment. In his study Knee-Deep in the Big Muddy: A Study of Escalating Commitment to a Chosen Course of Action, he showed that escalation was particularly pronounced when people were personally responsible for negative decision consequences. The interaction between responsibility and consequence was significant (p = <.019). Since then, there have been numerous studies investigating the escalation of commitment and the underlying effects. The findings are ambivalent, as the results often do not match or even contradict those of Staw (1976). There are many studies that used Staw's (1976) stimulus material, the A&S Financial Decision Case, or were based on his approach (Akinbobola & Ehigie, 2012; Armstrong, Coviello & Safranek, 1993; Bialek, Węgrzyn, & Meyers, 2021; Conlon & Parks, 1987; McCain, 1986; Morgan & Hansen, 2006; Pfeiffer, Schönborn, Mojzisch & Schulz-Hardt, 2007; Schoorman & Holahan, 1996; Schoorman, Mayer, Douglas & Hetrick, 1994; Singer, 1990; Singer & Singer, 1986). However, these studies did not test the interaction effect responsibility x consequence (Armstrong et al., 1993) and altered or excluded relevant aspects of the paradigm. For example, a different scenario and other variables were examined (Negrini, Riedl & Wibral, 2020; Pfeiffer et al., 2007) or the methodological approach was changed (Akinbobola & Ehigie, 2012; Bialek et al., 2021; Singer & Singer, 1986). For this reason, the planned study in the form of a direct replication should provide information on how robust and reliable Staw's (1976) results are if there are as few deviations as possible from the original study. Of particular interest is the replicability of the interaction effect personal responsibility x decision consequences. In addition, the reasons for the investment decisions are evaluated using content analysis. Armstrong et al. (1993) asked the participants to justify their decision, but did not analyze this. Other studies did not even include the justification in their design (Bialek et al., 2021; Negrini et al., 2020; Pfeiffer et al., 2007; Singer & Singer, 1986). The planned study therefore extends the existing literature with a replication of the study by Staw (1976), which not only records the participants' reasons for their decisions, but also evaluates them using content analysis.

However, in this present study, there were significant differences in the opposite direction for 5 five out of same 40 t-tests conducted by the original study, for the replication sample. Weak support for the relationship between approach-related emotions and passive CWB was found to be stronger than that between approach-related emotions and active CWB instead.

This lack of support was supported by the lack of significant results found in the 30 t-tests conducted comparing the significance in relationships between passive CWB and discrete emotions, versus active CWB and discrete emotions. However, this replication found weak support for the hypotheses in two out 30 t-test comparisons. 
Taking the difference in findings between the original and current replication into consideration, the results can be deemed as inconclusive. There is no significant difference from the original findings, and from the null.
This can be explained by the following reasons:
●	Some measurement tools differ from the original study.
●	Measurement tools were not situation specific as mentioned in original study as well
●	Cultural contexts and differences may have played a role in influencing individuals’ CWB and emotional experience

○	Different cultures value expression of emotions differently (Tsai, 2007)

title_r: Pre-peer review: Investigating information and skill transfer in neurodiverse groups using diffusion chain methodology: a replication study
abstract_r: Background: There have been many anecdotal reports that autistic people feel more comfortable and relaxed in autistic company. Our recent Diversity in Social Intelligence study examined this empirically, and found that an autism-specific environment facilitates learning and interaction for autistic people (Crompton et al., 2020). Our key findings indicate that (1) Autistic people transfer information with other autistic people as effectively as non-autistic people share information with one another; (2) information sharing breaks down when pairs are mis-matched: when one person is autistic and the other non-autistic, (3) feelings of rapport between people of the same neurotype accompany these info-sharing benefits; and (4) external observers can detect the lack of rapport apparent in mixed autistic / non-autistic interactions. These findings, for the first time, demonstrate that autistic people’s social behaviour includes effective communication (information, and skill sharing) and effective social interaction (positive rapport), which is in direct violation of the diagnostic criteria for autism. This represents the first empirical evidence that autistic people have their own repertoire social norms and cues, amounting to a uniquely autistic form of 'social intelligence'" This ground-breaking finding has profound implications for the characterisation of autism as a disorder, and practical implications for policy makers, practitioners, educators, clinicians and psychologists. However, pushing for dramatic changes in policy and practice would be premature without replication. This pre-registration is for a direct replication of the Diversity in Social Intelligence study in two parallel sites, from two continents, with both labs independent of the initial study. It will allow us to investigate whether these findings are replicated in independent samples. This rapid replication will allow us to explore this in a timely way and, if analogous results are found, make evidence-based recommendations to practitioners and policymakers. Replication Methodology: This replication study uses a diffusion chain methodology - a controlled, experimental form of the game "Telephone" - which has been effective in probing cultural learning between individuals in a social group (e.g. Flynn & Whiten, 2008; McGuigan & Graham, 2010). In this method, an experimenter models a complex behaviour to the first person in the chain. The person then has a chance to replicate the behaviour alone, before being paired with the next person in the chain and instructed to demonstrate the behaviour to them. Once more the second participant can practice the behaviour and then must pass it on to the next individual, and so on (see Figure 1). The diffusion chain methodology involves sequential pairs of participants completing the task, with two people in the lab at any one time, rather than a group task with all participants in the room. Tasks: We will replicate two of the diffusion chain tasks used in the original study: a storytelling task and a Rubik’s twist task. These tasks will provide raw data allowing us to operationalise the effectiveness of information transfer, and skill learning, between people. Measures: In addition, self-rated rapport will be measured after each diffusion chain interaction. We expect to find higher interactive rapport between two people of the same neurotype. Our hypothesis is that single neurotype chains (i.e. chains of all autistic people or chains of all non-autistic people) will result in more accurate and efficient transmission of information between people, and higher interactive rapport than mixed neurotype (i.e. mixed autistic-non-autistic) chains. Participants and conditions 216 participants (108 autistic and 108 non-autistic), matched for age and gender will be recruited and remunerated for their time. Participants will be allocated into one of three conditions: (1) Autistic: all participants are autistic (n = 72) (2) Non-autistic: all participants are non-autistic (n = 72) (3) Mixed: where half the participants are autistic, and half the participants are non-autistic (n = 72) For each of the three conditions, we will run twelve diffusion chains, each with six participants (n = 6 participants * n = 12 chains * n = 3 conditions = 216 participants). In the Mixed condition, participants will be arranged in an alternating order (autistic, non-autistic, autistic, etc.) so that each pair of people in the chain is “mis-matched” with a participant from the other diagnostic group. In the original study diffusion chains were eight participants long. Here we plan for chains of six people in length. The reason for this amendment is to maximise the value of the data collected, as explained below. Variations on the original study: In the original study we observed clear floor effects for participants in positions 7 and 8 in the chain (see Crompton, Ropar, Evans-Williams, Flynn & Fletcher-Watson, 2020). This occurred across all conditions and individual chains. In effect, by the time the information had been passed along six times, it was so degraded that participants had a minimal amount of information available to transfer. The mean difference in number of details recalled from the 1st to the 6th person in the chain was 21.56 (4.312 details per step) while the mean difference in number of details recalled from the 6th to the 8th person was 2.94 (1.47 details per step). On average the 6th person in the chain recalled 7.56 details while the 8th person in the chain recalled 4.61 details. Thus, we can clearly see how little information is available in the last part of a chain of 8 people. By reducing the number of participants in each diffusion chain to six, and increasing the number of diffusion chains, every participant will have a chance to provide meaningful data for analysis without floor effects. Having shorter chains will yield more powerful data (more chains, with the same number of participants), be more logistically achievable and cost-effective. The chains remain a direct replication of the data collected from the first six placed participants per chain, from the original study. Our research questions are: (1) Does performance on transmission tasks differ between autistic, non-autistic, and mixed conditions? (2) Does self-rated interactional rapport differ between autistic, non-autistic, and mixed conditions?

abstract_r:

item30: The original study did not report descriptive statistics needed for accurate power analysis. Based on the original study’s findings, β = -.19, b = -.32, SE b = .16, p = .043, we conducted a power analysis to confirm our required sample size.  Our replication of the original study’s simple linear regression in study 2 found that β = 0.003,  b = 0.004. SE b = 0.139, p = 0.976. The resultant regression equation was found to be insignificant and the estimations for the coefficients will thereby be inaccurate representations of the true effect. Pearson’s correlation was also low (r = .003, p = .976) and as such, we can conclude that was no significant linear relationship between maximising tendency and inaction inertia. Similar results were observed for the logistic regression, e^β = 1.05, p = .825. The lack of significance suggested that the effects were negligible when using maximising tendency to predict inaction inertia on the dichotomous item. Thus, since the measures for effect size in our regression (namely the Pearson’s correlation values and the coefficients) were insignificant, there was no linear relationship between maximising tendency and inaction inertia.

item31: Findings of regressing inaction inertia on maximising tendency did not reject the null hypothesis, R2=.000, F(1, 119) = .001, p > .05,  95% CI [-.270, .279]. 80% CI [-.175, .183].

item32: not significantly different from the original effect size

item33: informative failure to replicate

item34: Since we have defined a successful replication to be an exact or the closest possible replication of the original study, our replication could be judged to be a partial success. 
On one hand, by carrying out the replication study as close to the original as possible, the participants in our sample experienced the same intended stimulus as the participants in the US population of the original study. Recruited participants were all measured using the same scale (MTS) and judged on the same criteria as the original study. Besides, the instructions and procedure participants went through were similar to the original study. Ultimately, we created the closest replication possible such that the only differences were those that were impractical for researchers to control. Hence, the process of replicating the study was a success in following the original as closely as possible. 
On the other hand, our replication study faced informative limitations such as inadequate information given by the original authors, as well as practical limitations which can be attributed to the lack of resources such as providing remuneration. These limitations might have affected results and thus, we cannot judge our replication study to be a complete success. 

The failure of replication can be attributed partly to inadequate amount of information.   Lack of relevant details in the original paper, such as descriptive statistics, makes it difficult for present researchers to accurately estimate the required number of participants needed for a replication study with adequate power to sufficiently replicate the original effect. 

Furthermore, the time given to complete the replication study (10 weeks) was insufficient to gather a large enough sample size for the recommended power statistic of 1-β = .8. In addition, there were limitations in resources, unlike the original study whereby participants were paid. We were unable to provide monetary remuneration or any form of incentives to our participants for the completion of the survey materials. Hence, the lack of resources to incentivise might have caused the difference in results from the original study. This may be attributed to attentional differences since 128 responses were removed as a result of failing at least one manipulative or quality check, as compared to eight responses being excluded in the original study.

We judge this replication as inconclusive since the replication study will not find any statistically significantly results due to the limitations present. Hence, it might not be possible to conclude if maximizing tendency was related to inaction inertia in a job offer context, based on our study alone.

item37: One limitation was our sample population. We conducted the replication study in Singapore, whereby undergraduates were conveniently sampled on a university campus. This differed from the original study, where it was conducted in the United States using a participant pool from Amazon’s MTurk, a survey platform. Hence, our sample population was younger (M = 24.21, compared to M = 27.97 of the original sample), and they have fewer work experiences. As such, these undergraduates might possibly have a lower likelihood of experiencing inaction inertia as they seek work experiences and view the increase in salary as more attractive. Thus, the differences in sample populations might have caused bias in the measure of inaction inertia, hence influencing results. Besides, another limitation of our replication could be due to a small sample size of 121 participants, which reduced the possibility of detecting a significant effect because of a low statistical power. Furthermore, given that our sample participants were not incentivised to complete the survey, the lack of quality responses could have resulted in the differences in results observed. This was evidenced by the large quantity of participants that we had to exclude in our analysis compared to the original study. It was also possible that the recruited participants might not have a full understanding of the stimulus materials, which contributed to the lack of quality responses.

title_r: High Quality Direct Replications Matter: Response to Williams (2014)
abstract_r: We respond to Williams’ (2014) comments on our three failures to replicate of Study 2 fromWilliams and Bargh (2008). We clarify our conclusions on this topic, making clear that although the results of our studies cast doubt on the specific effect reported in Williams and Bargh (i.e., that instant hot and cold packs influence choice of reward for self or friend), a more complete understanding of the embodiment hypothesis in question requires consideration of relevant conceptual replications. Accordingly, we consider the strength of the evidence in the conceptual replications that Williams identifies and find that small samples appear to be the norm. We conclude that in order for researchers to move forward, future studies must take seriously issues of power, researcher degrees of freedom, and file drawer problems. Doing so will ensure that future studies are more informative tests of this hypothesis.

title_r: Replication study: The impact of cross-trial urgency on cognitive control
abstract_r: Previously it was shown that urgency enables stimulus-driven actions to bypass cognitive control in a specific time window. This was shown for eye movements (Salinas et al., 2019) as well as for manual responses (Poth, 2021). In these studies, the urgency was implemented by limiting the available time after a go-signal for executing a response to a target stimulus. Accordingly, the urgency was manipulated within one experimental trial. In this study, the previous paradigms are extended by now applying urgency over trials. Instead of limiting for responding within one trial, the available time for completing multiple trials is restricted. The participants have to perform a Spatial Stroop Task (see, Poth, 2021). Urgency is manipulated by asking the participants to complete either one (low urgency), two (mid urgency) or four trials (high urgency) within a time interval of nine seconds.

title_r: No Evidence for Unethical Amnesia for Imagined Actions: A Failed Replication and Extension
abstract_r: In a recent paper, Kouchaki and Gino (2016) suggest that memory for unethical actions is impaired, regardless of whether such actions are real or imagined. However, as we argue in the current paper, their claim that people develop “unethical amnesia” confuses two distinct and dissociable memory deficits: one affecting the phenomenology of remembering and another affecting memory accuracy. To further investigate whether unethical amnesia affects memory accuracy, we conducted three studies exploring unethical amnesia for imagined ethical violations. The first study (N = 228) attempts to directly replicate the only study from Kouchaki and Gino (2016) that includes a measure of memory accuracy. The second study (N = 232) attempts again to replicate these accuracy effects from Kouchaki and Gino (2016), while including several additional variables meant to potentially help in finding the effect. The third study (N = 228) is an attempted conceptual replication using the same paradigm as Kouchaki and Gino (2016), but with a new vignette describing a different moral violation. We did not find an unethical amnesia effect involving memory accuracy in any of our three studies. These results cast doubt upon the claim that memory accuracy is impaired for imagined unethical actions. Suggestions for further ways to study memory for moral and immoral actions are discussed.

title_r: Intuitive judgments in depression and the role of processing fluency and positive valence: A preregistered replication study
abstract_r: Background: Recent preliminary evidence indicates that depression is associated with impaired intuitive information processing. The current study aimed at replicating these findings and to move one step further by exploring whether factors known as triggering intuition (positivity, processing fluency) also affect intuition in patients with depression. Method: We pre-registered and tested five hypotheses using data from 35 patients with depression and 35 healthy controls who performed three versions of the Judgment of Semantic Coherence Task (JSCT, Bowers et al., 1990). This task operationalizes intuition as the inexplicable and sudden detection of semantic coherence. Results: Results revealed that depressed patients and healthy controls did not differ in their general intuitive performance (Hypothesis 1). We further found that fluency did not significantly affect depressed patients’ coherence judgments (H2a) and that the assumed effect of fluency on coherence judgments was not moderated by depression (H2b). Finally, we found that triads positive in valence were more likely to be judged as coherent as compared to negative word triads in the depressed sample (H3a), but this influence of positive (vs. negative) valence on coherence judgments did not significantly differ between the two groups (H3b). Conclusion: Overall the current study did not replicate findings from previous research regarding intuitive semantic coherence detection deficits in depression. However, our findings suggest that enhancing positivity in depressed patients may facilitate their ability to see meaning in their environment and to take intuitive decision.

title_r: Testing the Replicability of the Theory of Planned Behavior: A Large-Scale Multi-Sample Registered Replication Study
abstract_r: Identifying the determinants of social behavior, and the specific processes by which the determinants relate to behavior, are important in the development of theory to predict social behavior. Predicting behavior also has utility for organizations and stakeholders interested in developing effective interventions and strategies to promote behavior change. The theory of planned behavior (Ajzen, 1991) is a prominent social psychological theory developed to predict social behavior. The theory derives its assumptions from theories of attitude and social cognition (Albarracín & Johnson, 2019; Eagly & Chaiken, 1993; Fishbein, 1967), and focuses on predicting intentional behavior from sets of beliefs about future behavioral engagement. The theory has been tested in over 2000 studies, and over 30 meta-analytic syntheses. Cumulative findings indicate its efficacy in accounting for variance in behaviors across multiple domains. However, considerable unresolved heterogeneity in effects has been observed, which could be attributable to methodological artifacts or genuine variability across contexts, behaviors, and populations. In addition, some theory predictions, particularly interactions among constructs, have not been tested and replicated consistently. The current project will conduct a large-scale replication of the theory in general population and student samples adopting an identical protocol and measures. The result of the study will be a series of data sets testing theory predictions analyzed by meta-analytic structural equation modeling.

title_r: Acquiring the cardinal knowledge of number words: A conceptual replication
abstract_r: Understanding the way in which counting represent numerosities was shown to be a long-lasting process. As shown in the Give-a-number task, acquiring the meanings of verbal number words goes through successive developmental stages in which children first learn the cardinal meanings of small number words one at a time before generalizing the cardinal principle they have induced from the first three number words to all number words within their counting range. This acquisition would take about a year, and would be completed by the age of 3 ½ years. The aim of the present study was to provide a conceptual replication of the developmental sequence described in Wynn’s study nearly 30 years ago using the Give-a-number task. A first cross-sectional study was conducted on 213 Belgian children aged between 39 and 74 months using the Give-a-number task to examine the developmental pattern and the influence of age on this acquisition. The time span of acquisition was examined in a second study in which 34 children were tested five times every months between the age of 36 to 52 months. Results showed that acquiring the cardinal meanings of number words spread out over a protracted period, far more extended than assumed by Wynn. Furthermore, children do not generalize all-at-once to large number words, the cardinal knowledge they learned on small number words. Rather, number words were found to be learned one at a time in a really progressive manner. Results were discussed with regard to their implications for the existing theories and in relation with other tasks assessing the acquisition of verbal number symbols.

title_r: Merging Structural and Process-Related Approaches to the Study of Agreeableness: A Preregistered Replication and Extension
abstract_r: Agreeableness is one of the major domains included within prominent hierarchical models of personality like the Five-factor Model (FFM). (Low) agreeableness has shown to be the strongest correlate of a variety of antisocial behaviors relative to the other FFM domains. Though there is substantial evidence that (low) agreeableness is arguably the most important personality correlate of various antisocial behaviors, this evidence is descriptive and provides little information on the direction or processes underlying the relation. Process-related research has started to provide more insight into how agreeableness-related traits give rise to various antisocial and prosocial behaviors. The proposed study looks to first replicate previous research on some of the potential cognitive/emotional processes related to agreeableness, and then to conduct exploratory analyses to identify which, if any, of the empirically identified facets of agreeableness bear specific relations to the processes under study. Thus, the proposed project seeks to merge developments across important domains of personality research, structural research and process-based research, while also making use of open-science practices.

title_r: Re‑examining the effect of wage delegation : a replication study of Charness et al. (2012)
abstract_r: Experimental research has explored the effects of wage delegation on employee performance, with the pioneering attempt by (Charness et al., Am Econ Rev 102:2358–2379, 2012) in “The Hidden Advantage of Delegation: Pareto Improvements in a Gift Exchange Game”, published in the American Economic Review. We conducted a replication of their experiment for two main reasons: first, to validate the original findings that have influenced subsequent research, and second, to examine whether these results hold in contexts with reduced social proximity between workers and employers, a relevant issue due to the rise of remote work. Our online experiment, involving 410 participants, followed the original study’s design but used a different sample. We successfully replicated the main finding that wage delegation increases employee effort, though the effect was smaller and largely due to employees granting themselves higher wages. These results support the notion that with decreasing social proximity, formal controls increase in importance.

title_r: Model vs System Level Testing of Autonomous Driving Systems: A Replication and Extension Study
abstract_r: Offline model-level testing of autonomous driving software is much cheaper, faster, and diversified than in-field, online system-level testing. Hence, researchers have compared empirically model-level vs system-level testing using driving simulators. They reported the general usefulness of simulators at reproducing the same conditions experienced in-field, but also some inadequacy of model-level testing at exposing failures that are observable only in online mode. In this work, we replicate the reference study on model vs system-level testing of autonomous vehicles while acknowledging several assumptions that we had reconsidered. These assumptions are related to several threats to validity affecting the original study that motivated additional analysis and the development of techniques to mitigate them. Moreover, we also extend the replicated study by evaluating the original findings when considering a physical, radio-controlled autonomous vehicle. Our results show that simulator-based testing of autonomous driving systems yields predictions that are close to the ones of real-world datasets when using neural-based translation to mitigate the reality gap induced by the simulation platform. On the other hand, model-level testing failures are in line with those experienced at the system level, both in simulated and physical environments, when considering the pre-failure site, similar-looking images, and accurate labels.

title_r: A replication study of the association between the IL12B promoter allele CTCTAA and susceptibility to cerebral malaria in Thai population

title_r: Do Stereotypes Simplify Cognitive Processing? Examining The Cognitive Toolbox Through A Replication And Extension Of Macrae et al. (1994)
abstract_r: Stereotyping occurs in a wide variety of situations and can have severe and negative consequences. One potential explanation for the function of stereotypes offered by Macrae et al. (1994) is that they allow easier mental categorization of individuals and alleviate cognitive load. This can result in more attention for other tasks. In this thesis, I replicated Macrae et al.’s (1994) Study 1 using similar materials and procedures, while also addressing potential limitations to their research. Macrae et al. (1994) found that providing stereotype labels facilitated performance on a secondary task. In my replication study, I found no such facilitation effects. Further research needs to be done to fully understand the relationship between stereotyping and its potential to relieve cognitive load, but my study casts doubt on the reliability of Macrae et al.’s (1994) findings.

title_r: Giving and taking in dictator games – differences by gender? A replication study of Chowdhury et al. (Southern Economic Journal, 2017)
abstract_r: These data and code reproduce the results presented in the paper "Giving and taking in dictator games – differences by gender? A replication study of Chowdhury et al. (Southern Economic Journal, 2017)" by Korbinian von Blanckenburg, Eva Tebbe, and Anja Iseke, published in: Journal of Comments and Replications in Economics, Volume 2, 2023-1. Abstract: This study attempts to replicate experimental results from Chowdhury et al. published in Southern Economic Journal (2017). They study gender differences in the giving and taking variants of the dictator game. Using the same experimental design on a sample of German students our findings differ from Chowdhury et al. (2017). In contrast to the original study, we do not find support for an asymmetric gender effect. Our results indicate that, on average, both men and women allocate similar amounts in the giving and in the taking frame. Aditional analyses indicate that men are more likely than women to allocate nothing in the taking variant rather than in the giving variant, in line with Chowdhury et al. (2017).

title_r: Historical Communist Party Strength and Modern Party Loyalty. A Replication Study of Barceló (PNAS, 2021)
abstract_r: Replication data for “The Long-term Effects of War Exposure on Civic Engagement,” published September 2021, and “Corrections for Barceló, The Long-term Effects of War Exposure on Civic Engagement,” published online July 2023 and February 2024, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The corrections purport to address several issues in a 2021 publication, which we raised with both PNAS and the author. As we describe in our replication study, the corrections are themselves flawed and continue to lead to misleading findings. Barceló commits three major errors that render his research design inappropriate and his conclusions problematic. First, Barceló again commits a critical coding error that again leads him to attest incorrectly that he is clustering standard errors (SEs) at the provincial level, when in fact he is only using robust SEs, leading to false assertions of statistical significance and instrument strength. Second, Barceló miscodes his measure of South Vietnam. Third, Barceló overfits his model by including a linear transformation of his instrumental variable as a control. When these mistakes are addressed the provocative findings no longer hold.

title_r: A Conceptual replication of the differential price framing effect in the field
abstract_r: Across a series of 10 laboratory and online studies, Allard, Hardisty, and Griffin (2019) demonstrated an increased preference for premium, higher-priced products over standard products when consumers were presented with the additional cost of the higher-priced option (i.e., differential price framing; e.g., “for $20 more”) rather than with its total price (i.e., inclusive price framing; e.g., “for $60 total”); a phenomenon referred to as the differential price framing effect. In this paper, we conceptually replicate this effect in a field experiment that focuses on the application of a differential price framing strategy to a specific product format; namely, multipacks of identical products. Consistent with the differential price framing effect, the present study shows—based on 45,626 add-to-cart events and 30,426 completed product purchases on an online retailer’s website—that the choice shares of higher-priced options increase when a differential price framing strategy is used. However, compared to non-consequential add-to-cart activities, this bias is considerably less pronounced in actual purchase patterns.

title_r: A replication study of "Effects of Congruence and Preceding Trial Type on Stroop Test Reaction Times" by Hershman, Dadon, Kiesel & Henik
abstract_r: This Stroop study investigates whether cognitive conflicts, in particular task and information conflicts, also occur without a motor response and are reflected in pupil dilation and reaction times. The study is a partial replication of Hershman et al. (2023) and follows a within-subjects design with the factors reaction demand (response vs. rest) and stimulus congruence (congruent, neutral, incongruent). The dependent variables are reaction time (only in response trials) and pupil dilation (in all conditions). Based on the findings of the original study, we hypothesise that pupil dilation will be greater in incongruent conditions, and that reaction time differences between congruent and neutral stimuli will be minimal. The planned sample size is n = 36 (determined via power analysis). Stimulus order and key assignment will be randomised. Data will be analysed using repeated-measures ANOVA and supplemented by Bayesian RM ANOVAs. A significance level of p < .05 will be applied, and Bayes factors will be interpreted using standard thresholds.

title_r: Social Comparision and Self-Construal: A replication study
abstract_r: Does self-construal have an influence on the consequences of social comparison (as in Gardner et al. 2002)? Gardner et al. (2002, study 2) found in group to self comparisons interdependent self-construal was a factor that influences the consequences of social comparison. Participants were primed with interdependent or independent self-construal and then asked to judge the life-satisfaction of people based on yearbook pictures. Participants either got the feedback, that they outperformed their group in this “intuition”-task, but the group was doing badly, or they underperformed their group, but the group did well. The dependent variable was positive affect. Women in the independent prime condition showed a strong positive affective reaction, when outperforming the group, but negative affective reactions when underperforming the group, with the interdependent prime condition this pattern disappeared. For men there was no such interaction found. We will directly replicate this finding, only adding one variable in the beginning of the study: Gardner et al. (2002) explained the gender differences, with men and women having a different chronic self-construal. We will not merely assume these gender differences in chronic self-construal but measure it directly and look at its influence. The present research question is if self-construal (primed and chronic) influences the consequences of social comparison on affect (as in Gardner et al. 2002).

title_r: Evaluating the Family Stress Model in a sample of families of children with intellectual disabilities: A replication study
abstract_r: In broader, non-disability research, early-childhood poverty has been well recognised as a predictor of many negative outcomes across childhood such as poorer mental health and more internalising and externalising behaviour problems (Flouri, Midouhas & Joshi, 2014; Reiss, 2013). Additionally, the negative impact of childhood poverty expands across the life course, predicting later life outcomes such as adult attainment (Duncan, Ziol-Guest & Kalil, 2010). In many research studies, the Family Stress Model (FSM; Conger & Conger, 2002) has been used as a framework to explain the association between family poverty and child behavioural outcomes, proposing that family poverty influences parental outcomes which in turn affect the child (Gard et al., 2020). According to the FSM, the pressures that transpire from family poverty contribute to parental psychological distress, resulting in compromised family processes including harsher parenting strategies and poorer quality of family relationships. These compromised family processes then lead to poorer child development outcomes including potentially more internalising and externalising behaviours (Conger, Conger & Martin, 2010; Masarik & Conger, 2017). Using longitudinal data from families of non-disabled children, Neppl, Senia and Donnellan (2016) tested the FSM, evaluating the associations between maternal distress, parenting practices and child externalising behaviour problems. The findings were consistent with the FSM, determining that family poverty led to pressure experienced by the parents which in turn was associated with parental conflict and parental distress. The conflict experienced in the parent relationship was associated with harsh parenting and children’s behaviour problems. Intellectual disability research has established that children with intellectual disabilities are more likely to present with behaviour and emotional problems than non-disabled children (Emerson & Hatton, 2007). However, the difference in behaviour problems displayed by children with intellectual disabilities and non-disabled children can be largely explained by higher levels of family poverty (Emerson & Einfeld, 2010; Emerson & Hatton, 2007). According to Emerson et al. (2010) families of children with intellectual disabilities are more likely to experience poverty than parents of non-disabled children. Additionally, parents of children with intellectual disabilities are more likely to experience psychological distress (Totsika et al., 2011), and this is associated with their child exhibiting more behaviour problems (Hastings et al., 2006; Lecavalier et al., 2006; Neece, Green & Baker, 2012), and whether the family experience poverty (Emerson et al., 2010). Research has also explored parenting attitudes or the child-parent relationship as a predictor of later behaviour problems in children with intellectual disabilities. A more positive child-parent relationship predicts less behaviour problems exhibited by the child with intellectual disability (Norona & Baker, 2017; Totsika et al., 2014). Additionally, interventions that aim to reduce inconsistent and harsh parenting practices result in short-term improvements in the behaviour problems of children with intellectual disabilities (McIntyre, 2013; Petrenko, 2013; Tellegen & Sanders, 2013). Currently, research examining the FSM has maintained a focus on families of non-disabled children. However, as a developmental theory, FSM should be able to explain the impact of early adversity on child developmental outcomes in a variety of populations, such as in families of children with intellectual disabilities. Additionally, as intellectual disability research has supported the key risk factors in FSM as predicting children’s behaviour problems, FSM may represent a mechanism that explains how these risk factors interact with the relationship between family poverty and children’s behaviour problems in families of children with intellectual disability. We found one research study which evaluated the applicability of the FSM to explain the development of behaviour problems of children with intellectual disability. Using longitudinal data, Totsika et al. (2020) found evidence for a significant developmental pathway from early-childhood family poverty, through parental mental health, and adversarial parenting to the behavioural and emotional problems of children with intellectual disabilities. This study aims to replicate research from Totsika et al. (2020), evaluating the application of the FSM in families of children with intellectual disabilities. Therefore, we will examine the four-step theory of the FSM, testing the developmental pathway from childhood family poverty, through parental mental health, and child-parent relationship quality/ parenting practices to the developmental outcomes of children with intellectual disability. Additionally, we will also examine the children’s prosocial behaviours as an outcome, as previous research has shown that higher levels of maternal psychological distress are associated with fewer prosocial behaviours exhibited by the child with intellectual disability (Williams, Bailey & Hastings, 2022).

title_r: Enhancing sensorimotor adaptation of speech using tDCS over motor cortex and cerebellum: a replication study
abstract_r: Sensorimotor adaptation of speech plays an essential role in speech production. Specifically, speech processing relies on a dynamic interaction between the auditory and motor systems of the brain. Previous studies have indicated that the primary motor cortex (M1) and the cerebellum contribute to speech-motor adaptation. Anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) was used to increase excitability over the left M1 and the right cerebellum during a speech adaptation task in which participants compensated for a shift in the formant frequency fed back to them in real-time by altering the frequency in their speech production (Lametti, Smith, Freidin, et al., 2018). Stimulation over the left M1 drove participants to compensate for the shift in the first formant by adapting both the first and the second formant in their production, thereby producing speech closer to an existing vowel category. The shifts produced in both formants exceeded those produced by participants who received only sham stimulation. In contrast, anodal tDCS over the right cerebellum drove significantly greater adaptation in the first formant, but the second formant was unchanged. Here, we aim to replicate these findings. We will use software to provide the formant shift rather than the hardware setup used previously. We will also use a different location for the cathode electrode placement in the cerebellar stimulation since attaching it to the face may have impeded speech production in the original study. title_r: Disgust and the rubber hand illusion: A registered replication report of Jalal, Krishnakumar, and Ramachandran (2015)
abstract_r: Heightened experience of disgust is a feature of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), particularly in contamination-related OCD (C-OCD). Previous studies of the rubber hand illusion (RHI) reported that the sense of body ownership is related to the interaction between vision, touch, and proprioception. A recent study demonstrated a link between the RHI and disgust, reporting an interaction between these three perceptual modalities and disgust (Jalal, Krishnakumar, Ramachandran, 2015). However, there have been no direct replications of this initial study. We proposed a direct replication of Jalal et al.’s (2015) study. Based on a power analysis, we examined a minimum of 119 participants to determine whether placing contamination-related stimuli on a rubber hand causes OCD-like disgust among healthy participants while experiencing the RHI. In addition, we tested the cross-cultural validity of the previous findings, testing whether Japanese participants experience more intense disgust when a rubber hand and a participant’s hidden hand were stroked synchronously, compared with asynchronous stroking. This replication provides insight into potential applications of this study protocol in the treatment of OCD.

Study Title: Do Expectations and Perceptions of Personality Trait Change in College Students Match Reality?  

Authors: Andrew Rakhshani, Brent Donnellan, Richard Lucas, Courtney Brecheen, & Robert Ackerman

Description: 
	This study aims to conceptually replicate two studies (Herbst, McCrae, Costa, Feaganes, & Siegler, 2000; Robins, Noftle, Trzesniewski, & Roberts, 2005) that compared perceived versus actual personality change and extend these works by also evaluating anticipatory personality change. We will conduct secondary analyses on a large, longitudinal dataset of a student cohort followed across four years of college. We intend to emulate the analyses described in each of the target studies and conduct additional analyses relating to anticipated personality change.
	Herbst and colleagues (2000) sought to determine whether self-reported perceived change in personality was associated with actual changes based on 6 to 9-year follow-up data of middle-aged adults. Participants completed the 240-item NEO-PI-R at baseline and again at follow-up. At follow-up participants were also asked to report on how they had changed since their intake using two measures of change. The first was a single item measure reflecting three perceived change groups (i.e., changed a good deal, changed little, or stayed pretty much the same). The second asked whether participants increased, decreased, or stayed the same on each of the Big 5 dimensions (e.g., Extraversion: “compared to how you were six years ago, how lively, cheerful, and sociable are you now?”). Analyses and results were presented as follows: 
(1) frequencies of perceived change groups (52% stayed the same, 39% changed a little, 9% changed a good deal); 
(2) chi-square test of perceived change groups by gender (men: 54% stayed the same, 38% changed a little, 8% changed a good deal; women: 48% stayed the same, 41% changed a little, 11% changed a good deal; slightly more women reported change 2(2, N = 2,241) = 7.7, p = .02);
(3) compared stability coefficients across perceived change groups by Big 5 factor (see table below); 
 
(4) compared profile stability coefficients across perceived change groups (see table above); 
(5) compared baseline and post (respectively) factor and facet (cannot replicate) scores across perceived change groups (specific effect sizes were not reported; Respondents who felt they had changed a good deal scored significantly higher in Neuroticism and Openness and lower on Agreeableness than the other two groups on both administrations); 
(6) frequencies of perceived factor-level change (see note in table below); 
 
(7) compared mean level change from baseline to follow-up by direction of perceived change (the factor level perceived change measure) using repeated measures ANOVAs with Scheffe post hoc tests (these effect sizes were reported as partial eta squared for Time by perceived change group interaction; see table above); 
(8) correlation of perceived change by domain and residual gain score (“the raw change score corrected for initial level”) for the same domain (All five correlations were positive and significant, ranging in magnitude of .10 for Agreeableness to .24 for Neuroticism; On average, perceptions of change accounted for less than 3% of the variance in measured change); and 
(9) percentage of discordance of perceived change group and actual change (Same group had significant declines in all but Agreeableness; More group increased only in Neuroticism and Agreeableness; Less group showed significant declines in all but A; 80% of the comparisons are discordant for the self-perceived Same group, 60% for the More group, 20% for the Less group).
	
Robins and colleagues (2005) sought to determine (1) the extent and in what ways young adults think their personality changes and (2) how much perceived change was associated with actual change. Their study included a third purpose involving a host of additional measures that our dataset does not include so everything to follow will reflect the two parts we can replicate. They followed a group of 295 young adults for six waves across four years of college. Participants completed the 60-item NEO-FFI during the first week of college and again at the end of the fourth year. At the end of the fourth year, participants were also asked to indicate how they had changed (1 = decreased to 5 = increased) since entering college using a single item for each Big 5 factor. To assess actual personality change, they regressed each year four factor score on the corresponding week one factor score and saved the standardized residuals. Relevant analyses were presented as follows: 
(10) frequencies of perceived change grouped by decreased, stayed the same, and increased for each Big 5 factor (Almost everyone (98%) believed that they had changed on at least one factor; see table below); 
(11) actual mean-level personality change reported as Cohen’s d (see table below); 

 
(12) correlations between perceived and actual change by Big 5 factor (see table below); and 
 
(13) footnote noting comparisons of the intercorrelations among perceived changes and the intercorrelations among actual changes (In general, the pattern of intercorrelations was highly similar for perceived and actual change. In both cases, all of the intercorrelations were positive, except that change in Neuroticism was negatively correlated with change in each of the other four dimensions. The few discrepancies involved differences in magnitude rather than direction. For example, actual change in Conscientiousness correlated .25 with actual change in Extraversion, whereas perceived changes in these two variables did not correlate significantly (r = .10; ns). 

Replication:
We will replicate the exact analyses outlined and numbered above. There are a couple instances where the exact type of analyses is unclear. Specifically, for (3 and 5), it is unclear whether the authors conducted a t-test or ANOVA with contrasts; for (12), it is unclear which operationalization of perceived change grouping the authors used (three vs five groups). For these, we will use a t-test and both the group operationalizations, respectively. Results from the present study will be evaluated against those reported in the two target studies; conclusions will be based on the relative similarity of significance, direction, and magnitude of effect sizes reported across the studies.

Extension:
	In addition to the replications, we hope to extend this work by evaluating additional research questions and using more robust statistical models. First, we are interested in determining the extent to which young adults think their broad personality or individual Big 5 traits will change and whether this anticipatory change is associated with actual change. We will mirror all analyses note above by replacing perceived change with anticipatory change. Consistent with the “End of History Illusion” (Quoidbach, Gilbert, & Wilson, 2013) and self-enhancement literature, we hypothesize that participants will anticipate positive personality change. 
	Second, we are interested in determining whether optimism is associated with anticipatory personality change and/or actual personality change. Consistent with self-enhancement literature, we hypothesize that participants with greater optimism will anticipate greater positive personality change. 

 

	Third, we will analyze the above research questions (i.e., is perceived change associated with actual change; are optimism and anticipatory change associated with actual change) using latent growth curve models since we have eight measures of personality whereas both original studies only had two measures of personality, respectively. This procedure will provide a more reliable estimate of personality change. We will conduct these analyses in a structural equation modeling framework using the R package “lavaan.” We will test for measurement invariance using criteria recommended by Little (2013): change in CFI by .01; if scale invariance is not satisfied due to problems with 25% or fewer items, we will identify the one or two items to drop to achieve scale invariance; if there are more than two item, we attempt second order growth models or abandon this test. Else, models will first be run with freely estimated parameters such that the path estimate for the personality change slope at time one will be fixed to zero, time eight will be fixed to one, and paths in-between will be free to vary. Subsequent models will add constraints to test for linear and non-linear effects. We will set time zero to the midpoint of the study if we encounter strong correlations between the latent intercepts and slopes. If results do not change across models, conclusions will be made from the most parsimonious model; if results do change, a chi-square difference statistic will determine which model to base conclusions from. 

Known differences from original studies: Herbst and colleagues (2000) used the NEO-PI-R whereas we will be using the BFI; however, these two measures have factor convergences ranging from .71 to .84 without correcting for attenuation (Reynolds & Clark, 2001). The study duration (theirs: 6 to 9 years versus ours: 4 years) and sample descriptives (theirs: middle-aged college alumni versus ours: current college students) will differ between studies. 

Robins and colleagues (2005) used the 60-item NEO-FFI whereas we will be using the BFI; however, these two measures have mean factor convergence of .73 without correcting for attenuation (John & Srivastava, 1999). When the study took place (theirs: 1990s vs ours: 2010s) and sample descriptives (students from theirs: UC-B vs ours: UT-D).

Both of these studies used a subset of data from a parent study, both of which differed in the sort of variables collected from our parent study.

Name or brief description of dataset: The present study uses a subset of data collected from the “College Life Study.” The parent study was designed as a longitudinal study of college student adjustment and development.

Is this data open or publicly available? The variables used in these analyses will be posted when the paper is submitted.

How can the data be accessed? Robert Ackerman and Courtney Brecheen collected these data.

Date of download or access: Andrew Rakhshani and Richard Lucas will access these data after submission of this registration.

Is a codebook available? Packets of questionnaires and data keys are available upon request. 

How was data collected? 
Donnellan, Ackerman, & Brecheen, 2016: Data for this study come from an ongoing longitudinal study of college students at a public university in the Southwestern United States. Participants were initially recruited for the study toward the end of their first semester in their first-year orientation classes. Data for the current report were drawn from 1,158 total responses from college students ages 18 or older at the first wave of the study. Responses from 27 participants were discarded because they failed to answer affirmatively to a question “I answered all of these questions honestly” (25 responded “no” and 2 were missing responses). An additional 4 participants were discarded because they failed to answer any of the RSES items. Thus, the final sample size was 1,127 (55% men). Participants self-identified as Asian (38%), Anglo (39%), Hispanic (15%), African American (3%), or other or unknown (5%). The average age of the sample was 18.31 years (SD = 1.56, minimum = 18, maximum = 52, median = 18, mode = 18).

Have any of the authors worked with this dataset? 
Brent Donnellan, Courtney Brecheen, & Robert Ackerman: Have published from the first wave of this study (Donnellan, Ackerman, & Brecheen, 2016) and that study used the Big Five as criterion variables. Brent helped select measures for the study when it was being designed by Robert Ackerman with Courtney Brecheen. However, this registration and subsequent analyses will be completed by Richard Lucas and Andrew Rakhshani.
	Richard Lucas: No
	Andrew Rakhshani: No

	Brent Donnellan, Courtney Brecheen, & Robert Ackerman: Aware of the internal 
consistency estimates and stability coefficients for the Big Five domains. Aware of the distributions for the anticipated change items at Wave 1 and the perceived change items at the last wave. These have not been discussed with Andrew; these were discussed with Rich a long time ago, but he “does not recall this at all.” 
	Richard Lucas:  Reviewed the Time 1 and Time 8 questionnaire packets.
	Andrew Rakhshani: Reviewed the Time 1 and Time 8 questionnaire packets.

Sample size / Power analyses:
What is the sample size (to the best of your knowledge)? Number of complete BFIs:
	Time 1: 1267		Time 2: 361		Time 3: 450		Time 4: 277
	Time 5: 330		Time 6: 334		Time 7: 302		Time 8: 253
For the Robins et al. (2005) replication, we will only include participants that were 18 or 19 years old at wave one. This will remove very few participants so the above sample sizes should not change much.
How much power will the analyses have?
The research questions central to this project will focus on correlations. Using recommendations from Funder & Ozer (2019) for interpreting magnitude of correlations (.10 = small, .20 = medium, .30 = large), power was calculated for minimum (N = 253) and maximum (N = 1267) possible sample sizes at alpha = .005 (two-tailed). 
Power to detect r = .10 with N = 253 is .111
Power to detect r = .20 with N = 253 is .656
Power to detect r = .30 with N = 253 is .982
Power to detect r = .10 with N = 1267 is .777

Missing data:
What do you know about missing data in the data set already (e.g., overall missingness rate, information about differential dropout)?  
Nothing besides the sample sizes for the Big Five measures reported above.

The authors of this registration (Andrew and Rich) did not have access / exposure to the data. Brent had worked with this data but was not involved with this registration beyond providing information about the study description and sample sizes at each wave.

Inference criteria:
What criteria will you use to make inferences? Please describe the information you’ll use (e.g. specify the p-values, effect sizes, confidence intervals, Bayes factors, specific model fit indices), as well as cut-off criterion, where appropriate. We will use two-tailed tests with an alpha level of .005. With respect to replication analyses, findings that correspond in direction and significance to be considered replicable. We will qualify these conclusions based on the statistical power of each analysis.

The replication of previous studies is a robustness check. In situations in which research questions can be answered both by the original replication analyses and latent growth curve modeling, we will rely on the most parsimonious latent growth curve model to make conclusions. 
Sensitivity analyses will be completed to see if dropping non-18 or 19-year-olds for the Robins et al. (2005) replications produced different conclusions.

If the latent growth curve models do not run, the original replication analyses will be used to make conclusions. 

Exploratory analyses:

We will emulate the latent growth curve model depicted above except we will replace anticipatory change with perceived change in order to explore the relationships among perceived change, optimism, and actual change.

Study Title: Do Expectations and Perceptions of Personality Trait Change in College Students Match Reality?  

Authors: Andrew Rakhshani, Brent Donnellan, Richard Lucas, Courtney Brecheen, & Robert Ackerman

Description: 
	This study aims to conceptually replicate two studies (Herbst, McCrae, Costa, Feaganes, & Siegler, 2000; Robins, Noftle, Trzesniewski, & Roberts, 2005) that compared perceived versus actual personality change and extend these works by also evaluating anticipatory personality change. We will conduct secondary analyses on a large, longitudinal dataset of a student cohort followed across four years of college. We intend to emulate the analyses described in each of the target studies and conduct additional analyses relating to anticipated personality change.
	Herbst and colleagues (2000) sought to determine whether self-reported perceived change in personality was associated with actual changes based on 6 to 9-year follow-up data of middle-aged adults. Participants completed the 240-item NEO-PI-R at baseline and again at follow-up. At follow-up participants were also asked to report on how they had changed since their intake using two measures of change. The first was a single item measure reflecting three perceived change groups (i.e., changed a good deal, changed little, or stayed pretty much the same). The second asked whether participants increased, decreased, or stayed the same on each of the Big 5 dimensions (e.g., Extraversion: “compared to how you were six years ago, how lively, cheerful, and sociable are you now?”). Analyses and results were presented as follows: 
(1) frequencies of perceived change groups (52% stayed the same, 39% changed a little, 9% changed a good deal); 
(2) chi-square test of perceived change groups by gender (men: 54% stayed the same, 38% changed a little, 8% changed a good deal; women: 48% stayed the same, 41% changed a little, 11% changed a good deal; slightly more women reported change 2(2, N = 2,241) = 7.7, p = .02);
(3) compared stability coefficients across perceived change groups by Big 5 factor (see table below); 
 
(4) compared profile stability coefficients across perceived change groups (see table above); 
(5) compared baseline and post (respectively) factor and facet (cannot replicate) scores across perceived change groups (specific effect sizes were not reported; Respondents who felt they had changed a good deal scored significantly higher in Neuroticism and Openness and lower on Agreeableness than the other two groups on both administrations); 
(6) frequencies of perceived factor-level change (see note in table below); 
 
(7) compared mean level change from baseline to follow-up by direction of perceived change (the factor level perceived change measure) using repeated measures ANOVAs with Scheffe post hoc tests (these effect sizes were reported as partial eta squared for Time by perceived change group interaction; see table above); 
(8) correlation of perceived change by domain and residual gain score (“the raw change score corrected for initial level”) for the same domain (All five correlations were positive and significant, ranging in magnitude of .10 for Agreeableness to .24 for Neuroticism; On average, perceptions of change accounted for less than 3% of the variance in measured change); and 
(9) percentage of discordance of perceived change group and actual change (Same group had significant declines in all but Agreeableness; More group increased only in Neuroticism and Agreeableness; Less group showed significant declines in all but A; 80% of the comparisons are discordant for the self-perceived Same group, 60% for the More group, 20% for the Less group).
	
Robins and colleagues (2005) sought to determine (1) the extent and in what ways young adults think their personality changes and (2) how much perceived change was associated with actual change. Their study included a third purpose involving a host of additional measures that our dataset does not include so everything to follow will reflect the two parts we can replicate. They followed a group of 295 young adults for six waves across four years of college. Participants completed the 60-item NEO-FFI during the first week of college and again at the end of the fourth year. At the end of the fourth year, participants were also asked to indicate how they had changed (1 = decreased to 5 = increased) since entering college using a single item for each Big 5 factor. To assess actual personality change, they regressed each year four factor score on the corresponding week one factor score and saved the standardized residuals. Relevant analyses were presented as follows: 
(10) frequencies of perceived change grouped by decreased, stayed the same, and increased for each Big 5 factor (Almost everyone (98%) believed that they had changed on at least one factor; see table below); 
(11) actual mean-level personality change reported as Cohen’s d (see table below); 

 
(12) correlations between perceived and actual change by Big 5 factor (see table below); and 
 
(13) footnote noting comparisons of the intercorrelations among perceived changes and the intercorrelations among actual changes (In general, the pattern of intercorrelations was highly similar for perceived and actual change. In both cases, all of the intercorrelations were positive, except that change in Neuroticism was negatively correlated with change in each of the other four dimensions. The few discrepancies involved differences in magnitude rather than direction. For example, actual change in Conscientiousness correlated .25 with actual change in Extraversion, whereas perceived changes in these two variables did not correlate significantly (r = .10; ns). 

Replication:
We will replicate the exact analyses outlined and numbered above. There are a couple instances where the exact type of analyses is unclear. Specifically, for (3 and 5), it is unclear whether the authors conducted a t-test or ANOVA with contrasts; for (12), it is unclear which operationalization of perceived change grouping the authors used (three vs five groups). For these, we will use a t-test and both the group operationalizations, respectively. Results from the present study will be evaluated against those reported in the two target studies; conclusions will be based on the relative similarity of significance, direction, and magnitude of effect sizes reported across the studies.

Extension:
	In addition to the replications, we hope to extend this work by evaluating additional research questions and using more robust statistical models. First, we are interested in determining the extent to which young adults think their broad personality or individual Big 5 traits will change and whether this anticipatory change is associated with actual change. We will mirror all analyses note above by replacing perceived change with anticipatory change. Consistent with the “End of History Illusion” (Quoidbach, Gilbert, & Wilson, 2013) and self-enhancement literature, we hypothesize that participants will anticipate positive personality change. 
	Second, we are interested in determining whether optimism is associated with anticipatory personality change and/or actual personality change. Consistent with self-enhancement literature, we hypothesize that participants with greater optimism will anticipate greater positive personality change. 

 

	Third, we will analyze the above research questions (i.e., is perceived change associated with actual change; are optimism and anticipatory change associated with actual change) using latent growth curve models since we have eight measures of personality whereas both original studies only had two measures of personality, respectively. This procedure will provide a more reliable estimate of personality change. We will conduct these analyses in a structural equation modeling framework using the R package “lavaan.” We will test for measurement invariance using criteria recommended by Little (2013): change in CFI by .01; if scale invariance is not satisfied due to problems with 25% or fewer items, we will identify the one or two items to drop to achieve scale invariance; if there are more than two item, we attempt second order growth models or abandon this test. Else, models will first be run with freely estimated parameters such that the path estimate for the personality change slope at time one will be fixed to zero, time eight will be fixed to one, and paths in-between will be free to vary. Subsequent models will add constraints to test for linear and non-linear effects. We will set time zero to the midpoint of the study if we encounter strong correlations between the latent intercepts and slopes. If results do not change across models, conclusions will be made from the most parsimonious model; if results do change, a chi-square difference statistic will determine which model to base conclusions from. 

Known differences from original studies: Herbst and colleagues (2000) used the NEO-PI-R whereas we will be using the BFI; however, these two measures have factor convergences ranging from .71 to .84 without correcting for attenuation (Reynolds & Clark, 2001). The study duration (theirs: 6 to 9 years versus ours: 4 years) and sample descriptives (theirs: middle-aged college alumni versus ours: current college students) will differ between studies. 

Robins and colleagues (2005) used the 60-item NEO-FFI whereas we will be using the BFI; however, these two measures have mean factor convergence of .73 without correcting for attenuation (John & Srivastava, 1999). When the study took place (theirs: 1990s vs ours: 2010s) and sample descriptives (students from theirs: UC-B vs ours: UT-D).

Both of these studies used a subset of data from a parent study, both of which differed in the sort of variables collected from our parent study.

Name or brief description of dataset: The present study uses a subset of data collected from the “College Life Study.” The parent study was designed as a longitudinal study of college student adjustment and development.

Is this data open or publicly available? The variables used in these analyses will be posted when the paper is submitted.

How can the data be accessed? Robert Ackerman and Courtney Brecheen collected these data.

Date of download or access: Andrew Rakhshani and Richard Lucas will access these data after submission of this registration.

Is a codebook available? Packets of questionnaires and data keys are available upon request. 

How was data collected? 
Donnellan, Ackerman, & Brecheen, 2016: Data for this study come from an ongoing longitudinal study of college students at a public university in the Southwestern United States. Participants were initially recruited for the study toward the end of their first semester in their first-year orientation classes. Data for the current report were drawn from 1,158 total responses from college students ages 18 or older at the first wave of the study. Responses from 27 participants were discarded because they failed to answer affirmatively to a question “I answered all of these questions honestly” (25 responded “no” and 2 were missing responses). An additional 4 participants were discarded because they failed to answer any of the RSES items. Thus, the final sample size was 1,127 (55% men). Participants self-identified as Asian (38%), Anglo (39%), Hispanic (15%), African American (3%), or other or unknown (5%). The average age of the sample was 18.31 years (SD = 1.56, minimum = 18, maximum = 52, median = 18, mode = 18).

Have any of the authors worked with this dataset? 
Brent Donnellan, Courtney Brecheen, & Robert Ackerman: Have published from the first wave of this study (Donnellan, Ackerman, & Brecheen, 2016) and that study used the Big Five as criterion variables. Brent helped select measures for the study when it was being designed by Robert Ackerman with Courtney Brecheen. However, this registration and subsequent analyses will be completed by Richard Lucas and Andrew Rakhshani.
	Richard Lucas: No

consistency estimates and stability coefficients for the Big Five domains. Aware of the distributions for the anticipated change items at Wave 1 and the perceived change items at the last wave. These have not been discussed with Andrew; these were discussed with Rich a long time ago, but he “does not recall this at all.”
