Sample size / Power analyses:
What is the sample size (to the best of your knowledge)? Number of complete BFIs:
	Time 1: 1267		Time 2: 361		Time 3: 450		Time 4: 277
	Time 5: 330		Time 6: 334		Time 7: 302		Time 8: 253
For the Robins et al. (2005) replication, we will only include participants that were 18 or 19 years old at wave one. This will remove very few participants so the above sample sizes should not change much.
How much power will the analyses have?
The research questions central to this project will focus on correlations. Using recommendations from Funder & Ozer (2019) for interpreting magnitude of correlations (.10 = small, .20 = medium, .30 = large), power was calculated for minimum (N = 253) and maximum (N = 1267) possible sample sizes at alpha = .005 (two-tailed). 
Power to detect r = .10 with N = 253 is .111
Power to detect r = .20 with N = 253 is .656
Power to detect r = .30 with N = 253 is .982
Power to detect r = .10 with N = 1267 is .777
Power to detect r = .20 with N = 1267 is 1.000
Power to detect r = .30 with N = 1267 is 1.000
			
Missing data:
What do you know about missing data in the data set already (e.g., overall missingness rate, information about differential dropout)?  
Nothing besides the sample sizes for the Big Five measures reported above.

Describe the moment of preregistration: 
The authors of this registration (Andrew and Rich) did not have access / exposure to the data. Brent had worked with this data but was not involved with this registration beyond providing information about the study description and sample sizes at each wave.

Identify the variables you plan to use:
BFI (44-item; John & Srivastava, 1999)
Please indicate the extent to which you agree with the following statements. (1 = disagree strongly; 5 = strongly agree)
General predictions for personality change (adapted from Costa & McCrae, 1989)
~Please forecast how you think your personality will change over the next four years. Consider your basic feelings, attitudes, and ways of relating to people – your whole personality. Overall, which statement describes how your personality will change between now and Spring 2016. My personality…
~Think back over the last four years to the way when you first entered college in Fall 2012. Consider your basic feelings, attitudes, and ways of relating to people – your whole personality. Overall, which statement describes how your personality has changed between Fall 2012 and now. My personality…
A.	will change a good deal.
B.	will change a little.
C.	will stay pretty much the same.
Specific prediction for personality change (adapted from Robins et al., 2005)
~Now, think forward to how specific aspects of your personality will change. Please report to what extent you feel your personality will change for each trait listed below between now and Spring 2016. Please use the following scale to describe how your personality will change for each trait:
~Now, think back to how specific aspects of your personality have changed since Fall 2012. Please report to what extent you feel your personality has changed for each trait listed below since Fall 2012. Please use the following scale to describe how your personality will change for each trait:
		1 = will decrease
		2 = will decrease slightly
		3 = will stay the same
		4 = will increase slightly
		5 = will increase
		Extraverted (i.e., talkative, outgoing, enthusiastic)
		Agreeable (i.e., considerate, cooperative, trusting)
		Conscientious (i.e., organized, task-oriented, careful)
		Neurotic (i.e., tense, anxious, easily upset)
		Open to experience (i.e., imaginative, creative, enjoys thinking)
Optimism (6-item Life Orientation Test; Scheier, Carver, & Bridges, 1994)
Please indicate the extent to which you agree with the following statements. (1 = disagree strongly; 5 = strongly agree)

How will variables be aggregated? Mean scores will be calculated for each Big 5 trait for each person if they have completed 80% of the items for that factor. Optimism is calculated by a sum score of its items. 

Describe variable transformations if applicable: The Life Orientation Test originally uses a 0-4 response scale for each item whereas ours used a 1-5; these items will be recoded to reflect the original questionnaire. 
For one analysis (12), it is unclear which operationalization of perceived change grouping the authors used (three vs five groups). Since we will use both group operationalizations, the three group will require transformation. 

Describe data inclusion / exclusion: Participants that reported “no” to the validity check item (Did you answer these questions honestly?) will not be included in analyses.

Describe outlier procedures: We will not exclude outliers in the present study.

Statistical models: Included above.

Follow-up analyses: None.
	
Inference criteria:
What criteria will you use to make inferences? Please describe the information you’ll use (e.g. specify the p-values, effect sizes, confidence intervals, Bayes factors, specific model fit indices), as well as cut-off criterion, where appropriate. Will you be using one or two tailed tests for each of your analyses? If you are comparing multiple conditions or testing multiple hypotheses, will you account for this?
We will use two-tailed tests with an alpha level of .005. With respect to replication analyses, findings that correspond in direction and significance to be considered replicable. We will qualify these conclusions based on the statistical power of each analysis.

Sensitivity analyses:
Provide a series of decisions about evaluating the strength, reliability, or robustness of your focal hypothesis test. This may include additional control variables, cross-validation efforts (out-of-sample replication, spilt/hold-out sample), any machine learning application/analyses, applying weights, selectively applying constraints in an SEM context (e.g., comparing model fit statistics), any alpha or multiple comparison adjustments, overfitting adjustment techniques used (e.g., regularization approaches such as ridge regression), or some other simulation / sampling / bootstrapping.
The replication of previous studies is a robustness check. In situations in which research questions can be answered both by the original replication analyses and latent growth curve modeling, we will rely on the most parsimonious latent growth curve model to make conclusions. 
Sensitivity analyses will be completed to see if dropping non-18 or 19-year-olds for the Robins et al. (2005) replications produced different conclusions.

Statistical analysis backup plan:
Describe what you will do should your data violate assumptions, your model not converge, or some other analytic problem arise?  
If the latent growth curve models do not run, the original replication analyses will be used to make conclusions. 

Exploratory analyses:
If you plan to explore your data set to look for unexpected differences or relationships, you may describe those tests here. An exploratory test is any test where a prediction is not made up front, or there are multiple possible tests that you are going to use. A statistically significant finding in an exploratory test is a great way to form a new confirmatory hypothesis, which could be registered later in a different dataset.
We will emulate the latent growth curve model depicted above except we will replace anticipatory change with perceived change in order to explore the relationships among perceived change, optimism, and actual change.
We will also explore effects of demographic variables in the latent growth curve models.

title_r: Influence of the Big Five Personality Traits on subjective Valence and subjective Arousal – a Replication Study
abstract_r: Emotions and their connections to other phenomena are deeply integrated in psychologic research. Often emotional pictures are used to induce and measure them. Besides the older and not publicly available International Affective Picture Set (IAPS), there is the Open Affective Standardized Image Set (OASIS) recently used in science. These pictures are newer and for public use. The OASIS contains 900 colored pictures of four categories (humans, scenes, objects and animals) with a minimum of 134 pictures each. In some emotion induction methods like the OASIS, there is a heterogeneity in stimulus evaluation. They can be influenced by interindividual varying variables like e.g. age, gender or the personality. Regarding the Big Five personality factors, literature found connections of Extraversion (the tendency to behave e.g. energetic, assertive or outgoing) to stronger reactivity on positive and sometimes neutral stimuli. Neuroticism (the tendency to behave e.g. worried or anxious) was related to stronger reactivity on negative stimuli. For agreeableness (the tendency to behave e.g. appreciative or sympathetic), science provides mixed findings: both strong and weak agreeable people tend to evaluate positive stimuli more positive, and higher agreeableness is connected with stronger reactivity on negative pictures or with overall more positive affect. Ingendahl and Vogel (2022) pointed out a heterogeneity of normed valence evaluations of the OASIS and investigated personality influences (specifically Neuroticism, Extraversion and Agreeableness) as a possible reason. They conducted an online study with 3x30 pictures (10 positive, 10 negative, 10 neutral) of the OASIS and 901 participants who rated the pictures in valence. The researchers’ findings corresponded to earlier mentioned literature. Participants didn’t rate subjective arousal. Literature about this is mainly focuses on Neuroticism or Extraversion but provides only few and mixed findings. All in all, this study now aims to replicate the findings of Ingendahl and Vogel regarding subjective valence by using all 900 pictures of the OASIS. Furthermore, it aims to examine the influence of Neuroticism and Extraversion on subjective arousal.

title_r: Foodie Calls - A Preregistered Replication Study
abstract_r: When it comes to the question of who is going to pay on a first date, it is not always clear how the bill is shared. While the consensus is hard to reach in many societies, gender roles, which are greatly impacted by culture, play a huge role in determining the answer to this highly debated question. In societies where traditional gender roles and norms are clearly defined and exercised, it might be expected that it is usually men who pay the bill on a first date (Delucia, 1987; Jaramillo-Sierra &amp; Allen, 2013; Wu et al., 2021). In a study based on a US sample, Collisson and colleagues (2020) reported that some women, especially the ones with dark personality traits and traditional gender role beliefs are prone to abuse men in order to receive a free meal on a first date without feeling any actual romantic attraction. However, the impact of Dark Triad personality traits might be irrelevant in circumstances, if traditional gender roles are more explicitly pronounced in society because of the expected norms that suggest men should always pay. The aim of this study is to test the impact of the Dark Triad personality traits on the “foodie call” behavior, which refers to the situation “where a person, despite a lack of romantic attraction to a suitor, chooses to go on a date to get a free meal” (Collisson et al., 2020, p. 425). The study is designed as a pre-registered replication study. The materials are presented on the OSF website.

title_r: Are STEM Faculty Biased Against Female Applicants? A Robust Replication and Extension of Moss-Racusin and Colleagues (2012)
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

Abstract (as of 6/1/20): 

In a seminal study investigating gender bias in academic science, Moss-Racusin et al. (2012) found bias against female lab manager applicants with respect to competence, hireability, mentoring, and salary conferral. This topic will be revisited through four studies--two direct replications, one extension, and a meta analysis. The present set of studies, all using the same methods and materials as the original, will sample from a larger and broader pool of faculty, collectively representing the breadth of STEM disciplines at R1 universities across the United States. The proposed studies will have high power to detect smaller effect sizes than in the original. Furthermore, a priori criteria have been explicitly articulated for what will be accepted as hypothesis confirmation and replication, and for evidence of gender bias. The pre-registered data analysis plans will provide a strong test assessing the replicability of Moss-Racusin et al. (2012)’s finding that STEM faculty were biased against women who applied for a lab manager position.

title_r: Laminar fMRI in the human prefrontal cortex at 7T: A replication study of layer-dependent activity during working memory
abstract_r: This study aims to replicate Finn et al. 2019, specifically their “axial protocol”. Briefly, Finn et al. 2019 used VASO fMRI to measure cortical layer specific cerebral blood volume (CBV) changes during different periods of a delayed-response task in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC). They found that superficial layers were more active during the delay period when working memory items needed to be manipulated (alphabetization of a random letter sequence) compared to mere maintenance (remembering of the original letter sequence). In contrast, deeper layers were more active during the response period. The study by Finn et al. 2019 is the first that demonstrates the ability of high-resolution fMRI in humans to measure layer specific effects in the prefrontal cortex and thus opens the possibility to study high-level cognition layer-specifically non-invasively in human subjects. Given its importance for the field of cognitive neuroscience we think it is valuable to attempt replicating this seminal study and evaluate the robustness of its results. Moreover we want to confirm that the reported results are robust with respect to our specific slightly different experimental setup consisting of a different MRI scanner, different version and parameters of the SS-SI-VASO pulse sequence and differences in institutional constraints like maximal duration of human participant sessions. Lastly, the study by Finn et al. 2019 relied, like most layer fMRI studies to date, on a substantial amount of semi-manual or manual analysis steps including their ROI definition, gray matter segmentation and layer definition. In order to test whether less manual intervention can lead to comparable results we will limit ourselves to a more automatic analysis approach. As a consequence, our methods will follow Finn et al. 2019 closely and will only differ with respect to the above mentioned constraints. Here, we formulate and pre-register an analysis approach that automates some of the manual aspects of Finn et al. 2019. We believe this to constitute a fair attempt for replicating their results. In addition, we may explore the effects of additional analysis approaches (including manual analysis steps) on our results (see section on Exploratory analysis).

title_r: Investigation of the role of the right and left occipital face area in early face processing using neuronavigated repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation: A replication study
abstract_r: In day-to-day life, analyzing faces plays a crucial role for interactions with our surroundings. In their neuroanatomical model, Haxby et al. (2000) differentiate between a core system and an extended system for face processing in the brain. The core system is mainly responsible for early visual processing of face stimuli and consists of bilateral regions called the occipital face area (OFA), the fusiform face area (FFA) and the posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS). In this model, the OFA is supposed to process basic facial features before passing on the information to further processing at the level of FFA and pSTS. While the roles of pSTS and FFA have been intensively studied, the role of the OFA is still under debate (Pitcher et al. 2011). One of the studies that initially investigated the role of the OFA and led to a better understanding of its function was a study of Pitcher et al. (2007). In this study, Pitcher and colleagues investigated whether stimulating the OFA with repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) would impair early processing of faces. As a result, they were able to show that only the stimulation of the right OFA led to significant reductions in accuracy in a feature discrimination task of faces. In a series of subsequent rTMS studies, the authors therefore focused specifically on the role of the right OFA (Pitcher et al. 2008, 2009, 2011). At present, the functional role of the left OFA is still unknown. The present study has two goals. First, we aim to replicate the findings of the first experiment of Pitcher et al. (2007). More specifically, we aim to reproduce that rTMS targeted at the right OFA will disrupt accurate discrimination of face parts but has no effect on the discrimination of spacing between these parts. Second, we will investigate the role of the left OFA in face processing in more detail. As already discussed by Pitcher et al. (2007), a putatively deeper location of the left OFA might have made it more difficult to exactly target this region. Using neuronavigated rTMS with individual coordinates for each participant (a technique that was not yet used in the Pitcher et al. (2007) study), we aim to obtain more exact estimates for the disruption of face processing functions when stimulating the left OFA.

title_r: The Effect of Thinking About Being Excluded by God on Well-Being: A Replication and Extension
abstract_r: Prior research has provided initial evidence that thinking about being excluded by God lowers self-reported well-being in a Dutch sample of Christian students. The current research sought to replicate this finding in two studies. The first experiment recruited a USA sample of Christian students from a secular and religious school. The second experiment recruited a USA online sample of Christians contacted via Mechanical Turk. Results of these two studies replicated the initial finding that thinking about being excluded by God lowers self-reported well-being relative to thinking about being included by God, or contemplating that God created the earth. Moreover, a mini-meta analysis of the original study and the current two studies added the novel insight that thinking about being included by God increased well-being relative to contemplating that God created the earth. Overall, these results show how people’s perceived relationship with God may influence their quality of life.

title_r: The relationship between anhedonia and delay discounting task: a replication of Lempert and Pizzagalli (2010) study
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

summary: The purpose of this study was to replicate that of Lempert and Pizzagalli (2010), which examined the relationship between anhedonia and the delay discounting task (DDT). Patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) exhibit various symptoms such as depressive mood, anhedonia, and insomnia. Anhedonia is a key symptom of MDD and refers to a loss of positive feeling and a decrease in responsiveness to reward. The DDT has often been used to research MDD and reward responsivity. In DDT, a comparison is made between participants who choose to receive small rewards immediately and those who opt for larger rewards after a delay. Patients with MDD prefer an immediate reward because of their pessimism about the future and their impulsivity. However, in the case of high anhedonia, patients are assumed to prefer the larger rewards after a delay because of their decreased responsiveness to reward. Lempert and Pizzagalli (2010) examine how anhedonia affects DDT; they found a significant negative correlation (r = -0.42) between anhedonia and discounting rate. Thus, anhedonic participants appeared to prefer a larger reward after a longer delay. Lempert and Pizzagalli (2010) argued that anhedonic people have low impulsivity for immediate rewards. This finding is important in clarifying the decision mechanism in depression. However, in many fields of psychological study, there exists a question of reproductivity. The findings of Lempert and Pizzagalli (2010) also did not agree with those of other studies related to anhedonia and delay discounting rate (Cai et al., 2018; Pulcu et al., 2014). Therefore, we will conduct a replication study of Lempert and Pizzagalli’s (2010) study. We will conduct our study using the same setting and analysis as those of Lempert and Pizzagalli (2010)and examine the relationship between anhedonia and delay discounting rate.

title_r: Replication and extension of: Large language models associate Muslims with violence by Abid et al., 2021
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

The main purpose of this study is to replicate and extend the results in Abid et al. (2021; Nature Machine Intelligence). Building on preliminary evidence provided by the creators of GPT-2 and GPT-3 (state-of-the-art text generation algorithms; Radford et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020), the authors showed biased automated text generation when religious identities are cued in text completion prompts. GPT-3 completions for prompts formatted as “Two X walk into a” contained violent content much more often if X was replaced with “Muslims” rather than adjectives signifying other major religions. Since the smallest difference was found between “Muslim” and “Christian”, our replication attempt focuses on this more conservative measure of the model’s religion bias. However, we include the “Hindu” category as well to control for the impact of majority/minority difference between “Muslim” and “Christian”.
We extend these results by exploring whether naming specific individuals reduces the propensity of the model to rely on biased group-level representations. For instance, using “Y walks into a” where Y is replaced with a common Muslim name compared with names common among adherents of Christianity and Hinduism. 
We also examine whether the model is sensitive to differing degrees of genericity in the main referent of prompts, which can vary along a continuum. Generic kinds like “Muslim” lie near one end of the spectrum. Individual celebrities whose personal information presumably features strongly in GPT-3’s training data (from CommonCrawl.org), lie near the other end. Common names associated with social kinds like “Muslim” (e.g., Ali Islam) are somewhere in-between, albeit closer to the specific end of the genericity spectrum. We expect reduced bias as the specificity of the prompts are increased.

summary: The attached Word document contains structured, detailed descriptions of procedures for a replication of Abid et al.'s (2021) results, with particular attention paid to minor adjustments made by the current authors. It also contains theoretical and practical justifications for the extension based on the linguistic notion of genericity, as well as detailed information about the procedures and materials for that extension. Potential follow-up experiments are also mentioned.

title_r: Implicit Emotion Regulation - A Replication Study on the Counter Regulation of Emotions by Attentional Biases in Affective Processing.
abstract_r: Abstract We aim to replicate a study by Rothermund (2003; experiment 1) that investigated biases in the automatic allocation of attention to valence information as depending on current affective-motivational states. The main research questions are: a) Is it easier to allocate attention to words that are opposite in valence to the current affective-motivational state? (incongruency effect) b) Do incongruency effects only occur when attention needs to be shifted from a preceding stimulus to a target stimulus of opposing valence? (valence shift hypothesis) Our objective is to answer the research questions by investigating whether reaction times will be faster in a word categorisation task for words that differ in valence to the current affective-motivational state (as induced by performance feedback during the task), and whether this is only true when targets in consecutive trials differ in valence (valence shift). Participants: we aim to test 67 participants (based on power calculations) Study method: Within-subjects factorial design Factors: o Target Valence (positive vs negative) o Feedback Valence (positive vs negative) o Valence Shift (shift vs no shift) Dependent Variable: response time for word categorisation Study material: 32 positive and negative words (from Rothermund, 2003) Procedure: Participants will carry out a word categorisation task, in which the valence of a word has to be evaluated as positive or negative. For correct and fast responses, participants will receive a positive feedback. For erroneous or slow responses, they will receive negative feedback. Theoretical Background Considering its crucial role in maintaining physical and mental well-being (Gross and John, 2003; Diener, 2009), it is hardly surprising that psychological research has been increasingly focusing on the concept of emotion regulation. Braunstein, Gross and Ochsner (2017) describe two types of emotion regulation that are typically studied: explicit and controlled emotion regulation versus implicit and automatic regulation. These differ in terms of the level of conscious awareness (how aware we are of the regulation goal) and automaticity (how controlled versus automatic the change processes are). In the context of psychological resilience research, Schwager and Rothermund (2014) discuss mechanisms of implicit emotion regulation as critical for mental health. They argue that automatic affective processing lies at the core of resilience. In describing their Expanded Process Model of Resilience, they assume that automatic cognitive and affective regulatory processes happen first and function to change the accessibility of information; thereby allowing for a situation to be reassessed and motivation to be adjusted. The authors further explain that self-regulatory processes are influenced by biases in attention allocation toward positive and negative relevant information. Such biases are no rigid traits, however, but change depending on contextual factors. According to Rothermund (2011), there are two basic mechanisms that lead to a flexible adjustment of affective processing biases to valent information (positive or negative): 1) the control dependency principle and 2) the counter regulation principle. The control dependency principle posits that perceived control influences affective processing biases. That is, if the level of perceived control is high, attention will be preferably allocated to more negative information (problem focus), whereas, if the level of perceived control is low, attention will likely be drawn to positive information to aid reappraisal. The counter regulation principle, on the other hand, postulates that attention is preferentially allocated to information of opposing valence to the current affective-motivational state (Rothermund et al., 2008). Experiencing negative emotions will therefore make positive information more salient. In contrast, experiencing positive emotions is likely to direct attention to more negative stimuli. This theory is in line with contemporary concepts of resilience that describe it to be an adaptive process, counteracting functional and emotional deviations and helping them to return to a neutral level (Kalisch, Müller, & Tüscher, 2015). Importantly, affective processing biases happen in both directions to aid the maintenance of a balanced emotional state (Schwager & Rothermund, 2014). Various studies have suggested that affect and motivation exert an influence on cognition (i.e., information processing) by controlling selective attention (Derryberry & Tucker, 1991, 1994; Rothermund, 2003; Rothermund, Wentura, & Bak, 2001). In order to investigate the counter regulation principle, Rothermund (2003) assessed the relation between feedback-related affective-motivational states and the automatic processing of valence, by analysing effects of feedback on the speed of evaluative decisions. Motivational states were induced by positive/success or negative/failure feedback on the task that involved categorising simple valent words as positive or negative. Across three experiments, Rothermund (2003) found reaction times to be significantly faster for words opposite in valence to the current affective-motivational state. This incongruency effect only occurred, however, in situations in which attention had to be shifted between target words of opposing valence in two consecutive trials. The findings support the assumption of a counter regulation principle by showing that attention is automatically allocated to a stimulus that is different in valence to the current motivational state. Additionally, it supports the valence shift hypothesis proposed by Derryberry (1993). That is, incongruency effects of motivational states on affective processing only occur when attention has to be shifted between stimuli of opposing valence. The current study aims to replicate Rothermund’s (2003) findings by implementing his experimental design. We hypothesise that reaction times will be faster in the word categorisation task for words that differ in valence to the current motivational state. Furthermore, we expect to find an incongruency effect of feedback on the processing of target valence only in a situation involving a valence shift (i.e., when the targets of two consecutive trials differ in valence).

title_r: Tackett lab hormones replication project
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

summary: The present study is an attempt to reproduce, in an independent pre-adolescent sample, analyses from three studies examining the interaction between personality traits and hormones in predicting youth externalizing behavior.  The three papers are as follows: 

A. Reardon, K. W., Herzhoff, K., & Tackett, J. L. (2015). Adolescent personality as risk and resiliency in the testosterone-externalizing association. Journal of Research on Adolescence, 26, 390-402.

B. Tackett, J. L., Herzhoff, K., Harden, K. P., Page-Gould, E., & Josephs, R. A. (2014). Personality x hormone interactions in adolescent externalizing psychopathology. Personality Disorders: Theory, Research, and Treatment. 5, 235-246. 

C. Tackett, J. L., Reardon, K. W., Herzhoff, K., Page-Gould, E., Harden, K. P., & Josephs, R. A. (2015). Estradiol and cortisol interactions in youth externalizing psychopathology. Psychoneuroendocrinology, 55, 146-153. 

Sample: This replication effort will be conducted in an already-collected sample of 350 youth between the ages of 8 and 11. 

Variables: We will use variables indexing hormones, personality traits, and externalizing behavior. 

1. youth hormone levels as measured via a baseline sample of saliva collected 30 minutes after arrival to the lab. The samples were collected using a passive drool method, frozen, and immunoassayed in an independent lab. We will use the measurements of cortisol, testosterone, and estradiol (E2). 

2. parent-reported youth personality pathology traits as measured by the Dimensional Personality Symptom Itempool (DIPSI; De Clercq, De Fruyt, Van Leeuwen, & Mervielde, 2006). We will focus specifically on the higher-order trait dimension of Disagreeableness. 

3. parent-reported youth behavior as measured by the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL; Achenbach & Rescorla, 2001). We will focus specifically on the broadband Externalizing Problems scale. 

Hypotheses: We are aiming to replicate the findings from each of these three previous studies in a larger sample. This sample diverges from the original sample not only in size, but also in age (pre-adolescent versus adolescent) and in much greater racial/ethnic and socioeconomic diversity.

A. Reardon et al., 2015: This study demonstrated that testosterone was associated with externalizing behavior, but only for youth with low levels of self-regulatory personality. Thus, we hypothesize that testosterone will be predictive of externalizing behavior, but only for those youth high on disagreeableness. We hypothesize that there will be no relationship between testosterone and externalizing behavior for those youth low in disagreeableness. 

B. Tackett et al., 2014: This study found that testosterone was associated with externalizing behavior, but only when cortisol was low, and only among youth high on trait disagreeableness. Thus, we hypothesize that testosterone will be associated with higher externalizing behavior for those youth who have low cortisol and high levels of disagreeableness, and that there will be no relationship between testosterone and externalizing behavior for those youth low in disagreeableness or high in cortisol. 

C. Tackett et al., 2015: This study found that estradiol was associated with externalizing behavior, but only when cortisol was low and only among youth high on trait disagreeableness. Thus, we hypothesize that estradiol will be associated with higher externalizing behavior for those youth who have low cortisol and high levels of disagreeableness, and that there will be no relationship between estradiol and externalizing behavior for those youth low in disagreeableness or high in cortisol. 

Planned analyses: 

1. For the hormone variables (C, T, and E2), any extreme values will be winsorized. An extreme value will be defined as a value more than 3 standard deviations away from the mean, and this value will be replaced with the next highest observed value in the sample. 

2. We anticipate large skew values, as is typical for hormone variables, and thus all hormone variables will be log-transformed to reduce this skew. 

3. Because we anticipate that boys will have significantly higher T levels than girls, and that girls will have significantly higher E2 levels than boys, these two hormones will be standardized (z-scored) within gender, as is consistent with previous research on gonadal hormones (e.g., Mehta & Josephs, 2010). 

4. Age, gender, and time of waking will be used as covariates in all analyses, so these variables will be standardized. In addition, the predictor variable DIPSI Disagreeableness will be standardized. 

5. We will next create interaction terms: 
    a. T x Disagreeableness
    b. C x Disagreeableness
    c. E2 x Disagreeableness
    d. T x C
    e. E2 x C 
    f. T x C x Disagreeableness
    g. E2 x C x Disagreeableness

6. We will run regression analyses to test the central hypotheses of the three studies: 

A. Reardon et al., 2015: Full regressions testing the interaction between testosterone and disagreeableness will include age, sex, and time of waking as covariates in step 1, main effects for T and Disagreeableness in step 2, and the interaction term between T and Disagreeableness in step 3. 

B. Tackett et al., 2014: Full regressions testing the three way interaction between testosterone, cortisol, and disagreeableness will include age, sex, and time of waking as covariates in step 1, main effects for T, C, and Disagreeableness in step 2, the two-way interaction terms between T, C, and Disagreeableness in step 3, and finally the three-way interaction term between T, C, and Disagreeableness in step 4. 

C. Tackett et al., 2015: Full regressions testing the three way interaction between estradiol, cortisol, and disagreeableness will include age, sex, and time of waking as covariates in step 1, main effects for E2, C, and Disagreeableness in step 2, the two-way interaction terms between E2, C, and Disagreeableness in step 3, and finally the three-way interaction term between E2, C, and Disagreeableness in step 4. 

7. Additional analyses to examine potential moderators and specificity of the effects (some of which were directly examined in the previous publications) will include: 

    a. running the regressions using the parent-reported CBCL Internalizing Problems scale as an additional covariate, to test specificity of externalizing problems above-and-beyond general psychopathology. We hypothesize that associations will be smaller, but will still show unique associations with externalizing problems.
    b. running the regressions using the Pubertal Development Scale score (PDS) as a covariate instead of age, as hormone levels are affected by physical maturation. Age and pubertal status are highly correlated, so the pattern of results should largely be the same. Nonetheless, there is so little empirical data with these variables in child and adolescent samples that it is important to see how age and pubertal status covariates may differentially impact evidence for these associations, particularly across different stages of puberty. The current study offers substantial power to test this question in a early/pre-pubertal sample.
    c. running the regressions using the time of testing as a covariate, as hormone concentrations vary throughout the day. The pattern of results is anticipated to remain largely similar with this additional covariate. It will be examined because it is sometimes used as a covariate in similar research using a single baseline sample.
    d. running the regressions separately in boys and girls, a practice which is quite common in human psychoneuroendocrinological research, to examine whether the final pattern of results is similar for both boys and girls. We do not have strong a priori hypotheses for gender differences in these relationships, and the previous publications did not find meaningful evidence for gender differences. 
    e. running the regressions replacing the DIPSI Disagreeableness higher-order scale with the 12 lower-order facets of Disagreeableness. Facet-level analyses offer a more fine-grained examination of those aspects of self-regulatory personality that are involved in these associations (analyses are consistent with Tackett et al., 2014).
    f. examining race/ethnicity as a potential moderator. Evidence indicates different hormone levels across race/ethnic groups, but studies rarely have adequate racial and ethnic diversity to directly examine hormone-behavior associations between groups. Given the lack of previous studies on this specific research question, such analyses would be descriptive.

2. We anticipate large skew values, as is typical for hormone variables, and thus all hormone variables will be log-transformed to reduce this skew. 

3. The pattern of results is anticipated to remain largely similar with this additional covariate. title_r: HEXACO and FFM personality in relation with RIASEC vocational interests - replication study
abstract_r: The aim of this study is to revisit the relation between individual's personality and vocational interests in order to establish which one of the personality measures (HEXACO or Five-Factor Model) is the most accurate personality measure. Furthermore, this is a conceptual replication that aims to examine the validity and generalizability of the findings presented by McKay and Tokar (2012) by implementing the same methodology, but on a different population. This is a quantitative study that implements correlational design. After consenting to take part in the study, participants will be asked to provide a code word and fill out few sociodemographic information, and then to complete three questionnaires. Participants should fill the online survey individually, in a quiet space in order to provide the best accuracy of the answers. The entire process should take around 20 minutes. The data from this study will be analysed in IBM SPSS. Relationship between HEXACO personality measure and RIASEC vocational interests will be assessed by Pearson's correlation. Simultaneous regression will be conducted to compare HEXACO and FFM in relation with RIASEC. The significance level of <0.05 will be applied consistently. It is hypothesised that the results form McKay and Tokar (2012) will be validated, ie. HEXACO will show higher predictability of RIASEC vocational interests than FFM.

title_r: Does Speed of Recognition predict Two-Alternatives Forced-Choice Performance? Replicating and Extending Starns, Dubé, and Frelinger (2018)
abstract_r: Does the speed of single-word recognition errors predict performance in subsequent two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) trials that include the error item? Starns, Dubé, and Frelinger (2018) found effects of this kind in two experiments and account for them in terms of a continuous memory-strength signal guiding recognition decisions. In the 2AFC task, Starns et al. (2018) always paired an item that had been responded to falsely in a preceding single-word recognition task with an item that had been responded to correctly. Participants were instructed to identify and correct the error made in the single-word recognition test via their response in the 2AFC trial. As suggested by Malejka and Bröder (2016) for a source memory task, feedback regarding error items can indeed influence memory decisions. The present study is an adversarial collaboration that aims (a) to replicate Starns et al.’s (2018) results in a replication condition and (b) to test whether the effects of error speed reflect an artefact due to an error-correction strategy that uses response latency as a heuristic cue. For this purpose, we will implement a replication as well as an extension condition in which error feedback is removed. This study will contribute to the broader research question of whether a continuous memory-strength signal or discrete states underlie recognition decisions.

summary: This project reflects a replication and extension of the research reported in McPhetres & Zuckerman (2017). In addition to attempting to replicate their main finding that religious individuals endorse a lower standard of evidence for believing a religious claim relative to a scientific claim, we are extending this work to investigate whether religious and non-religious individuals treat negative or contradictory evidence of scientific and religious claims differently. Further, we are extending this work by exploring the potential relationship between evidence evaluation for confirmatory and contradictory evidence and individual difference measures in perceiving science as a credible enterprise, tendencies towards conspiracy ideation, and political orientation. Our pre-registration includes a thorough review of the relevant literatures, a description of how our study extends the original work of McPhetres & Zuckerman, a priori directional hypotheses and exploratory research questions. We are also pre-registering SPSS syntax that will be used for testing our a priori hypotheses.

item37: To manipulate the conditions that participants were in, we made use of vignettes where participants read about an interaction between the employee and another customer. The interaction could either be a neutral, uncivil or aggressive one. However, vignettes have limited ecological validity as participants were merely asked to imagine how they would behave in that situation. How they would react in real life might be different from how they imagined they would react. 

Our replication study relied on data collection from people who were conveniently available to participate in the study. Specifically, we recruited participants who were undergraduates studying in Singapore. This made our study susceptible to selection bias as we restricted the demographic of participants to include only undergraduates. This will lead to sampling error as our results will not be representative of the entire population in Singapore.

Our measures were self-reported, thus our results could be affected by common method bias. One major issue was the problem of social desirability. The participants tended to answer the questionnaire items in a manner that presented themselves in the best possible light.

In Hershcovis and Bhatnagar’s (2017) study, target-directed outcomes consisted of the dependent variables target evaluation, target support and tip percent. However, in our study, target-directed outcomes consisted only of the dependent variables target support and tip percent.

title_r: The role of metaphor in reasoning: a replication study
abstract_r: The importance of linguistic framing in reasoning has been well established. For instance, in their study, Thibodeau & Boroditsky (2011) explore how even subtle metaphors impact decision-making. This study will replicate the study conducted by Thibodeau & Boroditsky (2011). We explore how a metaphorically framed description of a socio-political issue, namely crime, in a fictitious city influences the suggestions made to solve the issue. title_r: The Possible Unemployment Cost of Average Inflation Below a Credible Target. A Replication Study of Svensson (American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics, 2015)
abstract_r: This paper replicates the main analysis of Svensson (2015) with some expansion to the original analysis, mainly for the United States. Overall, the replication exercise successfully confirms the conclusions of Svensson (2015). In both Sweden and the United States, empirical evidence sup- ports the existence of a non-vertical long run Phillips curve. The slope of the long run Phillips curve recorded -0.75 in Sweden and -0.23 in the United States. While the average inflation rate in the United States was very close to its targeted level, the average inflation rate in Sweden was 0.6 per- centage points below its targeted level over the sample period. The deviation of inflation rate from its targeted level in Sweden resulted in an unemployment cost equivalent to 0.8 percentage points over the sample period where the average unemployment rate recorded 7.4 percent compared with an estimated 6.6 percent had the average inflation rate been at its targeted level.

title_r: Replication Study: Coadministration of a tumor-penetrating peptide enhances the efficacy of cancer drugs
abstract_r: In 2015, as part of the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology, we published a Registered Report (Kandela et al., 2015) that described how we intended to replicate selected experiments from the paper “Coadministration of a tumor-penetrating peptide enhances the efficacy of cancer drugs“ (Sugahara et al., 2010). Here we report the results of those experiments. We found that coadministration with iRGD peptide did not have an impact on permeability of the chemotherapeutic agent doxorubicin (DOX) in a xenograft model of prostate cancer, whereas the original study reported that it increased the penetrance of this cancer drug (Figure 2B; Sugahara et al., 2010). Further, in mice bearing orthotopic 22Rv1 human prostate tumors, we did not find a statistically significant difference in tumor weight for mice treated with DOX and iRGD compared to DOX alone, whereas the original study reported a decrease in tumor weight when DOX was coadministered with iRGD (Figure 2C; Sugahara et al., 2010). In addition, we did not find a statistically significant difference in TUNEL staining in tumor tissue between mice treated with DOX and iRGD compared to DOX alone, while the original study reported an increase in TUNEL positive staining with iRGD coadministration (Figure 2D; Sugahara et al., 2010). Similar to the original study (Supplemental Figure 9A; Sugahara et al., 2010), we did not observe an impact on mouse body weight with DOX and iRGD treatment. Finally, we report meta-analyses for each result.

title_r: The positive-negative mode link between brain connectivity, demographics, and behavior: A pre-registered replication of Smith et al. 2015
abstract_r: In mental health research, it has proven difficult to find measures of brain function that provide reliable indicators of mental health and well-being, including susceptibility to mental health disorders. Recently, a family of data-driven analyses have provided such reliable measures when applied to large, population-level datasets. In the current pre-registered replication study, we show that the canonical correlation analysis (CCA) methods previously developed using resting-state MRI functional connectivity and subject measures of cognition and behavior from healthy adults are also effective in measuring well-being (a "positive-negative axis") in an independent developmental dataset. Our replication was successful in two out of three of our pre-registered criteria, such that a primary CCA mode's weights displayed a significant positive relationship and explained a significant amount of variance in both functional connectivity and subject measures. The only criteria that was not successful was that compared to other modes the magnitude of variance explained by the primary CCA mode was smaller than predicted, a result which could indicate a developmental trajectory of a primary mode. This replication establishes a signature neurotypical relationship between connectivity and phenotype, opening new avenues of research in neuroscience with clear clinical applications.

title_r: Replicating and Extending ``Because Their Treebanks Leak'': Graph Isomorphism, Covariants, and Parser Performance
abstract_r: Søgaard (2020) obtained results suggesting the fraction of trees occurring in the test data isomorphic to trees in the training set accounts for a non-trivial variation in parser performance. Similar to other statistical analyses in NLP, the results were based on evaluating linear regressions. However, the study had methodological issues and was undertaken using a small sample size leading to unreliable results. We present a replication study in which we also bin sentences by length and find that only a small subset of sentences vary in performance with respect to graph isomorphism. Further, the correlation observed between parser performance and graph isomorphism in the wild disappears when controlling for covariants. However, in a controlled experiment, where covariants are kept fixed, we do observe a correlation. We suggest that conclusions drawn from statistical analyses like this need to be tempered and that controlled experiments can complement them by more readily teasing factors apart.

title_r: A Replication Study of "Topic Modeling on Podcast Short-Text Metadata"
abstract_r: This report summarizes our efforts on replicating the key findings and methodologies introduced in the paper "Topic Modeling on Podcast Short-Text Metadata" from Valero et al. presented at the ECIR 2022. The original paper addresses the problem of effectively categorizing the wide and heterogeneous range of topics and discussions in the continuously growing podcast landscape. In order to achieve their goals the authors introduce a new method, called ’NEiCE’, to effectively extract the relevant topics out of the short-text metadata, like title and description, from a given podcast.

title_r: Reproduction Package for FSE 2024 Submission `A Replication Study of Interpolation-Based Hardware Model Checking for Software Verification'
abstract_r:
Reproduction Package A Replication Study of Interpolation-Based Hardware Model Checking for Software Verification Abstract This artifact is a reproduction package for the manuscript “A Replication Study of Interpolation-Based Hardware Model Checking for Software Verification”, submitted to FSE 2024. In the replication study, the transferability of the results reported by two prior publications on interpolation-based hardware model checking to software verification is investigated. The two publications are (1) Interpolation-Sequence-Based Model Checking (Vizel and Grumberg, 2009) and (2) Intertwined Forward-Backward Reachability Analysis Using Interpolants (Vizel, Grumberg, and Shoham, 2013). The purpose of this artifact is to reproduce the experiments conducted to validate the claims made in the above two publications. The artifact consists of source code, precompiled executables, and input data used in the evaluation of the replication study, as well as the results produced from the experiments. Specifically, it includes the source code and binaries of CPAchecker (at revision 44757 of branch “cfa-single-loop-transformation”), which implements the verification algorithms compared in the submitted manuscript, the SV-COMP ’23 benchmark suite, the experimental data generated from the evaluation, and instructions to run the tools and experiments. This reproduction package works best with the SoSy-Lab Virtual Machine, which runs Ubuntu 22.04 LTS. The VM has all the required dependencies installed. If you test this artifact with it, all installation steps below can be skipped. Contents This artifact contains the following items: README.*: this documentation fse2024-paper483.pdf: the manuscript submitted to FSE 2024 License.txt: license information of the artifact cpachecker/: a directory containing the source code and precompiled binaries of CPAchecker sv-benchmarks/: a directory containing the SV-COMP ’23 benchmark tasks used in our evaluation data-submission/: a directory containing the raw and processed data produced from our full evaluation (used in the manuscript, under paper-results/) and from a demo experiment (prepared for this reproduction package, under demo-results/) bench-defs/: a directory containing the benchmark and table definitions of the experiments (used by BenchExec, a framework for reliable benchmarking) This readme file will guide you through the following steps: Execute CPAchecker Perform experiments View the experimental results Execute CPAchecker System requirements for CPAchecker To execute CPAchecker, Java Runtime Environment (JRE) version ≥ 17 is required. For more information, please refer to cpachecker/INSTALL.md. Run verification algorithms in CPAchecker In the replication study, we compared the performance of three interpolation-based verification algorithms, namely IMC (McMillan, 2003), ISMC (Vizel and Grumberg, 2009), and DAR (Vizel, Grumberg, and Shoham, 2013). ISMC and DAR are the algorithms proposed by the two prior publications, respectively, and IMC is the first interpolation-based model-checking approach, which was used as the baseline in the two publications. All the algorithms have been implemented in CPAchecker. Below we list the commands to run the evaluated verification algorithms. These example commands use sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c as the input program. You can replace it with another program. IMC: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolation \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop imc.fallBack=false \ -setprop imc.loopBoundIncrementStrategyForBMC=CONST \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
ISMC: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolationSequence \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop imc.fallBack=false \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
DAR: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolationDualSequence \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop dar.fallBack=false \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
For more information on how to run CPAchecker, see cpachcker/README.md. Understand the output of CPAchecker The following is an example output shown on the console after an analysis is finished. 
[...redacted...] Verification result: TRUE. No property violation found by chosen configuration. More details about the verification run can be found in the directory "./output". Graphical representation included in the file "./output/Report.html".
There are 3 possible outcomes of the verification result: TRUE: the program is “safe”, i.e., it satisfies the given safety property FALSE: the program is “unsafe”, i.e., it contains a violation to the given safety property UNKNOWN: the analysis was inconclusive CPAchecker also generates an HTML report for conveniently browsing the results. Please refer to cpachecker/doc/Report.md for more information. Perform Experiments Install BenchExec We use BenchExec, a framework for reliable benchmarking and resource measurements, to perform our evaluation. Please follow the installation guide to set up the benchmarking environment. Experimental settings The settings are described in the XML file bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml. This XML file is used by BenchExec for limiting computing resources and scheduling runs. For the execution of a task, a resource limit of 2 CPU cores, 1800 seconds of CPU time, and 15 GB of memory is imposed. Run the Full Evaluation To run the full experiment over the 8813 benchmark tasks reported in the manuscript, execute the following command. 
benchexec bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml \ --tool-directory cpachecker/ -o results/ \ --read-only-dir / --overlay-dir . --hidden-dir /home/
Run Partial Evaluation The full evaluation requires roughly 6 months of CPA time on a 3.40 GHz core. To run the experiment on a subset of benchmark tasks, you could add -t <tasks_name> to the above command, where <task_name> refer to the task names defined in bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml. For example: 
benchexec bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml \ --tool-directory cpachecker/ -o results/ \ --read-only-dir / --overlay-dir . --hidden-dir /home/ \ -t ReachSafety-BitVectors
If you want to adjust the imposed resource limit, the following options can be used: 
-T <cputime_limit> -M <mem_limit>
For more information about these flags, please refer to benchexec -h. View the Experimental Results Generate Tables After the execution of an experiment, you can generate an interactive HTML by table-generator. Simply run: 
table-generator -x bench-defs/overall-slt-stats.xml \ -f html --no-diff -o results
Note that if the experiment is only performed on a single task set (via -t <tasks_name>), you have to replace bench-defs/overall-slt-stats.xml by bench-defs/subset-slt-stats.xml. Results from Our Experiments The results (both raw and processed data) of the partial run (on ReachSafety-BitVectors) and the full run obtained by our machines are in folders data-submission/demo-results/ and data-submission/paper-results/, respectively. The generated HTML tables are named overall-slt-stats.table.html under each respective folder. In the replication study, there are eight hypotheses extracted from the two prior publications. We list them below to make this document more standalone. For details, please refer to the bundled manuscript. Claims in the ISMC Publication H1.A: ISMC is faster than IMC on tasks with property violation. H1.B: ISMC is faster than IMC when IMC finds a proof only at high unrolling bounds. H1.C: Overall, ISMC is faster than IMC (by 30 % in this experiment). In our experiments, we confirmed H1.A also for software verification, but H1.B and H1.C did not hold. Claims in the DAR Publication H2.A: For DAR, the ratio between iterations using global strengthening to the total number of iterations is less than 0.5 in most tasks. H2.B: IMC finds a proof slower than DAR in many tasks even though it has a smaller convergence length. H2.C: DAR computes more interpolants than IMC. H2.D: DAR’s run-time is more sensitive to the sizes of interpolants than IMC. H2.E: Overall, DAR is faster than IMC (by 36 % in this experiment). In our experiments, we confirmed H2.A and H2.C also for software verification, but H2.B, H2.D, and H2.E did not hold. title_r: The mediating role of LMX between abusive supervision and work behaviors: A replication and extension
abstract_r: Purpose - – In a replication of a multi-source study by Xu Design/methodology/approach - – The authors collected multi-source data in order to minimize common method bias. The authors conducted regression analyses, Sobel tests, and bootstrapping techniques. Findings - – The authors found support that LMX mediates the negative relationship between abusive supervision and OCBO and OCBI. However, the authors could not replicate the mediating role of LMX in the association between abusive supervision and employees' performance. Similar results were obtained when the data were analyzed with the active-aggressive and passive-aggressive abusive supervision subscales. Research limitations/implications - – Due to the cross-sectional nature of the study, this study does not allow the authors to draw causal conclusions regarding the proposed relationships. Originality/value - – The authors replicated Xu

title_r: The effect of selective spatial attention on the development of secondary hyperalgesia: a replication study
abstract_r: Cognitive factors, such as attention, play an important role in the modulation of pain and in the development of pain chronicity. We attempt to replicate one such effect found in a previous study conducted by Filbrich et al., 2020, which shows how the experimental induction of central sensitization, a key factor in the development of secondary hyperalgesia, can indeed be modulated by selective spatial attention. Secondary hyperalgesia occurs after tissue injury. It refers to a condition of increased sensitivity to mechanical stimuli within the injured area and the surrounding skin. It is hypothesized that the intense and sustained activation of peripheral nociceptors enhances the responsiveness of the neurons in the central nervous system. This causes the phenomenon known as central sensitization which is considered to play a key role in the development of chronic pain. As in Filbrich (2020), we will manipulate the impact of selective spatial attention by asking healthy volunteers to selectively focus their attention on target stimuli applied on one of the two forearms while we apply high frequency stimulation on both forearms. To assess the effect of the manipulation, we will measure perceived intensity to mechanical pinprick stimuli on both arms at three different moments: at T0, before applying high-frequency stimulation (HFS), at T1, immediately after having applied HFS in combination with the selective attention task, and finally at T2, 20 minutes after the whole procedure. Moreover, at T2, we will estimate the extent of the area of secondary hyperalgesia on both arms by applying mechanical pinprick stimulation along two axes: (1) medial-later, and (2) proximal-distal. References 1)Filbrich, L., van den Broeke, E. N., Legrain, V., & Mouraux, A. (2020). The focus of spatial attention during the induction of central sensitization can modulate the subsequent development of secondary hyperalgesia. Cortex, 124, 193-203

item37: Firstly, the participant demographics in the replication study was different as compared to the original study. Our current study’s participants had a much smaller sample size in the current study (32 participants in our current study and 169 participants in the original study), and an average age that was almost 10 years younger than that of the original study, with twice the number of people being unemployed at the point of testing as compared to the original study. These differences could have contributed to our inability to replicate the findings of the original study, as the younger age group and differential employment status of participants in the current study could mean that they might have different types of thinking from participants in the original study, thus affecting their ratings of the perceived typicality of the situation.
Secondly, there is no compensation provided to participants, and this could have affected their motivation to pay attention to the items in the study, resulting in inattentiveness in their responses, that might not have been detected by the manipulation check questions. Singer (2002) found that monetary incentives can be used to motivate participation in individuals, and the authors of the original study (Motro & Ellis, 2017) similarly provided participants with monetary compensation should they be included in their data set. 
Thirdly, the fact that employee Pat shown in the video to participants was a White individual, it could have influenced the perceived psychological realism of the participants of our current study, as they are all Asians, and might have difficulty relating to the situation shown as Pat is of a different ethnicity.  Additionally, in this replication study, the participants were not told to imagine that they were the direct supervisor of Pat, the employee in the video, unlike in the original study as the researchers had deduced it was necessary only for the second hypothesis which was not replicated. Both of these factors might have lessened the psychological realism created for the participants in the present replication, which could have contributed to the non-significant finding.

title_r: Replication and Extension of Nozaradan, Peretz, Missal and Mouraux (2011)
abstract_r: Frequency tagging has been used to capture auditory entrainment to beat and meter in music. Specifically, Nozaradan, Peretz, Missal and Mouraux (2011) instructed listeners to imagine either a binary or ternary metrical pattern while listening to an isochronous auditory stimulus and recorded cortical responses using electroencephalography (EEG). The amplitude of brain activity was increased at beat-related frequencies in both imagery conditions. This study inspired other labs to use the frequency tagging approach to examine auditory rhythm perception, and in only 6 years, it has been cited over 250 times on Google Scholar. The frequency tagging technique has been used in several published papers since 2011 and it is being used increasingly in research presented at recent research conferences and symposia. However, this seminal study has not been replicated. This registered report will detail the results of multiple independent conceptual replications of Nozaradan et al. (2011), all of which will follow the same vetted protocol.

title_r: A replication study to re-assess the HEXACO and Five Factor Model of Personality in relation to RIASEC Vocational Interests.
abstract_r: This study aims to uncover a relationship between an individual's personality and vocational interests- meanwhile assessing the ‘best’ personality’ measure. As this study is replicating a previous study, we will be using the same methodology in order to validate its findings. This quantitative study used a correlational design, with questionnaires to collect the data. After providing informed consent and sociodemographic information participants will be presented, in a randomised order, the three questionnaires. This should be completed individually and in a quiet environment, so the participant can focus on answering the questions accurately. It should in total take around 20 minutes to complete. The data will be analysed separately using SPSS. Pearson correlation will assess the relationship between HEXACO personality measures and RIASEC interests. Simultaneous regression will compare HEXACO and FFM in relation to RIASEC. The significance level of <0.05 will be used consistently. It is hypothesised that the findings of this replication will validate the main results from McKay and Tokar (2012): HEXACO accounting for more incremental variance than FFM in regard to Holland’s RIASEC vocational interests.

title_r: GW4 21-22: Devaluation effects in food-specific response inhibition training: An independent conceptual replication
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

Food-specific inhibitory control training (F-ICT) is a behavioural intervention in which participants learn to associate certain food-types with the inhibition of behaviour. Research has demonstrated the effectiveness of such training in reducing food evaluations (e.g., Chen et al., 2016; Chen, Veling, de Vries, et al., 2018; Veling et al., 2013a), changing food choices (e.g., Veling et al., 2013b; Veling, Chen, et al., 2017), decreasing food intake (e.g., Lawrence, Verbruggen, et al., 2015; also see Allom et al., 2016) and even promoting weight loss (Lawrence, O’Sullivan, et al., 2015; Nederkoorn et al., 2010; Veling et al., 2014; see Jones et al., 2016 for a meta-analysis). This has led some researchers to suggest that F-ICT may be a cost-effective intervention with clinical utility (Carbine & Larson, 2019; Jones et al., 2016, 2018). 

One explanation for the effectiveness of F-ICT on health-related outcomes is provided by the Behaviour Stimulus Interaction (BSI) theory (Chen et al., 2016; Veling et al., 2008; Veling, Lawrence, et al., 2017), which proposes that during training food stimuli are devalued to reduce the response conflict caused by the need to inhibit motor responses towards (highly) appetitive items and thus facilitate task performance. In a series of six experiments using the Go/No-Go Task, Chen et al. (2016) examined the effect of of food-specific response inhibition training on stimulus devaluation by pairing appetitive stimuli with cues to respond (go stimuli) or with cues to not respond (no-go cues or the absence of cues). Providing evidence of stimulus devaluation, findings indicated that attractiveness ratings of no-go foods reduced after training whilst ratings of go-foods increased. This effect was then replicated in two preregistered experiments (Chen, Veling, Dijksterhuis, et al., 2018) and across obese and normal-weight individuals (Chen, Veling, de Vries, et al., 2018), showing consistently that no-go foods were rated as less attractive post-training compared to go-foods and untrained foods. 

The aim of the current study is to conceptually replicate the devaluation effect found by Chen et al. (2016) for food attractiveness ratings in a high-powered and representative sample, as well as exploring potential moderators of these effects.

title_r: Social Class and Social Working Memory Replication Study
abstract_r: Economic inequality in America has reached unprecedented levels with disparities between the haves and have nots impacting nearly every consequential life. Decades of work suggest that lower social class is also associated with diminished working memory and executive functioning (Hackman & Farah, 2009). Nevertheless, lower social class individuals consistently outperform their higher class counterparts on social cognitive tasks such as identifying emotions from facial expressions and adopting the visual perspective of others (Dietze & Knowles, 2020). Interestingly, successful performance on social cognitive tasks heavily relies on executive functioning and working memory processes in particular – the same resources lower social class is theorized to undermine. Why would lower social class be associated with diminished performance on nonsocial cognitive tasks but enhanced performance on social cognitive tasks, even if the two rely on similar underlying processes? In a pilot study, we used a standard test of social and nonsocial working memory developed by Meyer and Collier (2020) to investigate social class differences in working memory performance across social and nonsocial domains. We recruited 190 online participants through Prolific and found that lower social class predicted better social (but not nonsocial) working memory performance on two-load trials (b=-0.07, p=.006). In current pre-registered work, we seek to replicate this interaction between social class and memory type (social versus nonsocial). We will also conduct exploratory analyses to examine if social network density serves as a meaningful behavioral moderator or mediator of these effects.

title_r: Self Regulation Ontology Replication
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

summary: Previously (Eisenberg et al., 2019), our lab leveraged exploratory factor analysis (EFA) on the dependent variables (n=193 DVs) extracted from 522 individuals’ performances on a large range of tasks (n=37 tasks, n=129 DVs) and self-report surveys (n=22 surveys, n=64 DVs) broadly related to the psychological construct of ‘Self Regulation’. While 12 factors were recovered from the survey DVs, only 5 factors were recovered from task-derived DVs. of the 5 task factors, 3 (speeded information processing, caution, and perception/response) were strongly related to DVs that were parameters of drift diffusion modeling (DDM): drift rate, threshold, and non-decision time, respectively. This may indicate that DDM captures fundamental dimensions of cognition. Alternative, this could suggest that examining the data through the lens of DDM conceals otherwise fundamental cognitive factors that are central to other taxonomies in the literature (e.g., Miyake et al., 2000), like shifting, updating, and inhibition. 
	To investigate these possibilities, we plan to perform EFA and the subsequent analyses of Eisenberg et al. (2019) on the original data, replacing the DDM parameters with reaction time, accuracy, and within-subject reaction time standard deviation. We propose two competing hypothesis classes.  First, the factors recovered could be similar in number and occupy a similar factor space and axes as the original factors. For example, we could again find a 5-factor solution, but dependent variables that previously loaded on speeded information processing, caution, and perception/response may now load onto RT variance, accuracy, and mean reaction time, respectively. Within this class, a more specific outcome would be that these new factors provide worse fits to the data than the original factors. This would indicate that the additional assumptions of the DDM combined with the original modeling parameters produce dependent variables which better reflect the underlying psychological factor space. Alternatively, the new factors could better fit the data compared to the old factors, indicating that the additional assumptions of DDM distort the data in some way, and would encourage further investigation. 
	Second, the new factor solution may be fundamentally different in factor number and factor space/axes. For example, the original 5-factor solution may give way to a higher-dimensional solution in which dependent variables map onto more traditional psychological constructs like attention, working memory, shifting, inhibition, etc.  Alternatively, we may recover a set of factors more obscure that do not map cleanly onto the original factor solution or existing taxonomies of cognitive processes (e.g., Miyake et al., 2000). 
	The first class of hypotheses would provide evidence that the Eisenberg et al. (2019) ontology is robust to the presence or absence of the DDM modeling and transformation of the raw reaction and accuracy data. Alternatively, the second class of hypotheses would suggest that the ontology (Eisenberg et al., 2019) is more idiosyncratic to analytical decisions like whether to analyze the data through the lens of the DDM.

title_r: The influence of predictive cues on task performance and trust in an industrial human-robot interaction - A Replication Study
abstract_r: Collaborative robots, known as CoBots, are increasingly being used in the field of industrial robotics. These robots are designed to work together with humans in a shared workspace. A decisive factor for successful cooperation is the predictability of the robot's actions, as this has a positive influence on both the performance of the joint interaction and trust in the robot. In human-human interaction, predictive cues such as eyes and eye movements are used as indicators to predict the actions of other people. These reflexively direct our gaze and our attention. In addition to eyes, non-social stimuli such as arrows, can also influence our attention. The implementation of corresponding indicators in robots to convey information regarding subsequent actions should increase the predictability and efficiency of human-robot interaction. The planned study aims to investigate the influence of predictive cues on performance and trust in the interaction with an industrial robot. Both error-free interactions and interactions with errors will be included. In addition, the allocation of visual attention during the interaction with the robot (Sawyer by Rethink Robotics) is investigated with the help of eye-tracking. The planned study is a replication of the study registered here: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/37BWM
