Close Replication of Muñoz, De Los Reyes: The dark triad and honesty rules in romantic relationships

item29: 1.	Verbal description of the effect I am trying to replicate (optional)  The study “The dark triad and honesty rules in romantic relationships” by Muñoz and De Los Reyes (2021) examined the connection between the three traits of the dark triad (i.e., Psychopathy, Machiavellianism and Narcissism) and honesty rule endorsement in romantic relationships, defined as obligatory rules and discretionary rules. Obligatory rules consist of strict standards for honest communication, while discretionary rules provide the flexibility to determine when deception is appropriate. We are trying to replicate the following hypotheses:  1.	High Psychopathy positively predicts discretionary rule endorsement.  2.	High Psychopathy negatively predicts obligatory rule endorsement.  3.	High Machiavellianism positively predicts discretionary rule endorsement. 4.	Narcissism shows no effects on either honesty rule endorsement.   2.	It is important to replicate this effect because (optional)  With the replication crisis in mind, it is important to strengthen the confidence in the reliability of the reported effects, so that this replication study should promote the confidence in the postulated relationships between the dark triad traits and honesty rule endorsement (Brandt, 2014).  Further, in the original study, 98.05% of the participants were Hispanics and most of the participants were female. Thus, this replication study which will be conducted with a German sample and a more balanced gender ratio will help to answer the question concerning the generalizability of the findings of the original study to other contexts.   3.	The effect size of the effect I am trying to replicate is (optional)  1.	The effect size of the effect between psychopathy and discretionary rule endorsement is r = .26.  2.	The effect size of the effect between psychopathy and obligatory rule endorsement is r = -.10. This effect is mentioned as significant in the text but not in the attached bivariate correlation matrix.  3.	The effect size of the effect between Machiavellianism and discretionary rule endorsement is r = .28.  4.	The confidence interval of the original effect is (optional)  Not specified   5.	The sample size of the original effect is (optional)  Two different sample sizes are reported in the paper. According to the text, the sample size is N = 257, but according to the bivariate correlation matrix, the sample size is N = 258.    6.	Where was the original study conducted? (e.g., lab, in the field, online) (optional)  The original study was conducted online.   7.	What country/region was the original study conducted in? (optional)  The researchers are from University of Texas, but it is not clear in the text where the study was conducted in.  8.	What kind of sample did the original study use? (e.g. student, Mturk, representative) (optional)  The original sample consisted of n = 221 females, n = 35 males, n = 1 or 2 other (see Point 5). 95.33% of the participants were between 18 and 29 years old and 98.05% self-identified as Hispanic. No further information were given.  9.	Was the original study conducted with paper-and-pencil surveys, on a computer, or something else? (optional)  The original study was conducted on a computer.    Designing the Replication Study  10.	Are the original materials for the study available from the author? (optional)  -	No  11.	I know that assumptions (e.g., about the meaning of the stimuli) in the original study will also hold in my replication because (optional)  We will use validated and empirically tested questionnaires. For the assessment of the Dark Triad character traits, we will use the Short Dark Triad (SD3; Jones & Paulhus, 2014) which includes 9 items each for Machiavellianism, Narcissism and Psychopathy. It was already translated to German so we will use the translated version (Malesza et al., 2017). The other questionnaire we will use is a measure of honesty rules endorsement in relationships which includes 21 obligatory rule statements and 22 discretionary rule statements (Roggensack & Sillars, 2014). This questionnaire is written in English, so we will translate it to German. The translations will be checked by an English native speaker. By that we will make sure that the original meaning will not be distorted. For both questionnaires we will use a 5-point Likert-type scale (strongly disagree to strongly agree). We will also ask for participants age, culture and gender to rule out any impact on the effect.  12.	Location of the experimenter during data collection (optional)  Not applicable   13.	Experimenter knowledge of participant experimental condition (optional)  Not applicable   14.	Experimenter knowledge of overall hypotheses (optional)  All experimenters know about all hypotheses.   15.	My target sample size is (optional)  Our target sample size is N = 256, but we will collect N = 270 participants because of possible exclusions.  16.	The rationale for my sample size is (optional)  An a priori power analysis for correlation was conducted, assuming an effect size of r = .26 (which was smallest significant effect reported in the original study), setting Type I error rate at  = .05 and power at 99%.    Documenting Differences between the Original and Replication Study  17.	The similarities/differences in the instruction are (optional)  -	Different  18.	The similarities/differences in the measures are (optional)  -	Close   19.	The similarities/differences in the stimuli are (optional)  Not applicable   20.	The similarities/differences in the location (e.g., lab vs. online; alone vs. in groups) are (optional)  -	Exact  21.	The similarities/differences in remuneration are (optional)  The remuneration is not given in the paper. There will be no remuneration in our replication.   22.	The similarities/differences between participant populations are (optional)  -	Close   23.	What differences between the original study and your study might be expected to influence the size and/or direction of the effect? (optional)  Because we do not have the original materials there might be differences in the instruction text of the study and as already mentioned (see Point 11), we will self-translate the English questionnaire for honesty rules endorsement in relationships to German.   24.	I have taken the following steps to test whether the differences listed in the previous question will influence the outcome of my replication attempt (optional)  The translations will be checked by an English native speaker. By that we will make sure that the original meaning will not be distorted (see Point 11).  Analysis and Replication Evaluation  25.	My exclusion criteria are (e.g., handling outliers, removing participants from analysis) (optional)  We will exclude participants who don’t give their consent to participate and those who are younger than 18 years. If participants answer one of the attention check questions incorrectly, participants will be excluded afterwards.   26.	My analysis plan is (justify differences from the original) (optional)  First we will calculate descriptive statistics for all relevant variables (i.e, Machiavellianism, Psychopathy, Narcissism, obligatory rule endorsement and discretionary rule endorsement). Then, we will calculate an intercorrelation matrix for all relevant variables. Lastly, we will conduct two regression analyses with each trait of the dark triad as the predictor for obligatory rule endorsement and discretionary rule endorsement as dependent variables.   27.	A successful replication is defined as (optional)  We interpret our replication as success if the standard significance criterion (p < .05) is fulfilled and if the effect is in the same direction as the original effect (OSF, 2015).  28.	The finalized materials, procedures, analysis plan etc. of the replication are registered here:   We will use the OSF platform to register the necessary materials for the replication.

title_r: Will humans obey authority even though it can risk anothers life? A direct replication of the Milgram study.
abstract_r: One of the most famous studies in social psychology was completed by Stanley Milgram. Milgram's experiment's primary focus was on the conflict between obedience to authority and conscience of the participants (Milgram, 1963). Milgram was specifically interested in actions completed under World War II - can the horrible acts of nazi soldiers be explained with that they were only following orders from authorities? The procedure was that the participant was paired with one of Milgram´s confederates. The experiment conducted two roles - teacher and learner, the real participant was always the teacher. The learner was placed in a room and had electrodes attached to his arms. The teacher and researcher stayed in a room next door. Teacher´s room contained an electric shock generator and switches marked from 15 volts and up to 450 volts. The teacher was supposed to administer an electric shock every time the learner made a mistake, and also increase the level of the shock each time the answer was wrong. The experimenter also played an active role in the experiment and encouraged the teacher to continue to press on the switch, even though the learner protested. At the end of the experiment 65% of the participants continued to the 450 volts and all of the participants continued to 300 volts (Milgram, 1963). Milligrams' explanation about the findings was that the circumstances had such a big influence on the participants. With that in consideration the aspects of the situation such as the location, the behavior of the experimenter (authority) and the fact that the participants got paid could potentially change the behavior of the participants. But it is clear that people are more likely to follow orders given by authority. Milgram concluded that our aspects of moral and obedience carry enormous importance, but unfortunately those factors say little about how people will behave in different situations (Milgram, 1963). It has been many years since Milgram's experiment was completed. People's beliefs and attitudes have been through a dramatic change. Yet, it is important to replicate the study to see if those changes in our society have any kind of impact on the situations where participants may or may not agree to things that they find unpleasant. Another key question that should be answered by replicating this study is - are people still willing to harm others in pursuit of obeying authority? We found it important to replicate Millgram´s study also because one of the major weaknesses of the study is the biased sample. Participants in Milgram's study consisted of 40 males, all aged between 20-50 (Milgram, 1963). Due to the fact that all participants were white American citizens it would be interesting to implement study with participants all around the world, this may include different ethnicities, ages, genders and classes. This way it would be easier to generalize the study to the world population and see differences in actions if such will occur. We predict dramatic changes in attitudes over the years. We believe also that factors such as age and religion may influence people's behavior. Due to drastic changes in our society, this may also include politics factors, such as: development of democracy and human rights participants would not obeyed authority in the same way.

title_r: Associations Between Young Adult Smoking, Vaping, and COVID-19: A Replication and Extension
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

We describe a research plan of analysis to explore whether smoking and vaping are associated with the risks of COVID-19 among young adults. Our main goal is to replicate and extend the analysis reported in a prior study by Gaiha, Cheng, and Halpern-Felsher and published in the Journal of Adolescent Health in 2020. However, as we will explain in more detail in the Analysis Plan, our planned study will differ from the prior study in several ways. The GCH-F study and our replication and extension are examples of risk-factor epidemiology and estimate statistical associations. An overarching difference is that we plan to use a framework from health economics, together with applied econometric methods, to address the challenges of using observational data to study the research questions.

summary: This registration contains a description of our plans to collect data through online surveys, the survey instrument, and the plans for our statistical/econometric analysis of the data.

title_r: The influence of personality on texting whilst driving: a replication study with an extension.
abstract_r: The aim of this research is to replicate Harrison, M.A (2011). College Students’ prevalence and perceptions messaging while driving. Accident Analysis and Prevention. Study. The purpose of this study is to ensure the validity of the study. If the results are consistent across both studies, due to the difference in culture between the two studies, this will inform readers whether the results are replicable across culture. The first finding was that the sample population mean response was 3, indicating that they texted whilst driving on a few occasions. Furthermore, participants agreed that texting whilst driving was unsafe. In addition to this, participants agreed that texting whilst driving should be illegal. Participants disagreed with two statements, the first was that texting whilst driving is not distracting and texting whilst driving is only their business. Participants remained neutral regarding whether they will continue to text while drive, even though they are aware that it is dangerous. The most frequent answer was ‘never’ for whether they had experienced any consequences of testing whilst driving or engaging in reckless behaviour due to texting while driving. A second aim of the study is to extend the study and add to the field of research. This will be done by replicating Harrison, M.A (2011) sensation seeking Likert scale questionnaire to help gain an understanding into the reason for messaging while driving behaviours. Furthermore, I will analyse the relationship between sensation seeking and messaging while driving.

title_r: Migration, Diversity, and Economic Growth. A Replication Study of Bove and Elia (World Development, 2017)
abstract_r: A recent and well known paper, Bove and Elia (2017), argues that migrants' diversity, as captured by the indexes of both fractionalization and polarization, exerts a positive effect on GDP growth.In fact, by using the same dataset and methodology, we show that the impact of diversity cannot be distinguished from that of migration itself due to the very high correlation among the corresponding variables.Also, if one disentangles migration from diversity, following Alesina et al. title_r: Impact of the gene x environment interaction between BDNF Val66Met and childhood trauma on hippocampal gray matter volume – a multi-cohort replication study
abstract_r: In this project, we intend to replicate the study „Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor Val66Met Polymorphism and Early Life Adversity Affect Hippocampal Volume“ by Carballedo et al. (2013). In a Gene x Environment approach, we will be looking at childhood maltreatment (CM) as the environmental influence. Research indicates that childhood maltreatment plays a role in the onset, severity, and chronicity of depression (Nelson et al., 2017). Additionally, there is evidence that childhood maltreatment is linked to reduced hippocampal volumes, even among individuals who are free from any prior psychiatric conditions (Dannlowski et al., 2012; McCrory et al., 2011; Riem et al., 2015), suggesting that adverse experiences in childhood shape brain structure significantly (Opel et al., 2014). The genetic variable will be modeled through the polymorphism Val66Met, a single nucleotide polymorphism in the BDNF-gene. BDNF was found to be involved in developmental processes of the brain as it is a crucial regulator of synaptic formation and plasticity as well as neural development, growth, differentiation and plasticity (Huang & Reichardt, 2001; Lu, 2003; Nemeroff, 2016; Pang & Lu, 2004). The Val66Met genotype leads to decreased activity-dependent BDNF secretion from neurons and is associated with impairment in specific forms of learning and altered stress susceptibility (Frielingsdorf et al., 2010). Numerous studies and meta-analyses have explored the potential association between the rs6265 polymorphism and neuropsychiatric disorders like MDD, but findings remain inconsistent with both positive and negative results reported across different studies (L. Chen et al., 2008; Frustaci et al., 2008; Kanazawa et al., 2007; Verhagen et al., 2010). Given the ongoing replication crisis in psychological research (Open Science Collaboration, 2015) and other fields, it is crucial for us as researchers to prioritize the replication of previous findings using sufficiently large sample sizes. Particularly in the field of brain imaging, replication rates have remained disappointingly low, casting doubt on the credibility of results (Marek et al., 2022). Inspired by this challenge, we are motivated to undertake this study as a replication attempt of the findings reported by Carballedo et al. (2013).

title_r: The religiosity as social value hypothesis: A multi-method replication and extension across 65 countries and three levels of spatial aggregation.
abstract_r: Are religious people psychologically better or worse adjusted than their nonreligious counterparts? Hundreds of studies have reported a positive relation between religiosity and psychological adjustment. Recently, however, a comparatively small number of cross-cultural studies has questioned this staple of religiosity research. The latter studies find that religious adjustment benefits are restricted to religious cultures. Gebauer, Sedikides, and Neberich (2012) suggested the religiosity as social value hypothesis (RASV) as one explanation for those cross-cultural differences. RASV states that, in religious cultures, religiosity possesses much social value, and, as such, religious people will feel particularly good about themselves. In secular cultures, however, religiosity possesses limited social value, and, as such, religious people will feel less good about themselves, if at all. Yet, previous evidence has been inconclusive regarding RASV and regarding cross-cultural differences in religious adjustment benefits more generally. To clarify matters, we conducted 3 replication studies. We examined the relation between religiosity and self-esteem (the most direct and appropriate adjustment indicator, according to RASV) in a self-report study across 65 countries (N = 2,195,301), an informant-report study across 36 countries (N = 560,264), and another self-report study across 1,932 urban areas from 243 federal states in 18 countries (N = 1,188,536). Moreover, we scrutinized our results against 7, previously untested, alternative explanations. Our results fully and firmly replicated and extended prior evidence for cross-cultural differences in religious adjustment benefits. These cross-cultural differences were best explained by RASV. The purpose of this study is to replicate and extend work on the psychometric reliability of cognitive control event-related potentials (ERPs) as a function of increasing trials across three different tasks (Meyer et al., 2013, Psychophysiology). Our primary aim is a direct replication of Meyer et al. (2013) to determine the number of trials needed for adequate psychometric internal consistency (.70) of the error-related negativity (ERN) recorded during flanker, Stroop, and Go/no-go tasks using classical test theory estimates (i.e., coefficient alpha). We will use post-estimation contrasts to identify task differences in dependability and ICC estimates as function of the number of trials recoded.

title_r: When Do Comprehenders Mentalize for Pragmatic Inference? A partial replication study.
abstract_r: Description People commonly use indirect requests. The meaning of these indirect requests often hinges on the linguistic and social context in which they are embedded. For instance, "It's cold in here" may be interpreted as a comment or a request to adjust the heating. Trott and Bergen (2020) showed that when people read a narrative in which the protagonist was unaware of an obstacle (e.g., the car heater was broken) they were more likely to interpret the utterance, "it's cold in here" as a request (e.g., to turn the heater on), than when reading a narrative where the protagonist was aware of an obstacle. This suggests the protagonist's perspective was encoded whilst interpreting the meaning of the utterance. Trott and Bergen (2020) suggest that mentalising may be recruited to interpret the meaning of these ambiguous phrases at two points. Firstly, whilst reading and building a mental model of what the characters perspectives, for instance what they know or do not know (e.g., the heater’s broken), or secondly, when inferring the meaning of the indirect request (e.g., “it’s cold in here”). They found that mentalising, measured with the Short Story Task (Doddel-Feder et al., 2013), predicted performance on questions regarding knowledge states but not on inference-based questions. This suggests mentalising supports building a mental model of characters’ perspectives but that mentalising is less important when inferring the meaning of indirect requests. Trott and Bergen’s (2020) findings are significant as they have demonstrated that mentalising is recruited and used to different extents during different stages of reading. To investigate this, they designed eight pairs of narratives in which the protagonist was either aware or unaware of an obstacle to fulfilling a request (e.g., the heater is broken). A mixed experimental design was devised, with one within-subject condition (awareness), and one between-subject condition (group-type). There were two subgroups in the group-type condition (knowledge or inference). After reading the narrative, in the knowledge group participants were asked a knowledge-based question (“Does he know the heater is broken?”) and in the inference group, they were asked an inference-based question (“Is he making a request?”). In each group (knowledge or inference) the participants were assigned to one of two lists of narratives, counterbalanced for aware or unaware versions of the story. Our first aim is to replicate their finding that participants modulate their answers as a function of awareness in both the knowledge and inference groups. Our second aim is to see if, like Trott and Bergen (2020) mentalising predicts performance in the knowledge group but not the inference group. However, to further validate their findings, we will be using two different mentalising tasks. Recent adult research has shown that there is minimal coherence between mentalising tasks and it is likely that that different mentalising tasks are testing different aspects of mentalising (Warnell & Redcay, 2019). In a previous study, our results indicated that the Strange Stories (White, Hill, Happé, & Frith, 2009) was a more reliable text-based test of mentalising in adults than the Short Story Task after controlling for verbal abilities, and so we will use the Strange Stories as our first test of mentalising. Secondly, we will use a non-text-based test of mentalising Happé-Frith Animations (Campbell et al., 2006) to avoid overlapping language comprehension skills that may be common to the text-based inference tasks and Trott and Bergen’s (2020) paradigm (e.g., vocabulary and inferencing). This Happé-Frith animations task involves the participant describing relationships between moving shapes and the researcher coding their use of mental state language. Our third aim is to see whether mentalising still predicts performance in the knowledge group while controlling for reading comprehension, working memory, and age. Trott and Bergen (2020) used the Short Story Task mentalising and reading comprehension subsections to show mentalising predicted performance over reading comprehension. However, in our previous study we found there were high ceiling effects in the reading comprehension section of the Short Story Task, so we will use the Strange Stories Physical Stories (Happé, 1994) as a measure of reading comprehension. Next, we will examine whether mentalising predicts performance in the knowledge group whilst controlling for working memory, as working memory has been associated with reading comprehension (Kim, 2017) and mentalising (Zhao, Wang, & Apperly, 2018). Finally, as we have previously found that age was positively correlated with performance on language abilities and mentalising ability, we will also see if mentalising still predicts performance after controlling for age. title_r: Extreme weather, climate change, climate action and uncertainty distress: A replication study using network analysis.
abstract_r: Both extreme weather and climate change have been linked to distress and at times mental health problems. Pro-environmental actions have often been related to higher distress. The uncertainty distress model (Freeston et al., 2020) proposes that in real-world situations, perceptions of threat and uncertainty contribute to distress. Freeston, Sermin-Read, et al. (2023) recruited a community sample (N = 327) who completed an online survey. Network analysis was used to analyse the relationships between the variables. Exposure to extreme weather, perceptions of climate change, climate change distress and pro-environmental action were measured along with symptoms of adjustment disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, and uncertainty intolerance and behaviours. They reported there was variable exposure to extreme weather, but greater exposure was associated with more severe post-traumatic symptoms. Pro-environmental action was associated with greater severity of adjustment disorder symptoms. The perception that climate change was happening now was linked positively to pro-environmental action and negatively to perceptions of uncertainty about whether climate change was happening. The results replicated several findings from the emerging climate change distress literature and are consistent with some predictions of the uncertainty distress model, but not others. Aim: The main aim of the current study is to conduct a replication using network analysis with 1) improved measurement in some areas (see above and in measures section), 2) a larger and more diverse sample (see recruitment methods). The network analysis will follow the previous analysis as much as possible to facilitate comparison. Methods: The study will essentially replicate the previous study with the following modifications: inclusion of heatwaves; expand the type, timescale and impact of warnings; differentiated assessment of disruption; fuller range of emotional responses; shortened/improved versions of other measures. A larger sample will be sought, recruited to increase not only the diversity and representativeness of the sample, but also the geographical distribution and so the range of experiences of extreme weather. Results: Descriptive analyses of the participants, the experiences of extreme weather, and network analysis will be reported, based on the previous study.

title_r: Mild Uncertainty Promotes Checking Behavior in Subclinical Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: An online replication study
abstract_r: Previous research has shown that participants with high obsessive-compulsive tendencies (OC+) struggle when searching for an absent target. In studies supporting this notion, participants performed a visual search task in which they searched for a closed square among open squares. Results revealed no differences in target-present trials, however, in target-absent trials, OC+ participants searched longer. These findings were replicated and extended to a clinical sample, where they were found to be specific to patients with OCD and absent in those suffering from anxiety. These findings were discussed in the context of checking behavior in the face of mild uncertainty. In a recent conceptual replication study we designed, we did not find longer search times in target-absent trials for OC+ participants. That being said, our paradigm was not a direct replication of the original studies. Here we use the same stimuli from the original study, in an online sample to determine if our failure to replicate the effect was due to an overly easy task.

title_r: Factor Structure And Affective Composition Of The Chills: Replication And Extension
abstract_r: “The chills” refers to a set of bodily sensations (goosebumps, tingling, coldness, and shivers) that sometimes accompany strong emotion (Maruskin, Thrash & Elliot, 2012). Past factor analyses of the chills identified a multi-factor, hierarchical structure, consisting of four lower-order factors (goosebumps, tingling, coldness, and shivers) and two higher-order factors (goosetingles and coldshivers). Research on the affective nomological nets of particular chills factors provided additional evidence of the discriminant validity of the two higher-order and the four-lower-order factors (Maruskin, Thrash & Elliot, 2012; Wadsworth, 2019). Despite evidence of discriminant validity, most researchers have continued to treat the chills as a unitary construct. The goal of the present study is to replicate and extend evidence that the chills consists of a set of distinguishable sensations with distinct affective correlates. Specifically, I aim to (a) replicate the factor structure of the chills and (b) further test whether the four lower-order sensations show distinct relations to core affect variables. Using the narrative recall method, the present study assessed chills sensations and core affect during recalled chills experience. Results of factor analyses replicated the factor structure of the chills established by Maruskin et al. (2012). Results of circumplex analyses provided additional evidence of the discriminant validity of higher-order and lower-order sensations. Goosetingles tended to accompany pleasant states, whereas coldshivers tended to accompany unpleasant states. Furthermore, relative to goosebumps, tingling accompanied states lower on activation and higher on pleasure. Relative to coldness, shivers accompanied states lower on displeasure and higher on activation. These findings are consistent with but refine the conclusions of Maruskin et al. (2012) and point to the value of incorporating the affect circumplex in understanding the chills.

title_r: Effects of the Generic Masculine and its Alternatives in Germanophone countries. A Multi-lab Replication and Extension of Stahlberg, Sczesny, and Braun, 2001
abstract_r: In languages such as German, French, or Hindi, plural forms of job occupations and societal roles are often in a generic-masculine form instead of a gender-neutral form. Although meant as “generic”, this generic-masculine form excludes women from everyday language and might even entail the cognitive effect that listeners and readers will less likely think of women. Several studies have demonstrated this and related cognitive effects in the past. Due to the societal relevance of gender-neutral language, we propose a direct replication and extension of a classic study by Stahlberg, Sczesny, and Braun (2001, Experiment 2) in a multi-lab setting. We already present preliminary evidence showing that people indeed come up with more female exemplars when they are asked to name celebrities from several domains, such as politics and sports in gender-neutral forms compared to the generic-masculine form. The proposed multi-lab study will be conducted among 12 labs, collecting data from more than N = 2,000 participants.

title_r: Not toeing the number line for simple arithmetic: Two large-n conceptual replications of Mathieu et al. (Cognition, 2016, Experiment 1)
abstract_r: We conducted two conceptual replications of Experiment 1 in Mathieu, Gourjon, Couderc, Thevenot, and Prado (2016, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2015.10.002). They tested a sample of 34 French adults on mixed-operation blocks of single-digit addition (4 + 3) and subtraction (4 – 3) with the three problem elements (O1, +/-, O2) presented sequentially. Addition was 34 ms faster if O2 appeared 300 ms after the operation sign and displaced 5° to the right of central fixation, whereas subtraction was 19 ms faster when O2 was displaced to the left. Replication Experiment 1 (n = 74 recruited at the University of Saskatchewan) used the same non-zero addition and subtraction problems and trial event sequence as Mathieu et al., but participants completed blocks of pure addition and pure subtraction followed by the mixed-operation condition used by Mathieu et al. Addition RT showed a 32 ms advantage with O2 shifted rightward relative to leftward but only in mixed-operation blocks. There was no effect of O2 position on subtraction RT. Experiment 2 (n = 74) was the same except mixed-operation blocks occurred before the pure-operation blocks. There was an overall 13 ms advantage with O2 shifted right relative to leftward but no interaction with operation or with mixture (i.e., pure vs mixed operations). Nonetheless, the rightward RT advantage was statistically significant for both addition and subtraction only in mixed-operation blocks. Taken together with the robust effects of mixture in Experiment 1, the results suggest that O2 position effects in this paradigm might reflect task specific demands associated with mixed operations.

title_r: Conceptual replication and extension of the relation between the number line estimation task and mathematical competence across seven studies
abstract_r: A recent meta-analysis demonstrated the overall correlation between the number line estimation (NLE) task and children’s mathematical competence was r = .44 (positively recoded), and this relation increased with age. The goal of the current study was to conceptually replicate and extend these results by further synthesizing this correlation utilizing studies not present in the meta-analysis. Across seven studies, 954 participants, ranging from 3 to 11 years old (Age M = 6.02 years, SD = 1.57), the overall estimation-competence correlations were similar to those of the meta-analysis and ranged from r = −.40 to −.35. The current conceptual replication demonstrated that the meta-analysis captured a stable overall relation between performance on the NLE task and mathematical competence. However, the current study failed to replicate the same moderation of age group presented in the meta-analysis. Furthermore, the current study extended results by assessing the stability and predictive validity of the NLE task while controlling for covariates. Results suggested that the NLE task demonstrated poor stability and predictive validity in the seven samples present in this study. Thus, although concurrent relations replicated, the differential age moderation, lack of stability, and lack of predictive validity in these studies require a more nuanced approach to understanding the utility of the NLE task. Future research should focus on understanding the connection between children’s developmental progression and NLE measurement before further investigating the predictive and diagnostic importance of the task for broader mathematical competence.

title_r: Contralateral delay activity as a marker of visual working memory capacity: a multi-site registered replication
abstract_r: Visual working memory (VWM) is a temporary storage system capable of retaining information that can be accessed and manipulated by higher cognitive processes, thereby facilitating a wide range of cognitive functions. Electroencephalography (EEG) is used to understand the neural correlates of VWM with high temporal precision, and one commonly used EEG measure is an event-related potential called the contralateral delay activity (CDA). In a landmark study by Vogel and Machizawa (2004), the authors found that the CDA amplitude increases with the number of items stored in VWM and plateaus around three to four items, which is thought to represent the typical adult working memory capacity. Critically, this study also showed that the increase in CDA amplitude between two-item and four-item arrays correlated with individual subjects’ VWM performance. Although these results have been supported by subsequent studies, a recent study suggested that the number of subjects used in experiments investigating the CDA may not be sufficient to detect differences in set size and to provide a reliable account of the relationship between behaviorally measured VWM capacity and the CDA amplitude. To address this, the current study, as part of the #EEGManyLabs project, aims to conduct a multi-site replication of Vogel and Machizawa's (2004) seminal study on a large sample of participants, with a pre-registered analysis plan. Through this, our goal is to contribute to deepening our understanding of the neural correlates of visual working memory.

title_r: How strong is the rhythm of perception? A registered replication of Hickok et al. (2015)
abstract_r: Our ability to predict upcoming events is a fundamental component of human cognition. One way in which we do so is by exploiting temporal regularities in sensory signals: the ticking of a clock, falling of footsteps and the motion of waves each provide a structure that may facilitate anticipation. But how strong is the effect of rhythmic anticipation on perception? And to what degree do people vary in their ability to capitalize on these regularities? In 2015, Hickok et al. introduced a behavioural paradigm to assess how a rhythmic auditory stimulus affects perception of subsequent targets (Hickok G, Farahbod H, Saberi K. 2015 The rhythm of perception: entrainment to acoustic rhythms induces subsequent perceptual oscillation. Psychol. Sci. 26, 1006–1013. (doi:10.1177/0956797615576533)). They tested five listeners and found that perception (target detection accuracy) fluctuated rhythmically just like the sound rhythm. Here, we replicate the original finding, assess how likely the finding is to be observed for any individual, and quantify effect size in a large sample of adult listeners (n = 149). We introduce a model-based analysis approach that allows separate estimates of amplitude and phase information in target detection responses, and quantifies effect size for individual listeners. Together our results strongly support the presence of oscillatory influences on target detection accuracy, as well as substantial variability in the magnitude of this effect across listeners.

title_r: Revisiting Self-Efficacy in Computer Science: A Replication Study
abstract_r: Self-efficacy is a reliable predictor of academic motivation and achievement across academic disciplines and age groups (Lishinski et al. 2016; Zimmerman et al. 1992). Because self-efficacy can be improved through instructional experiences and tools, identifying students with low self-efficacy or strategies to increase it is valuable in computing education. For this reason, measurements of self-efficacy are important for educators and researchers. The goal of the study is to replicate the findings from Steinhorst et al. (2020) validation study of their newly designed self-efficacy measurement for introductory programming students. Additionally, the intention is to extend the work by incorporating new measures of general (i.e., domain-independent) self-efficacy to assess convergent validity and explore measurements over time. Students completed several instruments related to general self-efficacy once at the beginning and programming self-efficacy at the beginning and end of the semester. Half of the current studys scales were used in the original study, so this population can be directly compared to the original populations. New scales for general self-efficacy were added to examine convergent validity and potential differences between general and programming-specific self-efficacy. The results revealed robust internal consistency and construct validity of the Steinhorst instrument for both the introductory programming course and the data structures course, aligning with the general self-efficacy theory. Additionally, the findings highlight the Steinhorst Instrument's suitability for different languages and contexts. A significant insight from the study is the necessity for researchers and educators to modify the instrument accordingly, ensuring that items not covered in the curriculum are excluded. This research enhances researchers' and educators' understanding of the Steinhorst instrument's robustness for assessing programming self-efficacy across various educational contexts.

title_r: International adjustment of female vs male business expatriates. A replication study in Switzerland
abstract_r: Purpose - – Reasons for women’s underrepresentation in international assignments include stereotypical assumptions within organizations about their ability to adjust abroad and more broadly a lack of trust from the corporate headquarters. Female expatriates’ adjustment may strongly vary depending on the host country and on host-country nationals’ attitudes toward them. Yet up until today, very few studies have examined female expatriate adjustment in a single and non-Asian host country. The purpose of this paper is to address this gap by comparing the cross-cultural adjustment of male and female expatriates in Switzerland. Design/methodology/approach - – This study replicates Selmer and Leung’s (2003a) study design in order to compare adjustment of male and female expatriates working in multinational companies in the French-speaking part of Switzerland. Based on 152 valid questionnaires collected, the authors performed a multivariate analysis of covariance and further analyses of covariance to compare male and female expatriate adjustment. Findings - – The authors find that female expatriates have significantly higher interaction and work adjustment levels than their male counterparts, while no significant differences between men and women were observed in terms of general adjustment. These findings in a European context are consistent with those of Selmer and Leung in an Asian context. Originality/value - – Very few studies to date have examined the adjustment of female expatriates in a western host-country context, despite the fact that host-country cultural norms might strongly influence women’s experiences. The research brings new empirical evidence about cross-cultural adjustment of female and male expatriates in a western location. Contrary to persistent stereotypical assumptions, results emphasize again that women are able to adjust better or at least as well as their male counterparts.

title_r: Migration, Diversity, and Economic Growth. A Replication Study of Bove and Elia (World Development, 2017)
abstract_r: A recent and well known paper, Bove and Elia (2017), argues that migrants' diversity, as captured by the indexes of both fractionalization and polarization, exerts a positive effect on GDP growth. In fact, by using the same dataset and methodology, we show that the impact of diversity cannot be distinguished from that of migration itself due to the very high correlation among the corresponding variables. Also, if one disentangles migration from diversity, following Alesina et al. (2016), only migration maintains a positive impact on growth while diversity, as captured by fractionalization, turns out to be weakly and positively associated with growth, but limitedly to the 1980-2010 time span. Polarization, on the other hand, does not seem to exert any effect on growth. The question as to whether diversity is more or less beneficial in terms of economic growth remains therefore an intriguing one, and calls for more theoretical and empirical analyses, possibly based on less (geographically) aggregated data.

title_r: Meta-analysis and publication bias: How well does the FAT-PET-PEESE procedure work? A replication study of Alinaghi & Reed (Research Synthesis Methods, 2018)
abstract_r: This R-code produces the results of the replication study. Abstract of the paper: A meta-analysis is a tool for aggregating estimates of a similar “effect” across many studies. Publication bias is the phenomenon where literature is sample selected in favor of studies having statistically significant results and/or having estimates that satisfy pre-conceived expectations. A popular procedure used for conducting meta-analyses in the presence of publication bias is the FAT-PET-PEESE (FPP) procedure. In a recent paper published in \emph{Research Synthesis Methods}, Alinaghi and Reed (2018), utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, report that the FPP procedure does not work well when used in “realistic” data environments where true effects differ both across and within studies. AR’s findings are important because the FPP approach is dominant in the economics meta-analysis literature. I replicate their results and discover two mistakes, which I subsequently correct. The first mistake is found in a descriptive statistics table, misrepresenting the overview of simulated dataset. The second is associated with the fixed effect estimation, generating erroneous estimated effects and Type I error. Further, I extend their analysis by making their simulation environment even more realistic. Despite producing somewhat different results, my replications generally confirm AR’s conclusions about the unreliability of the FPP procedure in realistic data environments.

title_r: Second Phase: Replication and extension of Gantman et al. "The time course of moral perception: an ERP investigation of the moral pop-out effect"
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

This is a second round of data collection in our replication and extension attempt due to discrepancies that were discovered part way through initial data collection.

summary: During data collection for our experiment, we observed that accuracy levels on the behavioral task were much higher than reported in the original study. We eventually discovered that this was due to a discrepancy between our method, which was consistent with the method reported in the original article, and the method actually used in the original experiment. The original experiment displayed the word and mask above the fixation cross, while we displayed the word and mask at the location of the fixation cross.

Given that obtaining useful EEG data depends on observing the expected pop-out effect and that accuracy levels at or near ceiling performance make the pop out effect much harder to detect, we decided to terminate data collection before our pre-registered target and start a new round of data collection. Our target for the new round of data collection is 65 usable samples. 

Preliminary analysis of the data that we collected in the first round has helped us to tune our preprocessing pipeline and exclusion criteria. In addition to the pre-registered analysis plan from the first round of data collection, we are pre-registering the following EEG preprocessing steps:

We will extract only the four channels of interest: Cz, Pz, Fp1, and Fp2.
We will re-reference the data to the linked ears (A1 and A2).
We will filter the data using a 0.1 to 30Hz bandpass filter.
We will segment the data to windows from 400ms before the target word appears to 1200ms after. This is a 200ms cushion around the final segment target in order to avoid edge effects in our eyeblink removal step.
After segmentation, we will remove any segments where one or more channels has an absolute voltage fluctuation of 1000 microvolts or more.
We will then baseline correct the segments using only the -200 to 0ms portion of the segment.
We will then use a regression-based eyeblink removal process. This involves averaging Fp1 and Fp2 to generate a single "eye channel", using a 200ms wide triangle filter to detect rapid rises and falls in voltage that are consistent with an eyeblink and labeling those timepoints, computing a propagation coefficient using regression between the eye channel and Cz and Pz, and subtracting the voltage in the eye channel, multiplied by the regression coefficients, from Cz and Pz, at the time points identified as containing a blink. We will not attempt to regress out EOG signals since we do not have EOG-specific electrodes.
We will resegment the data to include just the -200 to 1000ms range.
We will remove any segments that still contain absolute fluctuations of 500 microvolts or more. 
We will apply baseline correction again.
If we need to analyze data from electrode sites other than Cz and Pz after applying the data-based method for selecting the individual electrodes described in the original paper, we will apply the above preprocessing steps to the data from those electrodes.

We are pre-registering the following behavioral data preprocessing steps:

If there is clear evidence that a subject inverted the response keys (e.g., accuracy well below 50% on one or both blocks), we will apply a correction that flips the responses on the relevant block. We observed this twice in our first round of data collection.

We are pre-registering the following exclusion criteria:

If the total number of usable EEG segments in any stimulus category after preprocessing is below 75% we will exclude the subject and collect data from another participant. In our first round this occurred for one subject. All other subjects had 90% or more usable segments.

title_r: The Foreign Language Effect on the Illusion of Causality: A Replication Attempt and an Explorative Analysis of the Mechanisms
abstract_r: Díaz-Lago and Matute (2019) supported in a series of two experiments that a cognitive bias, the illusion of causality, can be attenuated when the task eliciting this illusion is presented in a foreign language. This initial result is coherent with a certain set of literature (e.g., Circi et al., 2021; Del Maschio et al., 2022; Purpuri et al., 2024), which over the years has shown that the usage of a foreign language can influence decision-making in tasks commonly used to assess flawed reasoning processes (i.e., the Foreign Language Effect). Our study aims to achieve two primary objectives. First, we seek to replicate the original findings of Díaz-Lago and Matute (2019) with a more nuanced approach, utilizing suitable statistical inference tools to assess whether we can directly support the presence or absence of the effect, while also estimating the ES for the observed reduction in the illusion of causality. The second goal of our study is to provide an exploratory framework that may help identify which explanation(s), or combination thereof, could account for the Foreign Language Effect observed in the context of the illusion of causality. NOTE: A first explanatory and more detailed draft document of the experiment is outlined in the Files area of the main project (anonymized link: https://osf.io/hvgkx/?view_only=7098178875224cf3b0b6890b209432ea; see "CLT/FLE.pdf"). Additionally, this file is also available on the project’s GitHub page (under the "Files" tab: GitHub_IllusionofCausality_ForeignLanguage).

title_r: Does text generation improve learning from expository text? A conceptual replication attempt
abstract_r: The aim of the present study was to test the replicability of the text generation effect for learning with expository texts while systematically varying contextual factors that—based on extant literature—can be assumed to affect the occurrence and magnitude of the text generation effect. Seven experiments were conducted in which participants either read (control condition) or unscrambled sentences (generation condition) in expository texts. The experiments varied systematically on intentionality of learning, learning time constraint, retention interval, and study design. Contrary to expectations, no text generation effect could be found. Instead, some of the experiments even revealed a learning disadvantage for text generation compared to the reading control condition. In only one experiment (Experiment 6) and for just one of the learning measures, learners performed better when they had generated the texts. In sum, the results indicate that a generation effect is most likely to occur when learning is intentional, when learning time is unrestricted, and for immediate testing. The findings suggest that the applications of text generation in educational contexts are rather limited.

title_r: Functional co-activation of the default mode network in APOE ε4-carriers: a replication study
abstract_r: Structural and functional alterations of the brain in people genetically at-risk for AD are crucial in unravelling AD development. Filippini et al. found that the default mode network (DMN) is affected in young APOE ε4-carriers, with increased co-activation of the DMN during rest and increased hippocampal task activation. This work has been of substantial importance to the field, often being used to illustrate the trajectory of functional alterations of the DMN in APOE ε4-carriers from young adults and normal aging to MCI and AD. While multiple studies have been performed on DMN activation in older adults and those with MCI or AD, there are few studies on the effect of APOE ε4 on the DMN in young, healthy adults, of which Filippini et al. is the most highly cited. Moreover, this study only assessed a small sample size of 18 APOE ε4-carriers and 18 non-carriers. Therefore, we aim to replicate his early findings, using the APOE genetic variant, as well as a polygenic risk score, with the Human Connectome Project dataset. This dataset represents the population at large and therefore allows us to not only replicate earlier findings with substantially increased power, but also to study the wider polygenic nature of any effects and the generalisability of these results, as a broad spectrum of behavioural and demographic variations can be observed in the HCP cohort.

title_r: Infants’ Social Evaluation of Helpers and Hinderers: A Large-Scale, Multi-Lab, Coordinated Replication Study
abstract_r: Evaluating others’ actions as praiseworthy or blameworthy is a fundamental aspect of human nature. A seminal study published in 2007 suggested that the ability to form social evaluations based on third-party interactions emerges within the first year of life, considerably earlier than previously thought (Hamlin, Wynn, & Bloom, 2007). In this study, infants demonstrated a preference for a character (i.e., a shape with eyes) who helped, over one who hindered, another character who tried but failed to climb a hill. This study sparked a new line of inquiry into infants’ social evaluations; however, numerous attempts to replicate the original findings yielded mixed results, with some reporting effects not reliably different from chance. These failed replications point to at least two possibilities: (1) the original study may have overestimated the true effect size of infants’ preference for helpers, or (2) key methodological or contextual differences from the original study may have compromised the replication attempts. Here we conduct a pre-registered, closely coordinated, multi-laboratory, standardized study aimed at replicating the helping/hindering finding using a well-controlled video version of the hill show. We intended to (1) provide a precise estimate of the true effect size of infants’ preference for helpers over hinderers, and (2) determine the degree to which infants’ preferences are based on social features of the Helper/Hinderer scenarios.

title_r: The Incremental Validity of Average States: A Replication and Extension of Finnigan & Vazire (2018)
abstract_r: States refer to our momentary thoughts, feelings, and behaviors. Average states (aggregates across multiple time points) are discussed as a more accurate and objective measure of personality compared to global self-reports since they do not only rely on people’s general beliefs about themselves. Specifically, Finnigan and Vazire (2018) argued that, if average states better capture what a person is actually like, this should be reflected in their unique association with informant-reports of personality, and tested this idea based on two experience-sampling studies. Their results showed, however, that average self-reported states did not predict global informant-reported personality above and beyond global self-reports. In this research, we aimed at replicating and extending these results. We used data of five studies (total N = 806) that involved global self- and informant reports and employed a variety of different experience-sampling methods (time-based with different sampling schedules, event-based). Across all studies, the original results (i.e., no incremental effects of average self-reported states) were replicated. Furthermore, as an extension to the original study, we found that average other-reported states (provided by peers, results based on one study) did indeed predict global informant-reports above and beyond global self-reports. These findings highlight the importance of differentiating between method effects (global reports vs average states) from source of information effects (self vs. other). We discuss these results, focusing on the suitability of using informant-reports as a criterion variable and conceptual differences between assessment methods.

This study will attempt to replicate classic cross-cultural findings from the human mating literature. Specifically, we will examine sex differences in mate preferences across cultures (Buss, 1989); the multivariate effect size of these differences (Conroy-Beam et al., 2015); sex differences in the age of chosen long-term partners (Kenrick & Keefe, 1992; Buss, 1989), cross-cultural variability in mate preferences as a function of pathogen prevalence (Gangestad & Buss, 1993; Gangestad, Haselton & Buss, 2006), and cross-cultural variability in sex differences in mate preferences as a function of gender equality (Eagly & Wood, 1999; Gangestad, Haselton & Buss, 2006; Zentner & Mitura, 2012). 
Method
Participants
Data has already been collected, in person (not online), from participants in 45 different countries, n = 14,487 (7,961 female). Each study site collected data from both university populations and community samples. Due to a lack of records from about half of the sites, there is incomplete information about the percentage of each type of sample. From the sites that did keep records (n = 6,637), 47.14% (n = 3,129) came from community samples. Age of participants ranged from 18-91 years old (Mdn = 25, M = 28.79, SD = 10.64). Of the total sample, most participants reported being in ongoing, committed relationships (n = 9,236, 63.75%). 
Exclusion criteria. If data is unavailable for certain countries for the various indices used, those countries will not be included in those specific analyses (we will note in the paper which countries have been excluded due to lack of available data). Participants who were under the age of 18 when taking the survey were excluded from the sample. Participants who did not fill out any part of the mate preferences survey or did not report their sex were excluded from the sample as well. Two countries surveyed did not include the mate preferences portion of the survey (Serbia and Ukraine) and will not be included in analyses. 
Measures
Mate preferences. Participants completed a 5-item questionnaire on ideal mate preferences for a long-term romantic partner. Participants rated their ideal romantic partner on five traits: kindness, intelligence, health, physical attractiveness, and good financial prospects. All items were rated on bipolar adjective scales ranging from 1 (e.g. very unintelligent) to 7 (e.g. very intelligent).
Age. Participants reported their own age in years as part of a demographic questionnaire. Participants in relationships additionally reported the age of their actual long-term romantic partner. 
Pathogen prevalence. We will use a variety of measures of pathogen prevalence from the prior literature and from publicly available databases. These include the pathogen prevalence index developed by Low (1990) and used in Gangestad & Buss (1993); years of life lost to communicable diseases (Debruine et al., 2010); and years of life lost to infectious and parasitic diseases (WHO, 2015) and estimated deaths due to infectious and parasitic diseases (WHO, 2015). For the variables from publicly available databases, we collected the most recent available data in all cases.
Gender equality. We will use a variety of measures of gender equality from the prior literature and publicly available databases. We will use the Gender Development Index (GDI) and Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM) from Eagly and Wood (1999). We will additionally use updated gender equality measures including the Global Gender Gap Index (GGGI) (World Economic Forum, 2016), the Gender Inequality Index (GII) (United Nations Development Programme, 2015), and the updated version of the GDI (United Nations Development Programme, 2015). For the publicly available databases, we collected the most recent available data for all variables.
Control variables. We will include a series of four control variables.  These control variables will be GDP per capita (CIA World Factbook), latitude (CIA World Factbook), most common religion (CIA World Factbook), and world region (based on Gangestad, Haselton, & Buss, 2006). 
Analysis Plan
We will conduct all primary analyses using multilevel models. In these models, participants will be nested within countries. When possible, the models will include all random effects for both slopes and intercepts. Should we experience convergence issues with these models, we will have to adjust model parameters in an exploratory fashion (e.g. dropping random slope terms) and we will report our decisions clearly. Multilevel models provide several advantages over traditional approaches for analyzing this kind of cross-cultural data. These models will allow us to estimate sex differences in mate preferences overall in the data, as well as the variability in these sex differences across cultures based on the random effects. Using a single multilevel model to assess sex differences also minimizes both alpha inflation and the risk of Type II errors relative to the traditional approach of conducting multiple t-tests (e.g. Buss, 1989). For cross-cultural comparisons, these models take advantage of the nested nature of the data, yielding more statistical power relative to the traditional approach of calculating correlations based on aggregated nation-level data (e.g. Eagly and Wood, 1999). Finally, this approach lets us conduct all analyses within the same modeling framework, allowing clearer interpretation of the results.

These variables were chosen because they were each used in the papers we are replicating. 
 All data analysis will be conducted in R. All data and script will be made available at the time of publication.  
Sex Differences in Mate Preferences
To assess sex differences in mate preferences across cultures, we will fit five multilevel models, one for each preference (kindness, intelligence, health, good financial prospects, physical attractiveness). In these models the preference variable will be the outcome variable and participant sex (male or female) will be the predictor. Mate preference variables will be standardized across countries prior to analysis to provide slope values comparable to Cohen’s d. We will additionally plot country-level slopes against sample size from each country as in a funnel plot to assess the relationship between effect size and sample size. 
Actual Partner Age
We will fit one multilevel model to assess sex differences in actual partner age across cultures. In this model the difference between self and partner age will be the outcome variable and participant sex (male or female) will be the predictor. This difference will be standardized across countries prior to analysis to provide slope values comparable to Cohen’s d. We will additionally plot country-level slopes against sample size from each country as in a funnel plot to assess the relationship between effect size and sample size. 
Multivariate Effect Size
We will use the five preference variables to calculate the Mahalanobis distance (D) between males and females within each country. We will additionally calculate D separately for putatively sex-differentiated preferences (good financial prospects and physical attractiveness) and those not expected to be as strongly sex differentiated (intelligence, kindness, health). Logistic regression models will be trained in a random training set to predict participant sex using their ideal mate preferences; these models will then be applied to predict the sex of participants in a separate testing set. Each fold of this cross-validation will leave out 10% of the data for testing. The relevant outcome variable will be the percentage of participant sexes accurately predicted by the model in the testing set. This process will be repeated for 10,000 iterations to provide an estimate of predictive accuracy and estimated confidence intervals around this accuracy.

We will test for the effect of pathogen prevalence on ideal mate preferences in a series of multi-level models predicting preferences from nation-level pathogen prevalence indices. We will fit three multilevel models for each of the five mate preference variables. (2010). To create the third index using these variables, we will standardize and average the two variables for each country. We will check the validity of this new index by computing its correlation with the other two indices; however, we will use the index in analyses regardless of its relationship to others.

To examine the effect of nation-level gender equality on sex differences in mate preferences, we will fit a series of multilevel models predicting ideal mate preferences from sex and nation-level gender quality. Each model will have one of the five ideal preference variables as an outcome variable. These models will use the interaction of participant sex and a gender equality variable as the predictor, along with all relevant main effects. We will enter these three variables into a PCA and extract the first principle component. Scores on this principle component will be used as each country’s gender equality score. We will check the validity of this composite measure of gender equality by calculating its correlation with the other measures of gender equality; however, we will use this principle component regardless of its relationship to the other indices.

Method
Participants
Data has already been collected, in person (not online), from participants in 45 different countries, n = 14,487 (7,961 female). Each study site collected data from both university populations and community samples. Due to a lack of records from about half of the sites, there is incomplete information about the percentage of each type of sample. Exclusion criteria. If data is unavailable for certain countries for the various indices used, those countries will not be included in those specific analyses (we will note in the paper which countries have been excluded due to lack of available data). Participants who did not fill out any part of the mate preferences survey or did not report their sex were excluded from the sample as well. Two countries surveyed did not include the mate preferences portion of the survey (Serbia and Ukraine) and will not be included in analyses.

Mate preferences. Participants completed a 5-item questionnaire on ideal mate preferences for a long-term romantic partner. Participants rated their ideal romantic partner on five traits: kindness, intelligence, health, physical attractiveness, and good financial prospects. All items were rated on bipolar adjective scales ranging from 1 (e.g. very unintelligent) to 7 (e.g. very intelligent).

We will use the Gender Development Index (GDI) and Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM) from Eagly and Wood (1999). We will additionally use updated gender equality measures including the Global Gender Gap Index (GGGI) (World Economic Forum, 2016), the Gender Inequality Index (GII) (United Nations Development Programme, 2015), and the updated version of the GDI (United Nations Development Programme, 2015). Analysis Plan
We will conduct all primary analyses using multilevel models. In these models, participants will be nested within countries. When possible, the models will include all random effects for both slopes and intercepts. Should we experience convergence issues with these models, we will have to adjust model parameters in an exploratory fashion (e.g. dropping random slope terms) and we will report our decisions clearly. Multilevel models provide several advantages over traditional approaches for analyzing this kind of cross-cultural data. These models will allow us to estimate sex differences in mate preferences overall in the data, as well as the variability in these sex differences across cultures based on the random effects. Using a single multilevel model to assess sex differences also minimizes both alpha inflation and the risk of Type II errors relative to the traditional approach of conducting multiple t-tests (e.g. Buss, 1989). For cross-cultural comparisons, these models take advantage of the nested nature of the data, yielding more statistical power relative to the traditional approach of calculating correlations based on aggregated nation-level data (e.g. Eagly and Wood, 1999). This difference will be standardized across countries prior to analysis to provide slope values comparable to Cohen’s d. Logistic regression models will be trained in a random training set to predict participant sex using their ideal mate preferences; these models will then be applied to predict the sex of participants in a separate testing set. Each model will use the relevant ideal mate preference as the outcome variable and predict this variable using one of three pathogen prevalence indices. Each model will have one of the five ideal preference variables as an outcome variable. These models will use the interaction of participant sex and a gender equality variable as the predictor, along with all relevant main effects. Pre-registration: Sex Differences in Mate Preferences Across 45 Cultures: A Large-Scale Replication
This study will attempt to replicate classic cross-cultural findings from the human mating literature. Specifically, we will examine sex differences in mate preferences across cultures (Buss, 1989); the multivariate effect size of these differences (Conroy-Beam et al., 2015); sex differences in the age of chosen long-term partners (Kenrick & Keefe, 1992; Buss, 1989), cross-cultural variability in mate preferences as a function of pathogen prevalence (Gangestad & Buss, 1993; Gangestad, Haselton & Buss, 2006), and cross-cultural variability in sex differences in mate preferences as a function of gender equality (Eagly & Wood, 1999; Gangestad, Haselton & Buss, 2006; Zentner & Mitura, 2012). 
Method
Participants
Data has already been collected, in person (not online), from participants in 45 different countries, n = 14,487 (7,961 female). Each study site collected data from both university populations and community samples. Due to a lack of records from about half of the sites, there is incomplete information about the percentage of each type of sample. From the sites that did keep records (n = 6,637), 47.14% (n = 3,129) came from community samples. Age of participants ranged from 18-91 years old (Mdn = 25, M = 28.79, SD = 10.64). Of the total sample, most participants reported being in ongoing, committed relationships (n = 9,236, 63.75%). 
Exclusion criteria. If data is unavailable for certain countries for the various indices used, those countries will not be included in those specific analyses (we will note in the paper which countries have been excluded due to lack of available data). Participants who were under the age of 18 when taking the survey were excluded from the sample. Participants who did not fill out any part of the mate preferences survey or did not report their sex were excluded from the sample as well. Two countries surveyed did not include the mate preferences portion of the survey (Serbia and Ukraine) and will not be included in analyses. 
Measures
Mate preferences. Participants completed a 5-item questionnaire on ideal mate preferences for a long-term romantic partner. Participants rated their ideal romantic partner on five traits: kindness, intelligence, health, physical attractiveness, and good financial prospects. All items were rated on bipolar adjective scales ranging from 1 (e.g. very unintelligent) to 7 (e.g. very intelligent).
Age. Participants reported their own age in years as part of a demographic questionnaire. Participants in relationships additionally reported the age of their actual long-term romantic partner. 
Pathogen prevalence. We will use a variety of measures of pathogen prevalence from the prior literature and from publicly available databases. These include the pathogen prevalence index developed by Low (1990) and used in Gangestad & Buss (1993); years of life lost to communicable diseases (Debruine et al., 2010); and years of life lost to infectious and parasitic diseases (WHO, 2015) and estimated deaths due to infectious and parasitic diseases (WHO, 2015). For the variables from publicly available databases, we collected the most recent available data in all cases.
Gender equality. We will use a variety of measures of gender equality from the prior literature and publicly available databases. We will use the Gender Development Index (GDI) and Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM) from Eagly and Wood (1999). We will additionally use updated gender equality measures including the Global Gender Gap Index (GGGI) (World Economic Forum, 2016), the Gender Inequality Index (GII) (United Nations Development Programme, 2015), and the updated version of the GDI (United Nations Development Programme, 2015). For the publicly available databases, we collected the most recent available data for all variables.

Analysis Plan
We will conduct all primary analyses using multilevel models. In these models, participants will be nested within countries. When possible, the models will include all random effects for both slopes and intercepts. Should we experience convergence issues with these models, we will have to adjust model parameters in an exploratory fashion (e.g. dropping random slope terms) and we will report our decisions clearly. Multilevel models provide several advantages over traditional approaches for analyzing this kind of cross-cultural data. These models will allow us to estimate sex differences in mate preferences overall in the data, as well as the variability in these sex differences across cultures based on the random effects. Using a single multilevel model to assess sex differences also minimizes both alpha inflation and the risk of Type II errors relative to the traditional approach of conducting multiple t-tests (e.g. Buss, 1989). For cross-cultural comparisons, these models take advantage of the nested nature of the data, yielding more statistical power relative to the traditional approach of calculating correlations based on aggregated nation-level data (e.g. Eagly and Wood, 1999). Finally, this approach lets us conduct all analyses within the same modeling framework, allowing clearer interpretation of the results.

Each of these control models will include a standard set of control variables: latitude, GDP per capita, world region, and most common religion. These variables were chosen because they were each used in the papers we are replicating.

Sex Differences in Mate Preferences
To assess sex differences in mate preferences across cultures, we will fit five multilevel models, one for each preference (kindness, intelligence, health, good financial prospects, physical attractiveness). In these models the preference variable will be the outcome variable and participant sex (male or female) will be the predictor. Mate preference variables will be standardized across countries prior to analysis to provide slope values comparable to Cohen’s d. We will additionally plot country-level slopes against sample size from each country as in a funnel plot to assess the relationship between effect size and sample size. 
Actual Partner Age
We will fit one multilevel model to assess sex differences in actual partner age across cultures. In this model the difference between self and partner age will be the outcome variable and participant sex (male or female) will be the predictor. This difference will be standardized across countries prior to analysis to provide slope values comparable to Cohen’s d. We will additionally plot country-level slopes against sample size from each country as in a funnel plot to assess the relationship between effect size and sample size.

We will use the five preference variables to calculate the Mahalanobis distance (D) between males and females within each country. We will additionally calculate D separately for putatively sex-differentiated preferences (good financial prospects and physical attractiveness) and those not expected to be as strongly sex differentiated (intelligence, kindness, health). We will use bootstrapping to estimate 95% confidence intervals around these D values for each country. Finally, we will use a Monte Carlo cross-validated logistic regression to assess the ability of preferences to predict participant sex. Logistic regression models will be trained in a random training set to predict participant sex using their ideal mate preferences; these models will then be applied to predict the sex of participants in a separate testing set. Each fold of this cross-validation will leave out 10% of the data for testing. The relevant outcome variable will be the percentage of participant sexes accurately predicted by the model in the testing set. This process will be repeated for 10,000 iterations to provide an estimate of predictive accuracy and estimated confidence intervals around this accuracy.

We will test for the effect of pathogen prevalence on ideal mate preferences in a series of multi-level models predicting preferences from nation-level pathogen prevalence indices. We will fit three multilevel models for each of the five mate preference variables. Each model will use the relevant ideal mate preference as the outcome variable and predict this variable using one of three pathogen prevalence indices. The first will be the index developed by Low (1990) and used in Gangestad and Buss (1993). The second index will be the years of life lost by communicable diseases variable used by Debruine et al. (2010). To create the third index using these variables, we will standardize and average the two variables for each country. We will check the validity of this new index by computing its correlation with the other two indices; however, we will use the index in analyses regardless of its relationship to others. 
Gender Equality
